The price was to be fixed mutually from time to time but in no case it was to exceed the manufacturing cost plus 10 per cent profit thereon. Thereafter, another agreement was entered into between the assessee and the firm by which both the parties agreed to terminate mutually the earlier agreement. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to sell and the firm agreed to purchase running business of the assessee. As a consideration for the purchase of the bidi manufacturing business the firm was to pay to the assessee as ‘slump price’ of Rs. 5 lakhs. The IAC held that the assessee was holding an agency and the aforesaid amount received by the assessee was an amount towards termination of this agency, and, therefore, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held it as capital gain and directed the IAC to work out the taxable capital gains in accordance with the relevant provisions.

On appeal:

An incorporated limited liability company 'L' had a subscribed capital consisting of preference shares, ordinary shares and deferred shares. The assessee-company became the managing agents of said company under an agreement. Subsequently, the assessee acquired its ordinary shares and preference shares. On 10-10-1947, the assessee made a further acquisition of some deferred shares. Thereafter, the assessee agreed to make over its managing agency to 'K'. The terms included that 'K' should take over the deferred shares and also pay the assessee a further sum of certain amount as compensation for loss of future remuneration to the assessee as managing agent. The assessee sold during the relevant assessment year, the ordinary and preference shares which resulted in a loss. After adjusting this loss on the extra amount received on the sale of deferred shares, there was a net profit. The assessee did not return the amount as its income for the year on the ground that it was a capital receipt. The revenue disagreed and brought the amount to tax treating it as income. The Tribunal concurred with that view. It also declined to a make a reference.

On application under section 66(2):

There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

The assessees were engaged in business as merchants and agents of various companies having branch officer in different parts of India. Assessees’ agency with two of the Companies was terminated in the end of previous assessment year. During the assessment year under consideration i.e. 1929-30, assessee received from one of the companies whose agency had been terminated a sum as full compensation for cessation of the agency. The quotations were accepted on both sides as correctly expressing the nature of the transactions. While computing the assessable income of assessee, ITO took abovementioned receipts as profits and gains from business and also allowed certain deductions thereform in respect of compensation paid to various employees. Consequently the balances were included in the total income. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner and Commissioner confirmed the assessment. On further appeal, High Court held that sums in question were not incomes, profits or gains with in meaning of Act at all. In one part of its judgment the High Court seemed to hold that "compensation for loss of these agencies is a receipt in respect of a capital asset in the nature of goodwill. In another part of the judgment the payment seemed to be regarded as in the nature of compensation in lieu of notice.

On revenue’s appeal to the Privy Council :

The assessee-company had entered into an Agreement for Distribution, Manufacturing and Agency of products (ADMA 1997) with one BM Germany in 1997, by virtue of which the assessee acquired right to carry on above business, earlier carried out by BM Germany and its subsidiary. In 2004 RDG had acquired BM group all over the world and in the same year RDG unilaterally terminated certain obligations under 1997 agreement, which was challenged by the assessee in UK court and thereafter assessee and RDG entered into out of court settlement as per which the assessee and RDG mutually agreed to terminate the (ADMA 1997) and RDG paid compensation to assessee.

Said compensation was offered to tax under head 'Capital gain' by assessee contending that as it had transferred entire business and its rights under the agreement had been terminated, the amount received in consideration thereof was assessable as capital gain.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to hold that the proceeds received by the assessee company from RDG on account of termination of agency and distribution of products in India fell under the provisions of section 28(ii)(c) read with section 28(va)(a).

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was a distributor of products of foreign company for last 22 years. A joint venture company HTIPL, consisting of the assessee and the foreign company, was formed to manufacture the products of foreign company in India and also to market products of the foreign company manufactured abroad. Under an agreement entered into between the assessee and company HTIPL, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets like trained manpower personnel dealing with said products in India and detailed list of customers of said products and introduce HTIPL to all the customers both in public and private sectors for sale of said products. In view of transfer of above intangible assets, the assessee received certain compensation from HTIPL. The assessee treated that sum as a consideration for transfer of goodwill and offered same for taxation as long term capital gains. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had income from service contracts and commission from various parties; that it was a compensation received on termination of managing agency; that the assessee was carrying on several managing agencies and it gave up only one and continued with other; that the business structure of the assessee did not suffer and it was free to carry on the trade with other agencies; that the cancellation and compensation, therefore, was merely a normal incidence of business; and that the income of the assessee had increased in the subsequent years. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the amount received by the assessee was revenue receipt taxable in its hands. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had parted with a part of its apparatus to a joint venture and for the loss so suffered it had received compensation. He directed the Assessing Officer to tax the receipt as capital receipt.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee owned coal mines. Later, he along with other family members incorporated a company. By an agreement, the assessee transferred the management of entire business of working his collieries and mines to the company for consideration of royalty. On reference:

On reference :

On reference :

During the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company was operating, managing or administering many hotels belonging to others for a fee, as it had acquired certain skills and experience in managing big hotels in different countries of the world. The memorandum of association of the assessee-company authorised it not only to purchase and run hotels on its own account, but also to operate, manage or administer hotels belonging to others for a fee. The assessee-company agreed to operate the ‘S' hotel in Singapore in terms of an agreement and also provided supervisory services in the form of providing technical staff. In return, the assessee-company was to receive certain fee called 'management fee' which was calculated on the basis of gross operating profits as laid down in the agreement. This agreement was to run for an initial period of 10 years, but the assessee had option to ask for renewal of the said agreement for two further periods of 10 years each by mutual agreement. In 1975, however, the 'S' hotel/company went into liquidation and a receiver was appointed to take charge of its undertaking and properties. As the receiver wanted to sell the hotel to a third party, it entered into a supplemental agreement with the assessee in pursuance of which the assessee-company gave up its valuable rights to operate, manage or administer the 'S' hotel in consideration of a lump-sum payment.

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company received the aforesaid consideration amount and claimed it to be a capital receipt because the assessee received the same in consideration of giving up a capital asset.

The ITO held that in the case of the assessee-company, the contract to manage and administer 'S' hotel was entered into in the ordinary course of business and, therefore, the compensation received for termination of such agreement was nothing but a revenue receipt. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) was of the view that the assessee's business was not to buy and sell hotel operation agreements and as long as the agreements to manage and administer hotels which were long-term agreements were in force, the assessee-company could expect such agreements to yield income year after year and so each of the agreements constituted a source of the assessee-company's income. Therefore, he held that the receipt of compensation from the receiver of the 'S' hotel/company was nothing but a capital receipt. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference:

The assessee was carrying on sub-broking business with 'S' and had about 1800 clients. Said business was transferred to 'S' and for the transfer of goodwill, Rs. 1.11 crores were paid by 'S' to the assessee. Further, since the cost of goodwill was nil and the assessee had purchased the capital bonds with sale proceeds, it claimed deduction under section 54EC. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's claim of sale of goodwill holding that because of changes in the SEBI Regulations regarding share trading assessee could no more act as a sub-broker and, thus, when he could not have continued his business, there was no question of transfer of goodwill. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer taxed the sum of Rs. 1.11 crores under section 28(ii)(c) by treating the same as compensation for termination of agency.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that relationship between 'S' and the assessee was on principal to principal basis and the termination of the agreement between 'S' and the assessee was termination of agreement of two principals. He held that the amount in question was paid by 'S' as compensation for trading infrastructure of business of the assessee, and accordingly, same was to be treated as capital receipt. Accordingly, he directed the Assessing Officer to assess income under the head 'Income from capital gain' and allow exemption under section 54EC to the assessee.

It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

Firstly, in the instant case, it was certainly not the assessee's case before the Tribunal that the amount received towards goodwill was his income, nor did it appear to have been the case for taxing authority. The Tribunal apparently on its own motion came to that conclusion on the facts before it.

Following the decision in New India Life Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1957] 31 ITR 844 it could be said that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to do so.

As regards question whether capital gain arose in instant case, one has merely to read the definition of 'capital gain' to realise that transfer in question could not conceivably be a capital gain, because there was no transfer, sale or exchange of a capital asset. All that was done was to give the management of that asset to someone else. Therefore, the assessee in effecting the transfer of the management of the Coal mines to the company did not make any capital gain.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

The divesting of its management was really divesting the company of its property represented by its opportunity to carry on an activity for profit. The compensation paid was, therefore, for the loss of a capital asset and constitutes a capital receipt.

The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

The agency agreement entered into by the assessee with ‘HML’ in the year 1955 was a capital asset; the whole of it was not destroyed, lost or parted when the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ in the year 1960. It was merely an exploitation of the commercial assets in a different form. Till then, the recurring amount which the assessee was getting from ‘P’ was income. But by the arrangement arrived at on the basis of the second agreement, the whole of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee was parted with and lost. The question has presented some difficulty when the assessee gets some amount of compensation on termination of agency agreement from the principal itself. Sometimes, in a given case, such compensation, and especially with regard to the managing agency business, has been treated as revenue receipts. But, in the instant case, the type of agreement which the assessee entered into with ‘O’ even if it would have entered into with ‘P’ on payment of Rs. 50,000, would not have clothed the receipt with the chartered of a revenue receipt; still it would have been a capital receipt. This was clearly so, without presenting any difficulty, when the agreement was with another company. After having parted with all its rights of profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960, by a subsequent agreement executed in the year 1962, the assessee was left with no business activity in connection with the agency agreement with ‘HML’. The amount, therefore, received by it was not in lieu of compounded profit but surely in lieu of loss of profit-making apparatus.

What is received by way of price or compensation on disposing of circulating capital or stock-in-trade, namely, the trading asset, is ordinarily and generally revenue receipt. What, however, comes in the hands of the assessee on disposal of the capital assets referable to fixed capital is generally a capital receipt. What is capital asset in the hands of one may be a trading asset in the hands of another.

In the instant case the assessee was not parting with the benefits of a trading contract, rather it parted with its profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960; by utilising that apparatus it was earning profit from the agency business, and the whole of it was lost when he decided to retire on the receipt of Rs. 50,000. It was a sum paid to the assessee, truly a compensation for parting with its business, and the agreement entered into deprived the assessee of the benefit of its agreement entered in 1960, with ‘P’ which constituted the framework or whole structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus. For the reasons stated above, the receipt of Rs. 50,000 by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. The former only is treated as income, but not so with regard to the latter. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the firm itself was formed solely for the purpose of managing the company by entering into the agreement in question with the I.T.F. and there was no other business for it. If that was so, when on account of the loss of the managing agency the assessee-firm lost its business itself, the compensation received by it for that loss would be capital in nature. It is also generally held by the courts that lump sum amounts received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreements are capital in nature.

In the possible case, it was not possible to say that the agreement entered into between the assessee-firm and the I.T.F. under which the assessee-firm acquired the managing agency of the company was a contract, entered into in the ordinary course of business or a trading contract. It followed from the above discussion that the amount of compensation awarded to the assessee-firm was capital receipt and not a revenue receipt liable to tax. Though the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was capital in nature, none the less it was to be treated as "profits and gains of business" as provided under section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act and section 28(ii ) of the 1961 Act.

It was true that the assessee-firm did not enter into any agreement directly with the managed company. It was only the ‘I.T.F.’ which entered into the managing agency agreement with the managed company. But as per the terms of the agreement entered into between the ‘I.T.F.’ and the assessee-firm, the ‘I.T.F.’ assigned its rights under the managing agency agreement to the assessee-firm. The managed company also passed a resolution ratifying the assignment. The umpire awarded damages to the assessee-firm for its loss of managing agency commission, which the assessee-firm would have otherwise been entitled to, but for the breach of the agreement. It was only on the basis of the managing agency commission which the assessee-firm, would have received and estimating it, the umpire awarded the damages to the assessee-firm. What was relevant was whether the amount received was towards compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement or not. It mattered little who paid the amount. Therefore, the amount awarded to the assessee-firm must be deemed as profits and gains of business carried on by it and, therefore, it was income liable to tax.

In the instant case, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum monthly remuneration. Though some quantification was also involved in arriving at the actual damages, the compensation was awarded to the assessee-firm on the basis of the remuneration of so much per year as having accrued to it during the relevant years 1955-56 to 1959-60 (up to 14-8-1960). It was on that basis estimation of the damages was made by the umpire in the arbitration proceedings in awarding the compensation. As the assessee-firm employed the mercantile system of accountancy the relevant amounts as estimated by the umpire in the award must be deemed to have accrued to the assessee-firm during the relevant years.

Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of the revenue.

The agreement entered into between the parties clearly was one of the type which was entered into on principal to principal basis. The agreement showed that both the parties tried to protect their commercial interests by incorporating into an agreement provisions for this purpose. In this agreement, there was no provision whatsoever, which could be interpreted as the assessee acting as an agency of the firm for the purpose of manufacturing of bidies. The system of accounting arrived at in which the assessee could get the maximum profit of 10 per cent was for the mutual protection of the business interests of the parties. So far as the question of capital gain was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wholly wrong because in a slump transaction no such capital gain could arise because the sale was of a going concern. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals ) was to be reversed. Thus, as Rs. 5 lakhs was a sum received by the assessee in a slump transaction, i.e., as a going concern, no part of this amount was taxable either as revenue receipt or as capital gains.

There was no dispute that the portion of the compensation which represented past profits was a revenue receipt. The only question was whether the remaining portion was a revenue receipt or capital receipt. The remaining portion purported to be compensation given to the three partners for giving up: (i) the managing agency rights, (ii) the selling agency rights, and (iii) the goodwill. The managing agency rights vested with new firm (BJ). Similar was the case of the goodwill assuming that any goodwill had been built up by that time. 'BJ' continued to be in existence. It had not parted with managing agency rights nor its goodwill taken away. What had happened was that the partners representing the assessee firm in 'BJ' had surrendered their rights in partnership to the remaining partners and obtained certain payments for such surrender. This was not a case of parting with any agency rights. This was really a case of cancellation of a contract which had been entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such contracts are liable, in the ordinary course of business, to be altered or terminated on terms and any payment received in settlement of the rights as a result of the termination of the contract really represents the profits which the assessee would have made had the contract been performed. In the instant case, no deed of partnership had been entered into. Therefore, the same was terminable at will. Any of the partners of the firm could have brought the partnership to an end. Consequently, the possibility of termination of a partnership was inherent in the very course of business. Further the assessee-firm had various business activities; one of which was to join 'BJ' to carry on certain business activities. The assessee's representatives by entering into that agreement were merely carrying on a trading activity. Such being the case, it could not be held that the compensation paid for the termination of the contract was a capital receipt. It was not the case of the assessee that its only trading activity had come to an end. It had several activities. Just one of its trading had been put an end to. Hence, the amount received could not be considered as compensation for stopping its business.

As regards the transfer of the selling agency to 'BJ', this was not a right transferred under agreement as that right had been transferred to 'BJ' even at the time the partnership was formed. Further the trading structure of the assessee-firm was not affected. It merely replaced one trading activity by another with the aid of Rs. 35,01,000. In such circumstances, the amount received from the cancellation of agency did not represent the price paid for the loss of capital; it was of the nature of income. Therefore, the entire sum of Rs. 35,01,000 received by the assessee was a revenue receipt assessable under section 10 of 1922 Act.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

Since a managing agency is a creature of contract and since its formation, operation and termination are all to be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act, in so far as they apply, there was no force in the contention that a managing agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other manner. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the compensation amount was taxable profit within the meaning of section 10(5A).

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Even if it was assumed that the impugued payment was for surrendering of the managing agency, unless there was a finding that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency, this aspect would not support the revenue's stand.

Accordingly, the surplus arising out of the transaction of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains.

Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

On principle also it was difficult to understand why a distinction should be made between the destruction of the whole of the capital asset or a part of the capital asset. In either case, it was clear that the amount received as solatium for that destruction could not be profits arising out of the business of the assessee. The assessee was sought to be taxed under section 10 and the department had to satisfy that the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was profit made by the assessee in the course of its business or profit earned out of its business. Surely when Rs. 25,00,000 had been paid to the assessee for the cessation of its particular business, it could not be urged that this very sum of Rs. 25,00,000 were profits earned by the assessee in the course of its business.

Inasmuch as the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was received by the assessee in consideration of the termination of its managing agency, it was a solatium for the cessation of one of the several activities which the assessee company was entitled to carry on under the agreement, and if it was a solatium then it could not be looked upon as income but must be looked upon as representing the capital asset which had ceased to exist.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

[Para 7.1] Management right has now been included in the definition of 'property' and, therefore, is a 'capital asset' under section 2(14). This being so, taxability of any amount received against relinquishment of 'management right' has to be tested on the touchstone of provisions relating to computation of capital gain. The assessee argued that since management right is a capital asset, provisions relating to capital gain will apply and when such computation provisions are applied, they are unworkable. It is true that under the scheme of taxation of capital gain, it is not the entire sale consideration of an asset which is chargeable to tax but it is the 'profit or gain' arising on transfer thereof which is taxable. This observation is subject to the specific provisions of law which prescribe that in case of some category of capital assets, cost of acquisition is considered to be nil and, in those cases, full consideration accruing on transfer will become taxable. In the instant case, it is the stand of assessee that cost of acquisition of management right being indeterminate, no capital gain can be worked out and so the provisions are not workable. [Para 7.3]

Section 55(2) does not specify that cost of acquisition of 'management right' will be taken to be nil. In other words, there is no deemed cost of acquisition provided in the statute. No case has been made out by the Assessing Officer to show as to what was the cost of management right in the hands of assessee. Therefore, what has been brought to tax is the entire consideration for relinquishment of management right which runs contrary to the settled proposition of law, which was laid down by Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 5 Taxman 1/128 ITR 294. In this decision, the Supreme Court has laid down the proposition that machinery and charging provisions constitute an integrated code and where in the situation computation provision fails, it has to be assumed that such a transaction was not intended to be falling within the charging section and, therefore, the charge on account of capital gain must fail. [Para 7.3]

It is evident that the revenue has not established that the assessee was managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the company as no case has been made out by the revenue that the amount received by the assessee from CARE was on account of relinquishment of any managerial rights. Even assuming that the amount received by the assessee is relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, in view of ratio laid down by Supreme Court in the case of B.C. [Para 7.4]

In the above view, the amount received by the assessee is neither chargeable under section 28(ii)(a) nor under the head capital gain. [Para 7.5]

It was provided by the articles of association of the new company that the firm, should be appointed managing agents, and that this arrangement was part and parcel of the arrangements, whereby the Mills, in which the assessee admittedly held a share as karta, were sold by the partnership to the new company. If the partners should sell or assign their right to remuneration, as per clause 14 of the managing agency agreement it could not be said that the portion of the proceeds of sale attributable to HD's share, did not pass to him as joint family property. The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

It was not the case of the Department and it had never been their case that the capital asset in respect of which capital gain was made by the assessee and which was sought to be taxed was the shares and the managing agency. The whole of the reference was based upon the fact that the only capital asset concerned with was the shares and not the managing agency. Therefore, one must separate the managing agency from the shares in considering what was the value to be put upon the shares. The parties had put upon the shares a value which was much higher than the market value. Admittedly, it was an artificial value and it was artificial because the value put upon the shares was not the value of the shares alone but it was the composite consideration paid by the purchasers for obtaining the shares and also acquiring the managing agency. Under the circumstances, for the purposes of section 12B(2) the sale price of the shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. 65 per share.

Note : The case was decided in favour of assessee.

As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375. As regards the point that compensation was for past service of the firm, from a perusal of paragraph 2 of the agreement, it was clear that the promotion of the company by the partners of the firm was consideration for the appointment of the firm and for its tenure. It was a duly executed consideration. The period of 99 years was a fixed period. The firm was to continue for the whole of that period, unless it resigned the managing agency. It was not removable while the period of 99 years was still running. It could be removed only after the expiry of that period, and then also, only by a 3/4th majority of the shareholders of the company. It is clear that the situation in which the managing agency firm might resign or be removed prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years was not envisaged in the agreement at all. It followed that services rendered by the partners of the managing agency firm in promoting the company could not under the agreement for the basis of any compensation to be awarded to the firm for termination of the agreement either by its resignation or by its removal prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years. The compensation paid could not be consideration for past services.

It was paragraph 3 only of the agreement, which made provision for the premature termination of the managing agency. That paragraph contemplated termination only in one contingency, that of the company being wound up. If the company itself was wound up, the managing agency would be discontinued. In that event only, compensation as provided in paragraph 3(a) was payable. Thus it was clear that the compensation paid on the termination of the managing agency was not compensation for past services and was quite independent of that agreement. At the Tribunal stage this argument stood overruled when the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the payment was not collusive but was genuine and bona fide and further when it held that services were actually rendered by the firm in pursuance of the managing agency agreement after the company came into existence. In the face of the finding that services were actually rendered by the firm, which is a finding of fact, the argument that if any service was at all rendered, it was only the past service for promoting the company, stood overruled.

The result was that the compensation paid was receipt of a capital nature.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The concepts of capital and revenue expenditure are not defined anywhere in the statute, but there is no dearth of guidelines indicated by eminent judges in reported decisions both in England and in India.

In the instant case the assessee was not forced with any immediate or present danger to be averted, neither any financial problem confronted the board of directors for terminating the managing agency agreement nor was any economic difficulty to be surmounted by adopting this course. Plainly, the directors compounded a consolidated claim of the managing agents whose services were terminated apparently without any cause and the amount was paid for this purpose which, undoubtedly, resulted in an enduring benefit, from the economic point of view, for the assessee. Considering that the agreement which was being terminated was assignable and no managing agents were appointed to succeed in place of company ‘J’, there was brought into existence a clear advantage of an enduring nature, an advantage indistinguishable from a material or fixed asset for the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the assessee’s contention must fail and it was held that the payment of made to ‘C’ was not a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act, in the hands of the assessee.

In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

The subject-matter of appeal would get confined to the limits of the grounds specifically raised in the memorandum of appeal, the new grounds raised by the appellant with the previous permission of the Tribunal and the grounds urged by the respondent in support of the decree passed in his favour, even though the decision of the Court, against which the appeal is filed, is against him. It is thus clear that the Tribunal will have no jurisdiction to found its decision on grounds which have not been raised before it by any of the parties at all. In other words, it would not be open to the Tribunal to make out a new case for either the appellant or the respondent. The finding of the AAC was that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital loss and the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. Deducting the capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares, the total figure of the capital gain was arrived at, and from the total gain, the capital gain falling to the share of the assessee was computed at. In this context, it would not be reasonable to assume that by raising this ground the appellant was challenging the finding which was already in his favour, but it would be reasonable to hold that he was challenging the finding which was only against him, and that finding was that the value of the managing agency as on 1-1-1939, was nil. In dealing with this ground, the Tribunal itself observed that the said contention of the assessee related to the capital gains computed by the department.

There was no evidence to come to conclusion, that one of the lines of the business of the assessee-company was to promote companies and to sell out after the companies had been formed. Nor was it one of the regular lines of business of the assessee-company to acquire licences or permits and sell them. Nor even was it a regular line of business of the assessee-company to acquire managing agencies and sell them.

The licence obtained by the partnership, of which the assessee-company was a member, was a valuable asset and a capital asset in its hands. That capital asset was sold for a sum out of which the assessee received, its share of the receipt. It was capital receipt in its hands, and, therefore, the Assistant Commissioner was right in taking in view that being a capital receipt it fell within the scope of section 12B of 1922 Act. It was not assessable to tax as a trading receipt. Therefore, the claim of the assessee, that it was entitled to the benefit of section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act, was erroneous. It was in connection with the business activities of the assessee that the assessee received the sum. That it was a capital receipt in its hand did not make it any the less income from business, and it certainly could not be treated as something of a casual receipt or windfall.

Therefore, the amount in question was assessable to tax as capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act.

In the instant case, the Tribunal was fully justified in holding upon the materials before it that the profits arose from a transaction which was an adventure in the nature of trade. There was a singular paucity of material to establish that the intention of the assessee was to acquire the managing agency of the company. The assessee already had the managing agency of this estate even before its sale. The assessee was not able to place the agreement of managing agency which the assessee had with the previous owner. There was nothing to indicate that the sale of this estate by the said owners to another would have had the effect of terminating the assessee’s managing agency of that estate. There was nothing, therefore, to establish that the assessee had of necessity to acquire a large number of shares for the purpose of securing a capital asset, viz., the managing agency. Practically immediately after the formation of the company the assessee unloaded the majority of the shares it had acquired. Its intention was obviously not to retain these shares and the purchase itself was disassociated from any intention relevant to the acquisition of the managing agency. Had it been a case where the move for the purchase of the shares came from other parties and the assessee as and when any offer was made to it disposed of the shares, it could have justifiably inferred that the intention of the assessee was to keep these shares as an investment, that is to say, as a capital asset, the disposal of which under such circumstances not leading to any revenue income. But that the assessee, within less than a week after the acquisition of the shares started to invite offers for the sales of these shares, necessarily drove to the conclusion that even at the time of the acquisition of the shares the assessee must have had the intention of selling the shares.

The result was that the inference reached by the Tribunal that it was an adventure in the nature of trade which yielded the profit in question was amply supported by adequate material.

It was not merely an intermediary between the principal and its customers but was expected to employ staff; promote the sale and also to maintain warehousing facility. Thus, it was carrying on the business of GE by creating its own infrastructure and for the said purpose it had made huge financial commitments; the assessee was not entitled to act on its own behalf and for itself in respect of the goods entrusted to it. Thus, there was a relationship of agency with GE and not on principal-to-principal basis, as contended by the assessee. Thus, it could be seen that the amount received for termination of agency was a taxable receipt. However, the nature of the receipt is to be seen before bringing it to tax under section 28(ii)(c ). If the receipt is on termination of the agreements of agency and distributorship simplicitor, the compensation received is for the loss of revenue and, hence, a revenue receipt. In such a case, the agent/distributor can carry on business of a similar nature with any other principal. But if there is a restrictive covenant to deal with similar business, then all the agreements have to be considered in unison and not in isolation. By the restrictive covenant the assessee is not only losing the revenue but is also losing the revenue-generating source. As held by the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Ambadi Enterprises Ltd. [2004] 267 ITR 702/139 Taxman 96, one test for ascertaining as to whether what had received was a capital receipt or a revenue receipt is to find out whether the assessee had snapped its link with the profit making apparatus that had been transferred. [Para 16]

In the instant case also, the entire trained staff and the customer network were taken over by the GE and there was a restrictive covenant not to indulge in or to be associated with a similar business. In view of the same, the compensation received on account of termination of the agency and distributorship agreements and for entering into the non-compete agreement was a capital receipt which was not taxable as income from business or profession. [Para 17]

(3) The profits were to accrue by the operation of the Hind Roadways Corporation. (4) The loss was suffered by the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation at the instance of the Government.

On this premises which was clearly implied in the finding of the Tribunal, it appeared to be plain that the compensation was not for loss of profit of any business of the assessee but was to accrue out of a profit-making structure, viz., the corporation, of which the assessee was to be appointed the managing agent. With the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation, the prospect of the assessee becoming the managing agent of the corporation also vanished. Compensation was paid to him in lieu of the benefit which he might have derived by becoming the managing agent of the corporation. The corporation or the profit-making structure or the managing agency were only an asset of a capital nature. Compensation paid for the loss of a capital asset is not and cannot be taxable income.
