Sale deed executed by a general power of attorney holder after the death of the original owner was invalid: SC

M. S. Ananthamurthy v. J. Manjula [2025] 172 taxmann.com 7 (SC)

The suit property was originally part of 1 acre 8 guntas of land in Chunchaghatta Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bangalore South Taluk, owned by the original owner, M @ R. He developed the land into individual plots and sold them to various buyers.

The original owner executed a General Power of Attorney (GPA) and an Agreement to Sell in favour of the holder of the GPA. After the owner's death, the holder, in her capacity as a GPA holder, executed a registered sale deed in favour of her son, appellant No. 2.

The respondents contended that the sale deed was executed after the original owner's death and was, therefore, invalid. On the other hand, the respondents claimed that after the death of the original owner, his legal heirs sold the suit property to a person through a registered sale deed.

Later, the person sold the property to another person via another registered sale deed. Finally, the person gifted the suit property to her daughter, the answering respondent, through a registered gift deed.

The High Court ruled in favour of the respondents, and the matter reached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that a power of attorney derives its basic principles from Chapter X of the Contract Act, which provides for 'Agency' along with sections 1A and 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882. The relationship between the executant of a general power of attorney and the holder of the power is one of principal and agent.

A principal is bound by the acts done by an agent or the contracts made by him on behalf of the principal. Likewise, the power of attorney in the nature of the contract of the agency authorizes the holder to do acts specified by the executant or represent the executant in dealings with third persons.

In the present case, it is evident from the contents of the GPA executed by the original owner in favour of the holder that the holder was authorized to manage the property. However, the import of the word 'general' in a POA refers to the power granted concerning the subject matter. The test to determine the nature of POA is the subject matter for which it has been executed. The nomenclature of the POA does not determine its nature. Even a POA termed as a 'general power of attorney' may confer powers that are special in relation to the subject matter. Likewise, a 'special power of attorney' may confer powers that are general in nature concerning the subject matter. The essence lies in the power and not in the subject matter.

The holder of the POA did not choose to register the agreement to sell executed by the original owner in her favour. Even if such an argument were to persuade the Court, the document must have been registered as per section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act. In the absence of such registration, it would not be open for the holder of the POA to contend that she had a valid right, title and interest in the immovable property to execute the registered sale deed in favour of the appellant.

7. Oral gift of property to daughter on marriage excluded from 'one house' limit for Section 54F exemption: ITAT

Income-tax Officer v. Narasimha Reddy Duthala [2025] 174 taxmann.com 1073 (Hyderabad - Trib.)

The assessee sold unquoted shares for Rs. 92.49 crore and claimed Section 54F exemption by investing Rs. 43.83 crore in a house and Rs. 10.67 crore in a capital gains account. RAJESH DHAWAN*

Whether charging rent for displaying advertisement falls under advertising services?

No. The CESTAT in its judgment in the case of CCE v. Azad Publications [2007] 8 STT 242 (Delhi - CESTAT) held that permitting display of advertisement on its site and raising bills for realising rental charge is mere sub-letting to an advertising agency without providing services of the nature defined for advertising services and, hence, the activity of the respondent will not bring it under the definition of ‘advertising agency’.

Whether technical know-how generated for internal consumption sold out later falls under consulting engineer services?

No. In the case of Aksh Optifibers Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 252 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the appellants had developed certain technical know-how for themselves for the purpose of providing e-governance and rural governance in India and had named the project Gramdoot. Since the appellants could not implement the project themselves, they sold the technical know-how by agreement. It was held that since the agreement was for technology transfer and not for providing any technical know-how service and even the ownership of the technical know-how was transferred to the buyer, the demand of service tax was not sustainable.

Whether services provided by express cargo service transporters are different from courier agency services?

No. The Government in its Master Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated 23-8-2007 has clarified that "the nature of service provided by ‘Express Cargo Service’ provider falls within the scope and definition of courier agency".

Whether fee collected by an institution falls under commercial training or coaching services?

No. In the case of Magnus Society v. CC&CE [2009] 18 STT 193 (Bang. - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that education has a larger scope. Education may include coaching or training and not vice versa. Coaching or training is a very narrow activity, imparting skill in a particular discipline. But, education is a broader term, which is a process of development of personality of body, mind and intellect. Just because an institution collects fees from students, one cannot come to conclusion that it imparts commercial training or coaching. Institutions preparing students for entrance exams to universities are covered under commercial training or coaching services and not institutions offering degrees recognized by law.

Whether a computer engineering firm falls under consulting engineer services?

Yes. The Finance Act, 2008, with effect from May 16, 2008, has amended the definition of ‘taxable service’ to bring back the computer software engineering consultancy service under the service tax net and to provide that services provided by a consulting engineer in relation to advice, consultancy or technical assistance in the disciplines of both computer hardware engineering and computer software engineering shall also fall under consulting engineer service.

Whether an organization formed for charitable purposes is liable for service tax?

Yes. The CESTAT in its judgment in the case of Punjab Ex-Servicemen Corpn. v. CCE [2009] 18 STT 121 (New Delhi - CESTAT) held that an organization may be charitable organization established for some purpose, but may still engage in commercial activities, as without any commercial activities, the income required for charitable purpose cannot be generated. For levy of service tax it is the activity of an organization, which is relevant and not objective.

Whether the person manufacturing the sign boards falls under advertising services?

No. In the case of Star Neon Sign v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 223 (New Delhi - CESTAT), it was held that the person who is only writing or preparing the sign boards at the behest of his customers cannot be called as advertising agency. There was no evidence on record to show that the relationship between the customers and the appellant was of advertising agent, which is necessary for imposition of service tax.

Whether assisting a person in acquiring shares in a company falls under management consultant services?

No. In the case of K.R. Alloys Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 20 STT 392 (Bang.- CESTAT), the Tribunal held that the appellants were not carrying out activity of management but they were manufacturers. Incidental help in acquisition of shares does not fall under ‘management consultant service’.

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent services - Wholesale business of Indian made foreign liquor 5.2 The assessee-corporation was established by the State Government with a view to undertake wholesale business of Indian made foreign liquor to ensure good quality at fair price, and to end certain undesirable practices. There was an agreement between the assessee and the various manufacturers/suppliers of liquor under which the manufacturers/suppliers were to supply the liquor on FOR (destination) basis to various depots maintained by the assessee. The assessee was required to sell liquor only to dealers who were licensed by the State Excise Commissioner. The Commissioner had held that ownership of liquor had never been transferred to the assessee; that the invoices were prepared by the assessee on behalf of principal; that it collected the landing price and the commission from the retailers; that it was a consignment agent and the commission paid to the assessee shall be subject to service tax under the heading ‘C&F agent’. Accordingly, he confirmed service tax demand along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner had held that the assessee-corporation was a procurement agent for the State Government.

According to the Tribunal, if that view was accepted, then the assessee would be rendering the services to the State Government and the State Government would become the recipient of services. It had not been shown that the State Government was required to pay any charges to the assessee for the so-called services rendered. In view of the above, the assessee could not be considered as an agent rendering services to the State Government for consideration, in spite of the fact that the agreement between the assessee-corporation and the supplier of liquor referred to the assessee as a procurement agent.

The Tribunal held that as regards the relationship between the assessee and the supplier of the liquor, it was found that transfers were in the nature of sale and purchase. The licence granted to the assessee-corporation was also for purchase and sale of liquor and the agreement clearly referred to prices on F.O.R. destination basis. Overlooking all these evidences, it would not be proper to conclude that there was no sale by the assessee and that it was acting as procurement agent. At any rate, it was not undertaking any agent’s function for the supplier of liquor or the manufacturer supplier of liquor. Notwithstanding the fact that the assessee had chosen to describe its income from sale of liquor as commission in the balance sheet, it was to be viewed that the assessee-corporation was engaged in purchase/sale of liquor and could not be considered as C&F agent.

There was a difference between a payment made as compensation for the termination of an agency contract and an amount paid as solatium for the cancellation of a contract entered into by a businessman in the ordinary course of business. In an agency contract, the actual business consists in the dealings between the principal and his customers, and the work of the agent is only to bring about that business. What he does is not the business itself but something which is intimately and directly linked up with it. The agency may, therefore, be viewed as the apparatus which leads to the business rather than the business itself. Considered in this light, the agency can be held to be of the nature of a capital asset invested in business. But this cannot be said of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such a contract is part of the business itself, not anything outside it as is the agency and any receipt on account of such a contract can only be a trading receipt [CIT v. Rai Bahadur Jairam Valji [1959] 35 ITR 148 (SC)]. Also see, Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC).

Compensation paid for termination of a managing agency business is a payment in relation to said business as such said receipt was obviously related to that business and was not or income from a new and independent source and, therefore, previous year relevant to that receipt would be same as previous year for managing agency business itself [Chidambaram Mulraj & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 102 ITR 7 (SC)].

Compensation for unilateral termination of agreement - Where agreement entered into by assessee-company to develop and construct buildings on land owned by another company was unilaterally terminated by land owner company and under a settlement agreement compensation was paid to assessee for annulment of its rights to carry on business and for being deprived of potential income which would have arisen to it from carrying on such business, said compensation would constitute trading receipt in hands of assessee [Ansal Properties & Industries Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 86/[2011] 196 Taxman 45 (Delhi)].

INCOME DERIVED BY CERTAIN TRADE, PROFESSIONAL OR SIMILAR ASSOCIATION [SECTION 28(iii)]

'Performing specific services', meaning of - The words 'performing specific service' mean conferring particular benefits on the members. With reference to a trade, professional or similar association, the performing of specific services must mean conferring on its members some tangible benefit which otherwise would not be available to them as such except for payment received by the association in respect of those services. Thus, amount received in the nature of entrance fee and other subscription fees from its members for allowing their application for enlisting names of companies not already on quotations list so that shares and stocks of said companies might be placed on the stock market chargeable to tax u/s 28(iii) [CIT v. Calcutta Stock Exchange Association Ltd. [1959] 36 ITR 222 (SC)].

Other incomes taxable under appropriate heads of income - The plain reading of section 28(iii) suggests that the income derived by a trade association from specific services rendered by it should be brought to tax. From such a reading, no exclusion of any other type of income can be implied if such other income can otherwise be taxed under other provisions of the 1961 Act [CIT v. Shree Jari Merchants Association [1977] 106 ITR 542 (Guj.)].

GENERAL

Transfer of part asset - The words 'the transfer of a capital asset' occurring in section 45 cannot be interpreted as a transfer of the entire capital asset and not a part of the same [National Products v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 755 (Kar.)].

Capital asset on the date of transfer - It is necessary that property transferred must be a capital asset on date of transfer and not that such property should have been capital asset also on date of its acquisition by the assessee [Arun Sunny v. DCIT [2009] 184 Taxman 498 (Ker.)]. Also see, A. R. Dahiya v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 141 Taxman 449 (P&H).

CAPITAL GAINS OR NOT

Gift for tax avoidance - Where assessee transferred its shareholding, as a gift, in a company to step-down company created in a tax haven country and the said step-down company transferred stake in favour of a third-party investor for a consideration, sole intention of assessee being escape rigour of Indian tax laws, therefore, assessee was liable to tax u/s 45 [PCIT v. Redington (India) Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 136 (Mad.)].

Inherited property - Where assessee inherited certain land, leased out same on payment of ground rent and ultimately sold it after decades, profit arising from sale of land was to be taxed as 'capital gains' [CIT v. Administrator of the Estate of Shri E. F. Dinshaw [2012] 22 taxmann.com 57/208 Taxman 193 (Mag.) (Bom.)].

Intangible assets - Sale of brand names, trademark, copyright and goodwill in journals sold/transferred would clearly be a case of sale of capital asset and exigible to capital gains [CIT v. Mediworld Publications (P.) Ltd. [2011] 11 taxmann.com 374/200 Taxman 1 (Delhi); CIT v. ABB Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 338/[2022] 284 Taxman 350 (Kar.)].

Where collection of assets of undertaking transferred in slump sale included intangible assets like goodwill and intellectual property whose cost of acquisition could not be determined, said sale could not be assessable to capital gains [CIT v. AKZO Noble India Ltd. [2020] 121 taxmann.com 216/[2021] 276 Taxman 259 (Cal.)].

Malba - Proceeds of malba, i.e., material left over after demolition of a structure, would be taxable under the head 'Capital gains' and not under the head 'Income from other sources' [CIT v. Ribu Saggi [2014] 45 taxmann.com 371/223 Taxman 150 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Owelty - Amount of owelty (i.e., compensation deposited to settle inequalities in partition) represents immovable property and would not attract capital gain tax [CIT v. Ashwani Chopra [2013] 30 taxmann.com 299/213 Taxman 490 (P&H)].

Pledge of shares - No capital gains arise where there was no transfer of shares but shares have been pledged for the purposes of obtaining loan [CIT v. Reliance Communication Infrastructure Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 302/[2013] 212 Taxman 177 (Bom.)].

Sale of business as a going concern - Where business is sold as a going concern valuing plant and machinery, etc., surplus arising over and above the difference between WDV and actual cost has to be taxed u/s 45 [CIT v. Artex Mfg. Co. [1997] 93 Taxman 357 (SC)].

Shares - Where assessee-company purchased shares of a private limited company from funds received from its holding company and after some time it had sold said shares to its holding company, profit arising from sale of shares had to be taxed under head 'Capital gains' [CIT v. Renato Finance & Investment Ltd. [2013] 33 taxmann.com 262/218 Taxman 312 (Bom.)].

Where assessee-director received huge amount as non-compete fee but real and true nature of transaction was sale of shares and transfer of control and management of company, amount in question was to be taxed as capital gains in hands of assessee [CIT v. Shiv Raj Gupta [2014] 52 taxmann.com 425 (Del.), SLP granted inShiv Raj Gupta v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 3/244 Taxman 191 (SC)].

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : “An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

2.2-11 Transferor can claim exemption from capital gains -The tax treatment of the transferor is not at all relevant in the grant of depreciation to the transferee in respect of cost of intangible asset. Thus, the transferee will be eligible to claim depreciation even if the transferor is not subject to tax on account of, say,

◆ applicability of section 47(xii)/(xiii)/(xiv) of the Act, exempting the transferor from capital gains tax.

◆ the transferor claiming exemption by applying the ‘No cost’ principle as laid down in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294 (SC) and in Voltas Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [1998] 64 ITD 232 (Mum.) (in respect of trademark).

◆ applicability of double taxation avoidance agreement.

2.2-12 Sale and lease back - It may be noted that if an intangible asset is sold and then taken for use from the transferee, Explanation 4A to section 43(1) may apply if the transferor has already obtained depreciation on the asset. Under this Explanation, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on the written down value of the transferor at time of transfer of the intangible asset, although he may have acquired the intangible asset for a higher sum. To illustrate, if the written down value of an intangible asset is Rs. 20 lakhs in the hands of the transferor and if he sells the asset for Rs. 50 lakhs, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on Rs. 20 lakhs by virtue of the provisions of Explanation 4A.

It may be noted that the aforesaid Explanation does not apply if the transferor has not claimed any depreciation on the intangible asset. In such an event, the actual cost for the transferee shall not be restricted to the written down value of the transferor and he will get depreciation on his cost of acquisition.

CIT [2000] 243 ITR 158, held that cancellation of sale of assets cannot be such a subsequent event so as to change the nature of the receipt of the forfeited amount. 6.15-2e WHETHER A RECEIPT IS CAPITAL OR REVENUE - The principles that can be deduced from various decisions of the Indian and the foreign courts for determining whether a particular amount received by an assessee is capital or revenue in nature are as under :

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

■ Profit motive is not decisive of the question, whether a particular receipt is capital or income.7

■ The question whether the payer is compelled to pay has no relevance in the determination of the character of the receipt. It may be that the payee has no legal claim for payment and the payment is made voluntarily, yet the receipt may be of revenue character.8

A voluntary payment is a profit of employment if it accrues by virtue of the employment notwithstanding that there may not be any legal obligation to make the payment. If, however, the payment is in the nature of a personal gift to him, it is not regarded as a payment for services but as a mere present.8

■ The voluntary payment to a lawyer by a person who is not a client but who has benefited by the lawyer’s professional services to another is taxable.1

■ The fund out of which the money came is not material.2

■ General payments made by way of donation to a company out of benevolence or feeling of charity would not entail income in the hands of the recipient.3

■ Amounts received in settlement of a right under trading contract are trading receipts.4

6.15-2f COMPENSATION - WHETHER REVENUE OR CAPITAL - About the receipt of compensation the law is that as discussed below :

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

■ Compensation for surrender of industrial licence - In CIT v. Automobile Products of India Ltd.1, the Bombay High Court held that where the termination of the activity is not a necessary incident of the business of the assessee and the extinction and surrender of the industrial licence and the collaboration agreement have impaired the profit-making structure of the assessee, the amount received by it as compensation will be a capital receipt.

But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

Extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset

The booklet "How to compute capital gains published by the Income Tax Department" explains 'extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset' as under:

"This covers every possible transaction which results in destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation of all or any bundle of rights in a capital asset."

For example, termination of a lease or of a mortgagee interest in a property. In the case of CIT v. Grace Collis [2001] 115 taxmann 326 (SC) the Supreme Court held that the definition of 'transfer' in section 2(47) also contemplates the extinguishment consequent upon the transfer thereof.

Therefore, the expression 'transfer' does include the extinguishment of rights in a capital asset independent of and otherwise than on account of transfer.

Tracing the history of "extinguishment of rights"

If legislative history is traced, the Indian Income-tax Act 1922(the 1922 Act) did not contain any specific provision corresponding to section 2(47) of the Act defining 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset, though section 12B of the 1922 Act relating to capital gains spoke of "sale, exchange or transfer", as attracting capital gains. The "transfer" was mentioned in juxtaposition of "sale and exchange"- The term juxtaposition means the fact of two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect.

Reference to relinquishment was not mentioned in the said provision. Section 12B of the 1922 Act was recast by the Finance (No.3) Act,1956 wherein it was mentioned that ".the tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head "Capital Gains" in respect of any profits or gains arising from the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer of a capital asset effected after the 31st day of March, 1956, and such profits and gains shall be deemed to be income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place" In other words, the phrase " relinquishment" was added but the other phrase "extinguishment of any rights (therein)" about which this discussion centers around was placed in a separate clause by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1984 with effect from 01-04-1985 when the section 2(47) of the Act was recast apparently with the object of avoiding any ambiguity and repetition of the expression in the charging section though the phrase " extinguishment of any rights (therein)" had also been in the statute book since the inception of the 1961 Act itself.

This clause gives an artificially extended meaning to the expression 'transfer' and expands the same to include the cases of extinguishment of any rights and the compulsory acquisition which were conspicuous by their absence in the 1922 Act.

The Supreme Court as early as 21st February 1978 in the case of Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 803/2 SCC 50 (a Bench consisting of 7 Hon'ble Judges) with regard to transfer of a right in a property by extinguishment observed as under-

6.1-2 Contracts 'relating' to business

The amended section 28(ii)(e) covers any contract "relating" to the business. Hence, it would cover contracts relating to purchases, sales or services or any other aspect of a business including joint venture agreements, distribution, etc.

6.1-3 Contracts 'relating' to acquisition of capital assets

Since the amended section is very widely worded it would cover contracts relating to acquisition of capital assets and hence on a literal reading, the compensation or other payment at or in connection with termination of such contract would be taxable as business income under section 28(ii)(e). On the other hand, Courts have held that giving up the right to obtain conveyance of immovable property or to claim specific performance is a transfer, assessable as capital gains [CIT v. Smt. Laxmidevi Ratani [2005] 147 Taxman 642 (MP); CIT v. Vijay Flexible Container [1990] 48 Taxman 86 (Bom.); Asian PPG Industries Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 38 SOT 114 (Mum. - Trib.); Asstt. CIT v. United Motors (I) Ltd. [2009] 32 SOT 399 (Mum. - Trib.)]

Thus, it is possible that a receipt is taxable as capital gains as well as under section 28(ii)(e) on its literal reading, if such receipt is in connection with the termination of the contract. In such circumstances, it could be argued that the provision may be so construed as being applicable to cases other than those relating to transfer of a capital asset. See for instance a case such as Patel Brass Works v. CIT [2007] 163 Taxman 279 (Guj.). In CIT v. T. P. Sidhwa [1981] 6 Taxman 91 (Bom.), the Bombay High Court explained the Supreme Court judgment in Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v. CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 and stated that "whether an income falls under one head or the other has to be decided according to the common notion of practical men, for the Act does not provide any guidance in the matter. In other words, the heads of income must be decided on the nature of the income by applying practical common notion and not by reference to the assessee's treatment of income". Now, under the common notion, gains of the type mentioned above should fall under capital gains and not profits and gains of business which is ordinarily not meant to cover capital receipts.

Further, the Explanatory Memorandum reads as follows:

"Under the existing provisions of the Act, certain types of compensation receipts are taxable as business income under section 28. However, the existing provisions of clause (ii) of section 28 is restrictive in its scope as far as taxation of compensation is concerned; a large segment of compensation receipts in connection with business and employment is out of the purview of taxation leading to base erosion and revenue loss."

Thus, the intent is to bring within the scope of the law cases that presently fall outside resulting in base erosion and revenue loss and not cases which are already covered under the head capital gains.

Scope of provision - Section 45(5) read as a whole not only deals with reworking but also with the change in the full value of the consideration (computation) and since the enhanced compensation/consideration (including interest u/s 28 of the 1894 Act) becomes payable/paid under 1894 Act at different stages, the receipt of such enhanced compensation/consideration is to be taxed in the year of receipt subject to adjustment, if any, u/s 155(16), later on. The Calcutta High Court in the case of Principal CIT v. ITC Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 88 (Calcutta) held that sum received for relinquishment of right to operate hotel under operating license agreement is revenue receipt.

In this case the assessee-licensee was running the hotel owned by the licensor along with the licensor's employees under an operating license granted by the licensor under an Operating licence agreement, and the licence was terminated by the licensor, and the assessee received the compensation by way of settlement of all disputes in relation to the agreement as per the Arbitrator's award as per consent terms.

The following substantial question was referred to the High Court—

"Whether receipt of money by the Assessee on account of relinquishment of its right to operate a hotel as a licensee would constitute capital receipt exposing the Assessee to capital gains tax or the same shall be treated as business receipt?"

The High Court held that "as it is a compensation received for loss of trading operation of running the hotel under the agreement and not for the loss of any asset of enduring value the amount received is a revenue receipt and not a capital receipt."

Paragraph 29 of this judgment is the highlight of this decision and the same is extracted below—

"Vide in Commissioner of Income Tax, UP, Lucknow v. Gangadhar Baijnath, Generalganj, Kanpur (1972) 4 SCC 28 (para 14) Hon'ble Supreme Court noted that one way of distinguishing capital from revenue receipts, is to take the classical economists' distinction between fixed capital and circulating capital receipts in respect of former is capital while the latter is not. Fixed capital is what is retained by the owner and turned to profit while circulating capital is parted with in order to yield profit. The ITC had not (made) any fixed capital investment to run the hotel under the "Operating Licence Agreement". On the other hand, from perusal of various clauses of the agreement it appears that the ITC has introduced some circulating capital to run the hotel. Therefore, from Classical Economists distinction point of view also, the receipts of Rs. 32.42 crore by the ITC from the ELEL being not for transfer or loss of any capital asset but at best in lieu of circulating capital introduced to operate the hotel, is "revenue receipt" arising from the trading contract i.e. "Operating Lisence Agreement". Mere use of the word "relinquishment" in the "Settlement Agreement" and in the "Consent Terms" without disclosing any rights in any capital asset or relinquishment any rights in any capital assets, is not decisive rather establishes that the receipt is not capital receipt."

Redemption of preference shares is relinquishment and transfer

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 509 (SC) the Court held that redemption of preference shares is clearly 'sale' by the shareholder to the company and would come within the purview of 'transfer' in view of the following:

A reading of sections 77, 80 and 85 of the Companies Act, 1956 [now sections 67, 55 and 43 of the Companies Act, 2013] makes it clear that when a preference share is redeemed by a company, what a shareholder does is, to sell the shares to the company. Such a transaction is nothing but sale of the preference shares by the shareholder to the company.

That is why after specifically laying down in section 77(1) of the said Act [now section 67(1) of the 2013 Act] that no company shall have the power to buy its own shares, it was necessary to specify in sub-section (5) thereof [sub-section (4) of section 67 of the 2013 Act] that this provision shall not affect the rights of a company to redeem any preference shares issued by it.

If redemption of preference shares did not amount to sale, it would not have been necessary to specifically provide that the restriction imposed upon a company in respect of buying its own shares will not apply to redemption of preference shares issued by the company.

The Court held that the assessee had purchased the preference shares at less than face value. When the shares were redeemed by the company, she received more than what she had paid for the shares. In order to get this amount the assessee had to give up or abandon or surrender the shares held by her. The meaning of the word 'relinquish' as given in Webster's Comprehensive Dictionary International Edition 1984, is: (1) to give up; abandon; surrender, (2) to cease to demand; renounce; to relinquish a claim, (3) to let go (a hold or something held).

6.15-5D Capital gains - Profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset are chargeable to income-tax under the head ‘Capital gains’. The charging section envisages transfer of capital asset and the profits and gains arising on account of such transfer.

The expression ‘transfer’ has been defined in section 2(47) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 as including sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any rights therein, or compulsory acquisition thereof; or conversion of a capital asset into stock-in-trade, or transaction involving the allowance of the possession which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of an immovable property, etc.

Since the transfer as contemplated is one as a result whereof consideration has passed to the assessee or has accrued to him, extinguishment or relinquishment of rights must relate to that ‘capital asset’ corporeal or incorporeal. It is, therefore, obvious that transfer of a capital asset in order to attract liability to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ must be a ‘transfer’ as a result whereof some consideration is received by or accrues to the assessee. If the transfer does not yield any consideration, there can be no question of capital gains. If the transfer takes effect on extinguishment of a right in the capital asset, there must be receipt of consideration for such extinguishment to attract liability to tax.1

The word ‘transfer’ also covers cases which result in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise of all or any of the bundle of rights which a person has in the capital assets.1 It is only when consideration is received in respect thereof.

The word ‘transfer’ is comprehensive and is regarded generally as comprehending within its scope transfers both voluntary and involuntary. In the absence of a distinct genus or category, no presumption can arise that the word ‘transfer’ in section 2(47) must be construed in the sense of a voluntary transfer, because the words ‘sale’, ‘exchange’ and ‘relinquishment’ are in the normal acceptation of those terms voluntary acts, and, therefore, if an existing title of a capital asset is extinguished and a new one created, there is within the meaning of section 2(47) a ‘transfer’ of capital asset, and the fact that the divestiture of title takes place under a law relating to compulsory acquisition of property would make no difference. The compulsory acquisition of capital asset may be a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 2(47), but is not sale. These expressions are not synonymous conveying the same meaning. Had this been so, and also the expression ‘sale’ as embracing within its scope ‘compulsory acquisition’ of an asset, there would have been no need to refer to both these expressions in the inclusive definition of ‘transfer’ in section 2(47). One of the purposes of the inclusive definition is to expand the concept defined. The meaning of the expression ‘transfer’ was extended to cover the compulsory acquisition of an asset along with sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any right therein, etc.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

Corporate veil lifting - Tax avoidance

The courts have been stepping into pierce the corporate veil when fiscal or legal obligations are sought to be bypassed by a corporate entity. The Supreme Court has upheld the right of the tax authorities to go behind the corporate façade to look at the economic realities of transactions, if the shell of the corporate entity is used for tax evasions or to circumvent tax obligations [see Juggilal Kamlapat v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 702 (SC) and CIT v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd. [1967] 63 ITR 609 (SC)]. The courts have been upholding the revenue’s right to disregard the consequences of transactions even in respect of those which are genuinely undertaken if their purpose is to avoid tax that would otherwise be payable. The taxing authority is entitled and is indeed bound to determine the true legal relations resulting from a transaction. If the parties have chosen to conceal by a device the legal relation, it is open to the taxing authority to unravel the device and determine the true character of the relationship. It is the duty of the court, in every case where ingenuity is expended to avoid and taxing legislation, to go behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs. The court is not be satisfied with form and leave well alone the substance of a transaction [Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. v. Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. [1986] 157 ITR 77 (SC)/Ess Ess Kay Engg. Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 151 ITR 636 (Punj. & Har.)]

In Juggilal Kamlapat’s case the Supreme Court exercised the right of unraveling a colourable device of tax evasion. In that case the assessee- firm was a managing agent of a company. The Tribunal held that the reason for terminating the managing agency was not a true reason but was merely a fake one and the whole transaction was a hoax for the purpose of evading income-tax both in the hands of the payer and the payee. The Tribunal also found that that there was only a change of personnel in the managing agency and not a change in office and that the assessee had no right of compensation for any loss of office. The question for consideration was whether the compensation received by the assessee could be treated as capital receipt on the ground that it arose out of the destruction of capital asset, viz., the managing agency. The Supreme Court held that the managing agency business carried on by the assessee- firm was not destroyed or lost to the four individual partners who constituted the assessee-firm. What happened was that the individuals who constituted the assessee-firm became the directors of the newly- formed company and in this new capacity they undertook the conduct of the managing agency business and as shareholders continued to benefit from the profits of that business flowing to them in the shape of dividend instead of as a share of profits from the assessee-firm. In other words, the managing-agency asset was enjoyed by four individual partners in a different capacity with the same object of profit-making. There was, therefore, no destruction of the apparatus of the profit- making asset, i.e., the managing agency contract. It was obvious that there was an intimate connection in this case between the managing agency business of the assessee-firm and the payment of a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs and, therefore, this amount represented as a revenue receipt. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee - company was managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies and also held majority of their conversion shares - 'D' company made an offer to assessee to purchase conversions share of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency - Assessee accepted said offer - Subsequently, agreement was modified and as per new agreement, assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in favour of 'D' company, resigned from it - Revenue authorities brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act amount of compensation received by assessee-company on account of resigning managing agency agreement - Whether since transaction in its true legal character was relinquishment of managing agency and was neither a sale nor transfer thereof, High Court rightly held that assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset. On principle also it was difficult to understand why a distinction should be made between the destruction of the whole of the capital asset or a part of the capital asset. In either case, it was clear that the amount received as solatium for that destruction could not be profits arising out of the business of the assessee. The assessee was sought to be taxed under section 10 and the department had to satisfy that the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was profit made by the assessee in the course of its business or profit earned out of its business. Surely when Rs. 25,00,000 had been paid to the assessee for the cessation of its particular business, it could not be urged that this very sum of Rs. 25,00,000 were profits earned by the assessee in the course of its business.

Inasmuch as the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was received by the assessee in consideration of the termination of its managing agency, it was a solatium for the cessation of one of the several activities which the assessee company was entitled to carry on under the agreement, and if it was a solatium then it could not be looked upon as income but must be looked upon as representing the capital asset which had ceased to exist.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

FACT: The assessee-company entered into an agreement with a firm. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to manufacture ‘bidies’ as per the specifications, such as shape, size, quality and standard, of the firm. The assessee was also free to manufacture bidies for any person, firm or company. It was also provided that the assessee should purchase its own raw materials at its own discretion but, however, the wrapping paper and printed label bearing firm’s trade-mark were to be supplied by the firm. The price was to be fixed mutually from time to time but in no case it was to exceed the manufacturing cost plus 10 per cent profit thereon. Thereafter, another agreement was entered into between the assessee and the firm by which both the parties agreed to terminate mutually the earlier agreement. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to sell and the firm agreed to purchase running business of the assessee. As a consideration for the purchase of the bidi manufacturing business the firm was to pay to the assessee as ‘slump price’ of Rs. 5 lakhs. The IAC held that the assessee was holding an agency and the aforesaid amount received by the assessee was an amount towards termination of this agency, and, therefore, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held it as capital gain and directed the IAC to work out the taxable capital gains in accordance with the relevant provisions.

On appeal:

HELD: The agreement entered into between the parties clearly was one of the type which was entered into on principal to principal basis. The agreement showed that both the parties tried to protect their commercial interests by incorporating into an agreement provisions for this purpose. In this agreement, there was no provision whatsoever, which could be interpreted as the assessee acting as an agency of the firm for the purpose of manufacturing of bidies. The system of accounting arrived at in which the assessee could get the maximum profit of 10 per cent was for the mutual protection of the business interests of the parties. The IAC was, therefore, wrong in holding it as an agency.

So far as the question of capital gain was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wholly wrong because in a slump transaction no such capital gain could arise because the sale was of a going concern. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals ) was to be reversed. Thus, as Rs. 5 lakhs was a sum received by the assessee in a slump transaction, i.e., as a going concern, no part of this amount was taxable either as revenue receipt or as capital gains.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee held certain shares of company ‘G’ and was also managing agent of said company - During relevant accounting year, one ‘T’ made offer to assessee to purchase of aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ held by assessee also managing agency rights of assessee - Assessee accepted aforesaid offer and thereafter wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting his resignation from office of managing agents and further recommended ‘T’ to be appointed as managing agents in his place - Company ‘G’ accepted said letter - Whether resignation by assessee of managing agency and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, was nothing but mode of performance of agreement to sell managing agency arrived at between assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were attracted - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee, who was one of partners of managing agency firm and was director of managed company, received his share of compensation from managed company in terms of arbitration award for premature termination of managing agency agreement - Assessee claimed amount so received to be capital receipt and hence not liable to tax - Whether amount in question was capital receipt and not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes

not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes FACT: There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :
