On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court : HELD: The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts

be ignored altogether but must be taken into consideration along with other relevant circumstances.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued. A managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at the rate of 20 per cent of the profits was not the same thing as a managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at 10 per cent of the profits. There was a distinct deterioration in the character and quality of the managing agency viewed as a profit-making apparatus and this deterioration was of an enduring kind. The reduced remuneration having been separately provided, the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 must be regarded as having been paid as compensation for that injury to or deterioration of the managing agency.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid and received not to make up the difference between the higher remuneration and the reduced remuneration but was in reality paid and received as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous terms as to remuneration as it was in terms expressed to be. In other words, so far as the managed company was concerned, it was paid for securing immunity from the liability to pay higher remuneration to the assessee firm for the rest of the term of the managing agency and, therefore, a capital expenditure and so far as the assessee firm was concerned, it was received as compensation for the deterioration or injury to the managing agency by reason of the release of its rights to get higher remuneration and, therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax.

DE in India. The said license(s) allegedly expired in the month of February 2003. The assessee’s stand adopted throughout is that the said alleged termination of license by Disney was in violation of the agreement regarding AMPL. It appears to have filed a petition before the Company Law Board (predecessor to the National Companies Law Tribunal Law) and got an interim order against DE. The said other entity thereafter went for the appeal before the Bombay High Court. [Para 5]

■ Now comes the dispute between the parties. The assessee and DE entered into an agreement wherein the latter entity transferred its shareholding in AMPL at 51 per cent to MEL (a wholly owned assessee’s subsidiary) for US $ 1 and further agreed to pay it an amount of US $ 10 million as compensation for erosion in the value of its investment in AMPL. Suffice to say, it is this compensation received by the assessee from DE has been assessed under the head business income under section 28(ii)(b) in the assessment findings at page 4 and upheld in the Commissioner (Appeals) detailed discussion hereinabove. [Para 6]

■

Both the parties reiterate the respective stands against and in support of taxability of the impugned compensation. The assessee’s stand is that the said compensation as capital receipt not chargeable to tax under section 4 itself by quoting the catena of case law, the focus is only qua applicability of section 28(ii)(b) as once the same is held as not attracted, all other aspects thereof would indeed stand rendered infructuous. [Para 7]

■

The assessee is not 'managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of an Indian company' in clause (a) to (b) or otherwise in clause (c) so as to render its compensation as taxable under the head business income. The assessee’s agreement clause (10) that both the above parties had decided about 'expert professional, technical and managerial advice and services' by the former to the latter entity. Neither the agreement clause between assessee and DE nor the assessment order and the Commissioner (Appeals), as the case may be, have proved the assessee to be a managing agency qua 'whole or substantially whole…….' in the foregoing terms. [Para 9]

■

The Commissioner at this stage also sought to buttress the point that the assessee had infact received 'non-compete fee' as per clause (9) of the agreement which is taxable under section 28(va) as inserted by the Finance Act, 2002 with effect from 1-4-2003. There is no such addition made by both the lower authorities. The relevant assessment findings could not be revisited so as to add a new head upon in section 254 proceedings before the Tribunal. The impugned compensation is not assessable under section 28(ii)(b) once it is not the managing agency in the foregoing terms. The assessee’s former twin substantive grounds raised in the instant appeal are accepted therefore. This being the outcome qua applicability of section 28(ii) against the department, it is further concluded that the assessee’s endeavour to make the impugned sum is rendered academic in nature. [Para 10]

. In such a case, it is the board of directors collectively who can be said to be managing the business affairs of the company. Therefore, the assessee was not managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the company and the impugned amount cannot be related to the three rights referred to in the Addendum. [Para 7.1] Management right has now been included in the definition of 'property' and, therefore, is a 'capital asset' under section 2(14). This being so, taxability of any amount received against relinquishment of 'management right' has to be tested on the touchstone of provisions relating to computation of capital gain. The assessee argued that since management right is a capital asset, provisions relating to capital gain will apply and when such computation provisions are applied, they are unworkable. It is true that under the scheme of taxation of capital gain, it is not the entire sale consideration of an asset which is chargeable to tax but it is the 'profit or gain' arising on transfer thereof which is taxable. This observation is subject to the specific provisions of law which prescribe that in case of some category of capital assets, cost of acquisition is considered to be nil and, in those cases, full consideration accruing on transfer will become taxable. In the instant case, it is the stand of assessee that cost of acquisition of management right being indeterminate, no capital gain can be worked out and so the provisions are not workable. [Para 7.3]

Section 55(2) does not specify that cost of acquisition of 'management right' will be taken to be nil. In other words, there is no deemed cost of acquisition provided in the statute. No case has been made out by the Assessing Officer to show as to what was the cost of management right in the hands of assessee. Therefore, what has been brought to tax is the entire consideration for relinquishment of management right which runs contrary to the settled proposition of law, which was laid down by Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 5 Taxman 1/128 ITR 294. In this decision, the Supreme Court has laid down the proposition that machinery and charging provisions constitute an integrated code and where in the situation computation provision fails, it has to be assumed that such a transaction was not intended to be falling within the charging section and, therefore, the charge on account of capital gain must fail. [Para 7.3]

It is evident that the revenue has not established that the assessee was managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the company as no case has been made out by the revenue that the amount received by the assessee from CARE was on account of relinquishment of any managerial rights. Even assuming that the amount received by the assessee is relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, in view of ratio laid down by Supreme Court in the case of B.C. HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the income-tax Act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessee, holder of two-third shares of a company and also managing agent of said company, sold its entire shareholding in one block to a third company gaining some profit and  surrendering said managing agency-No finding on record that assessee was a dealer in managing agency and transaction was a colourable one-Whether surplus realised out of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains-Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee-company had held two-third shares of company A and was also its managing agent. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold all these shares to company B at a profit of Rs. 3,14,519 and claimed that the surplus realised was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains. The ITO took the view that the assessee had acquired these shares to procure the managing agency and it had, in fact, carried on multifarious activities in various lines including banking, financing of various companies as well as managing agency. He, accordingly, held that the entire profit from the sale of these shares represented business profit. On appeal, the AAC held that a major portion of the sale proceeds was relatable to the assessee's right to the managing agency which passed along with the shares. He further held that in view of the numerous agencies which the assessee carried on, this transaction involving the giving up of the managing agency was of a revenue nature. Consequently, the AAC upheld the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the assessee had parted with an asset of enduring nature and observed that nothing had been received by the assessee as price for its foregoing managing agency rights. What it had legally received was the value of the shares though it could not be denied that it received a higher value because the shares carried with it the managing agency rights. Further, the Tribunal was of the view that it was concerned with the true and legal realisation resulting from the transaction which appeared to be that of the sale of shares and that the shares were not the assessee's stock-in- trade It, accordingly, held that the impugned profit was liable to be taxed as capital gains and not as revenue gains.

On reference:

HELD: Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Even if it was assumed that the impugued payment was for surrendering of the managing agency, unless there was a finding that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency, this aspect would not support the revenue's stand.

Accordingly, the surplus arising out of the transaction of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains.

The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction. It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

It is thus clear that the Tribunal will have no jurisdiction to found its decision on grounds which have not been raised before it by any of the parties at all. Deducting the capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares, the total figure of the capital gain was arrived at, and from the total gain, the capital gain falling to the share of the assessee was computed at. In this context, it would not be reasonable to assume that by raising this ground the appellant was challenging the finding which was already in his favour, but it would be reasonable to hold that he was challenging the finding which was only against him, and that finding was that the value of the managing agency as on 1-1-1939, was nil. In dealing with this ground, the Tribunal itself observed that the said contention of the assessee related to the capital gains computed by the department.

These being the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was neither competent nor justified in interfering with the finding of the AAC as regards the transaction of sale and holding that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gains. The assessee's contention that the managing agency had value as on 1-1-1939, had been accepted by the Tribunal, and in view of this finding of the Tribunal, and in the light of the observations herein made, the amount of capital gains would have to be computed afresh.

It was true that the assessee-firm did not enter into any agreement directly with the managed company. The managed company also passed a resolution ratifying the assignment. The umpire awarded damages to the assessee-firm for its loss of managing agency commission, which the assessee-firm would have otherwise been entitled to, but for the breach of the agreement. It was only on the basis of the managing agency commission which the assessee-firm, would have received and estimating it, the umpire awarded the damages to the assessee-firm. What was relevant was whether the amount received was towards compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement or not. It mattered little who paid the amount. Therefore, the amount awarded to the assessee-firm must be deemed as profits and gains of business carried on by it and, therefore, it was income liable to tax.

In the instant case, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum monthly remuneration. Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of the revenue.

the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt. As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act. Where on a consideration of the circumstances, payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business, nor deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business, and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated) the receipt is revenue : Where by the cancellation of an agency the trading structure of the assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss of what may be regarded as the source of the assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipt.

In the instant case, on a review of all the circumstances, there was no doubt that what the assessee was paid was to compensate him for loss of a capital asset. It matters little whether the assessee did continue after the determination of its agency with the company to conduct the remaining agencies. The transaction was not in the nature of a trading transaction, but was one in which the assessee parted with an asset of an enduring value. The court was therefore, unable to agree with the High Court that the amount received by the appellant was in the nature of a revenue receipt.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

On reference : HELD: As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375. As regards the point that compensation was for past service of the firm, from a perusal of paragraph 2 of the agreement, it was clear that the promotion of the company by the partners of the firm was consideration for the appointment of the firm and for its tenure. It was a duly executed consideration. The period of 99 years was a fixed period. The firm was to continue for the whole of that period, unless it resigned the managing agency. It was not removable while the period of 99 years was still running. It could be removed only after the expiry of that period, and then also, only by a 3/4th majority of the shareholders of the company. It is clear that the situation in which the managing agency firm might resign or be removed prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years was not envisaged in the agreement at all. It followed that services rendered by the partners of the managing agency firm in promoting the company could not under the agreement for the basis of any compensation to be awarded to the firm for termination of the agreement either by its resignation or by its removal prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years. The compensation paid could not be consideration for past services.

It was paragraph 3 only of the agreement, which made provision for the premature termination of the managing agency. That paragraph contemplated termination only in one contingency, that of the company being wound up. If the company itself was wound up, the managing agency would be discontinued. In that event only, compensation as provided in paragraph 3(a) was payable. Thus it was clear that the compensation paid on the termination of the managing agency was not compensation for past services and was quite independent of that agreement. At the Tribunal stage this argument stood overruled when the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the payment was not collusive but was genuine and bona fide and further when it held that services were actually rendered by the firm in pursuance of the managing agency agreement after the company came into existence. In the face of the finding that services were actually rendered by the firm, which is a finding of fact, the argument that if any service was at all rendered, it was only the past service for promoting the company, stood overruled.

The result was that the compensation paid was receipt of a capital nature.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i)  of the Income-tax Act 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee firm was agent of ‘HML’ - It assigned its agency rights to ‘P’ which agreed to pay part of its profits subject to minimum sum per annum - Subsequently, by another agreement, assessee transferred its rights under assignments to ‘O’ for lump sum consideration - Whether by second agreement assessee had parted with its profits making apparatus and, therefore, amount recived by it from ‘O’ was capital receipt - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was appointed as agent of ‘HML’ in 1955. In 1960, the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ according to which ‘P’ took over the business of the assessee and agreed to pay 31 per cent of its profits subject to a minimum of Rs. 25,000 per annum. Subsequently, by another agreement in 1962, the assessee transferred its rights under the agreement of 1960 for a consideration of Rs. 50,000 to 'O'. The ITO held the sum of Rs. 50,000 to be a revenue receipt of the assessee and taxed it as its income . The AAC maintained the addition in appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal deleted the sum of Rs. 50,000 from the income of the assessee, holding that it was a capital receipt.

On reference :

HELD: The agency agreement entered into by the assessee with ‘HML’ in the year 1955 was a capital asset; the whole of it was not destroyed, lost or parted when the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ in the year 1960. It was merely an exploitation of the commercial assets in a different form. Till then, the recurring amount which the assessee was getting from ‘P’ was income. But by the arrangement arrived at on the basis of the second agreement, the whole of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee was parted with and lost. The question has presented some difficulty when the assessee gets some amount of compensation on termination of agency agreement from the principal itself. Sometimes, in a given case, such compensation, and especially with regard to the managing agency business, has been treated as revenue receipts. But, in the instant case, the type of agreement which the assessee entered into with ‘O’ even if it would have entered into with ‘P’ on payment of Rs. 50,000, would not have clothed the receipt with the chartered of a revenue receipt; still it would have been a capital receipt. This was clearly so, without presenting any difficulty, when the agreement was with another company. After having parted with all its rights of profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960, by a subsequent agreement executed in the year 1962, the assessee was left with no business activity in connection with the agency agreement with ‘HML’. The amount, therefore, received by it was not in lieu of compounded profit but surely in lieu of loss of profit-making apparatus.

What is received by way of price or compensation on disposing of circulating capital or stock-in-trade, namely, the trading asset, is ordinarily and generally revenue receipt. What, however, comes in the hands of the assessee on disposal of the capital assets referable to fixed capital is generally a capital receipt. What is capital asset in the hands of one may be a trading asset in the hands of another.

In the instant case the assessee was not parting with the benefits of a trading contract, rather it parted with its profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960; by utilising that apparatus it was earning profit from the agency business, and the whole of it was lost when he decided to retire on the receipt of Rs. 50,000. It was a sum paid to the assessee, truly a compensation for parting with its business, and the agreement entered into deprived the assessee of the benefit of its agreement entered in 1960, with ‘P’ which constituted the framework or whole structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus. For the reasons stated above, the receipt of Rs. 50,000 by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The ITO was of the opinion that by the transfer of the management of the mines to the company the assessee made a capital gain.

On appeal, the Appellate Commissioner upheld the order of ITO but reduced the amount of capital gain.

On further appeal, though the Tribunal held that the company would have been required to pay higher amount of royalty if it had not paid certain amount on account of goodwill. The Tribunal, thus, opined that the assessee had capitalised a part of his income. It accordingly, concluded that the amount paid to assessee was liable to be taxed at the rates appropriate to 'income' and not at the rates appropriate to capital gain.

On reference:

HELD: Firstly, in the instant case, it was certainly not the assessee's case before the Tribunal that the amount received towards goodwill was his income, nor did it appear to have been the case for taxing authority. The Tribunal apparently on its own motion came to that conclusion on the facts before it.

Following the decision in New India Life Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1957] 31 ITR 844 it could be said that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to do so.

As regards question whether capital gain arose in instant case, one has merely to read the definition of 'capital gain' to realise that transfer in question could not conceivably be a capital gain, because there was no transfer, sale or exchange of a capital asset. HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether amount received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreement are capital in nature - Held, yes - ‘ITF’ was managing agent of a company - Under an agreement, it transferred managing agency to assessee firm - Due to some disputes arose subsequently between assessee and ‘ITF’, assessee had to resign from office of managing agency and in arbitration proceedings, received damages towards compensation for loss of managing agency commission - Whether compensation received by assessee was capital receipt and not revenue receipt - Held, yes - Whether, however, said amount would be treated as ‘profits and gains of business’ under section 28(ii) of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and compensation was awarded to assessee on basis of remuneration as having accrued to it during earlier five assessment years, compensation must be deemed to have accrued to assessee during said years - Held, yes

FACT: ‘ITF’ was managing agent of a company. Under an agreement ‘ITF’ transferred the managing agency of company to the assessee firm. The assessee firm took over the management of the company in pursuance of the general power of attorney executed by the ‘ITF’ in its favour. Thereafter due to some disputes, the ‘ITF’ asked the assessee firm to resign from the office of managing agency. The matter was ultimately referred to arbitrators who awarded compensation to the assessee for loss of the managing agency commission. The ITO held that the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was compensation for the loss of commission which the assessee-firm would have otherwise earned, but for the breach of the terms of the agreement and brought to tax the amount of the compensation for the assessment year 1963-64 on the basis that it was a revenue receipt. The appeals of the assessee were dismissed by the AAC and the Tribunal. On the question of the assessee-firm's accounting being of mercantile system and, therefore, it should be held that the amount received by the assessee-firm should be attributable to respective years on accrual basis, the Tribunal held that the amount received could not be apportioned in the manner in which the assessee-firm sought.

On reference :

HELD: There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. The former only is treated as income, but not so with regard to the latter. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the firm itself was formed solely for the purpose of managing the company by entering into the agreement in question with the I.T.F. and there was no other business for it. If that was so, when on account of the loss of the managing agency the assessee-firm lost its business itself, the compensation received by it for that loss would be capital in nature. It is also generally held by the courts that lump sum amounts received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreements are capital in nature.

In the possible case, it was not possible to say that the agreement entered into between the assessee-firm and the I.T.F. under which the assessee-firm acquired the managing agency of the company was a contract, entered into in the ordinary course of business or a trading contract. It followed from the above discussion that the amount of compensation awarded to the assessee-firm was capital receipt and not a revenue receipt liable to tax. Though the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was capital in nature, none the less it was to be treated as "profits and gains of business" as provided under section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act and section 28(ii ) of the 1961 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B of the Indian  Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was partner in a firm - Said firm sold shares of a company together with its managing agency rights at an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share though market value of share was Rs. 46 only - Whether full value must be true value and not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset and, hence, for purposes of section 12B of 1922 Act sale price of shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. at 65 per share - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a firm. The said firm by agreement dated 7-9-1946 sold shares in a company together with the managing agency right of said company which it was holding to another firm for an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share, though the market value at the time was Rs. 46 per share. The department held that for purposes of computation of capital gains of assessee partner, the sale price of each share should be taken at Rs. 65 while the assessee contended that the market value of Rs 46 should be taken into account. The Tribunal upheld the decision of the department.

On reference:

HELD: The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether share of a partner in partnership concern is property and, thus, a capital assest within meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Assessee and ‘G’ were partners in three partnership firms which were managing agents of three mills - Assessee’s share in one concern was transferred to ‘G’ in exchange for G’s share in other concerns and additional sum of Rs. 1,00,000 - Whether transaction in question involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets and had all elements of sale and, thus, sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was assessable to tax as capital gains - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

HELD: Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

On reference : HELD: In the instant case, the Tribunal was fully justified in holding upon the materials before it that the profits arose from a transaction which was an adventure in the nature of trade. There was a singular paucity of material to establish that the intention of the assessee was to acquire the managing agency of the company. The assessee already had the managing agency of this estate even before its sale. The assessee was not able to place the agreement of managing agency which the assessee had with the previous owner. There was nothing to indicate that the sale of this estate by the said owners to another would have had the effect of terminating the assessee’s managing agency of that estate. There was nothing, therefore, to establish that the assessee had of necessity to acquire a large number of shares for the purpose of securing a capital asset, viz., the managing agency. Practically immediately after the formation of the company the assessee unloaded the majority of the shares it had acquired. Its intention was obviously not to retain these shares and the purchase itself was disassociated from any intention relevant to the acquisition of the managing agency. Had it been a case where the move for the purchase of the shares came from other parties and the assessee as and when any offer was made to it disposed of the shares, it could have justifiably inferred that the intention of the assessee was to keep these shares as an investment, that is to say, as a capital asset, the disposal of which under such circumstances not leading to any revenue income. But that the assessee, within less than a week after the acquisition of the shares started to invite offers for the sales of these shares, necessarily drove to the conclusion that even at the time of the acquisition of the shares the assessee must have had the intention of selling the shares.

The result was that the inference reached by the Tribunal that it was an adventure in the nature of trade which yielded the profit in question was amply supported by adequate material.

The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

The very fact that the board was prepared to go to such lengths and offer a much higher price than the ruling market price for the share showed their anxiety to buy the shares even at a considerable premium only with an eye to some other advantage, namely, the acquisition of the managing agency. If it were a purely business deal, there was no reason why the board should not have ensured that the purchase was made at the prevailing market rate which on that day was much lower. The bona fides of the transactions had not been challenged and, therefore, the extra rate sanctioned and the extra rate per share actually offered would, in court's opinion, clearly indicated an object other than the mere object of making profit in the way of business from the shares. To commence with, therefore, it was clear that the intention of the company was to buy the shares only with a view to acquiring the controlling interest in the NGME Ltd. and, thereby acquiring its managing agency.

The shares were purchased and sold within a short time, but that they were sold within a short time might equally be compatible with the shares being sold in the ordinary course of business as being sold on capital account because the assessee-company failed to attain its main objective, namely, the acquisition of the managing agency of the company whose shares they had been purchased. It all depended upon the circumstances established. Therefore, not much could be made of the fact that the shares were sold away within a short time after their purchase. The intention of the assessee-company in purchasing the shares. The dealings of the company with those shares after the purchase clearly indicated that their whole intention was to purchase the shares with a view to acquiring the managing agency and not with a view to dealing with those shares in the way of business. At the time of sale also, that in the case of the first lot of shares of NGME Ltd. as well as the second lot of the ACE Ltd., appropriate resolutions were passed by the board of directors and each resolution clearly explains the reason why those shares were being sold so abruptly. In the case of NGME shares it was clear that the objective failed because the then managing agents already had held more than 50 per cent of the shares of the company and it was impossible for the assessee-company to get hold of the managing agency. The main objective having failed, those shares were naturally sold off. So far as the ACE shares were concerned, it was clear not only from the resolution authorising their sale, but also from the correspondence and the alarming reports that the company was in a very bad way and acquiring the managing agency of such a company would not only reflect adversely upon the assessee, but cause them difficulty at the time of resale. Collectively, the assessee would also be involved in the misfeasance or misconduct of the erstwhile managing agents.

It is now settled law that where shares in a company are purchased as a part of the transaction of acquiring the managing agency of the company, the shares purchased for that purpose would themselves be of a capital nature and any profit or loss resulting from the purchase or sale of such shares cannot be treated as a revenue loss or profit, but must be treated as a profit or loss on capital account. The sole object and intention of the dealings in shares of the assessee in question before the Court was the acquisition of the managing agencies of the companies whose shares they had purchased and the managing agency itself would undoubtedly be a capital asset. Therefore, whatever gain accrued as a result would be on capital account.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Since the additional remuneration was based on the profit and unless the amount of profit was known, it was not possible to hold that the additional remuneration accrued at the end of the relevant accounting year. The department was not able to show that under provision of the agreement, the additional remuneration became due prior to the approval in the General Body Meeting. Therefore, it was to be held that the view of the Tribunal that the income did not accrue to the assessee on or before 31-03-1970 and the additional remuneration received by the assessee was not liable to be included for the assessment year 1970-71 appeared to be in order.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipts - Assessment year 1944-45 - By an agreement assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent of a company - During relevant accounting year managed company received offer from another company, company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as managing agents - Said offer was accepted by managed company and it asked assessee to retire - Assessee received certain amount by way of compensation towards termination of managing agency - Majority of shareholders of company ‘J’ were members of assessee-firm - Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was not casual receipt and it did arise out of business of assessee and, therefore, was not exempted under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

HELD: The instant case was not one of a change of opinion by the successor as on the findings of the Tribunal the predecessor being unaware of the nature of the receipt had no occasion to form any opinion and the case was simply one of omission or may even be one of negligence and where the successor became aware of the omission or negligence. The case of a change of opinion simpliciter occurs only where without reference to the papers on the record or books or information from any outside source the same person who formed the opinion originally, changes that opinion subsequently by process of contemplation or by mere thinking about it a second time. It followed that action under section 34 of the 1922 Act was validly taken.

The Tribunal was also justified in holding that the receipt was a revenue receipt liable to tax.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

Iqbal Ahmad and R.S. Pathak for the Applicant.

Gopal Behari for the Respondent.

8. When assessee is not disposed of any asset, then amount received cannot be regarded as compensation in respect of loss of an enduring asset. 9. Payments made in settlement of trading rights under a trading contract are trading receipts, but where a person is prevented from doing business and injury is inflicted an capital asset, then the compensation will be capital and if injury is to stock in trade, then the compensation so received will be revenue in nature. [Para 11]

Considering the above principles, in the instant case, the compensation received by the assessee from HTIPL was revenue in nature and was taxable accordingly. The reasons were (i ) the assessee was carrying on business of agencies/distributorship. It had lost only one. This business apparatus was not impaired. It was its business to deal in agencies. The impugned agency was not the sole bread earner for the assessee. It lost one trading item and continued with others, (ii ) what had been done with HTIPL was only a business arrangement. A legal structure had been erected wherein the same business of distributorship of products in question would continue but under different banner and in partnership with HTIPL in a joint venture. This was no stoppage of business as such. In place of deriving income from foreign company directly, it would derive income for the same job from HTIPL as a share in joint venture. The business apparatus, if any, had been remodelled in a different form to suit the principal i.e., the foreign company. The income flow had not been stopped from this source. So, what had been done through this resource transfer agreement was only a business arrangement or business re-organisation whereby the assessee’s income or source of income was not affected (iii) what was transferred to HTIPL was not an asset, as no such asset had been acquired by the assessee. It did not figure in the balance sheet. It was claimed by the assessee that intangible asset had been transferred. In fact, it was found that the customer data base as such was not transferred on an absolute ownership basis. The assessee was not prevented from using the same. What was done was that HTIPL would use the same database henceforth after the termination date. No legal ownership or intellectual copyright was claimed over this database. At least no evidence was placed in support of the claim that customer database was a copyright protected or intellectual property right protected asset. The transfer of employees/staff also was merely a transfer of a resource, which could have been otherwise also built up. This was again a normal business arrangement and was only a condition of joint venture. Further, arrangement with foreign company was only modified vis-a-vis the assessee. Earlier there was an arrangement of foreign company directly with assessee. Now it was again with assessee but in a joint venture. In commercial parlance, nothing had changed except form of relationship which was only a more suitable and convenient trade arrangement. Hence, transfer of employees and staff was not helpful to support the argument that there was a transfer of asset and, hence, the compensation so received was capital in nature; (iv) in fact HTIPL only received certain benefits in terms of resource transfer which would help the joint venture in running the business. [Para 12]

Those resources (employees and customer database) were not the part of balance sheet. They were also not a part of definition of ‘asset’ as given in section 2(14), ‘property’ of any kind held by an assessee. [Para 13]

As held in CIT v. National Insurance Co. Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 37 (Cal.), a property is a bundle of rights, which the owner can lawfully exercise to the exclusion of all others. He is entitled to use and enjoy it as he wishes. The property can be either corporeal or incorporeal. Though it does not always mean physical property but it does mean the right, title, interest in a property. Property also includes rights such as trade marks, copyrights, patents and even intellectual rights capable of transfer or transmission. They also include beneficial rights to a thing considered as having money value especially with reference to transfer/succession and their capacity to be injured. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the revenue had sought to make employees and customer database as same sort of right. For it to be right, there should be (i) possession (ii ) ownership to the exclusion of others; (iii ) transferability/succession (iv) some money value; (v) or created by statute. Employee could not fall under the definition of capital asset as they did not fit under the concept of ‘property’. Though the customer database had been formed over the years but had not been actually transferred to HTIPL. It had been only allowed to be used by it. [Para 15]

So far as the argument of the assessee that what had been received by the assessee was for ‘goodwill’ was concerned, those two items alone did not form goodwill. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipt - Assessment year 1942-43 and 1944-45 - Assessee-company was incorporated with an object of carrying on business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, etc. - Assessee invested certain amount with a newly incorporated sugar company with a condition that assessee was to be given managing agency in a company to be erected in future - That company, however, could not be erected - During relevant accounting years assessee sold shares acquired by it and made certain profit - Whether object of assessee in buying shares in sugar company was purely to obtain managing agency of new mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from inception no intention whatever on part of assessee to re-sell shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them - Held, yes - Whether therefore investment of money in purchase of shares was of a capital nature and profits arising out of sale of shares were of a capital nature and were not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with an object to undertake and carry on the general business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, export and import agents, clearing and forwarding or house or land agents. In 1933 another sugar company was incorporated. Managing director of the assessee entered into an agreement with the sugar company in March 1933, whereby the assessee-company was to invest Rs. 5,00,000 in the sugar company in lieu of which it was to be given the managing agency of the third mill of the sugar company not in existence at the time.

The third mill was, however, not erected and the agreement about acquiring the managing agency fell through. The managing director died in December 1940, and the assessee decided to sell all the shares in 1941. The excess amount realized on sale of these shares was taxed by the ITO, as revenue receipts, the first in the assessment year 1942-43 and the second in 1944-45. The assessee-company's contention that the excess was in the nature of capital appreciation was not accepted. This order was confirmed by the AAC and the Tribunal.

On reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The exact nature of the business which the assessee was doing was admittedly not clear from the record but it was not denied that the memorandum of association of the assessee did not authorise it to purchase and/or sell shares as dealers nor was it denied that beyond this isolated transaction of purchase and sale the assessee did not deal in shares. It seemed that the object of the assessee in buying shares was purely to obtain the managing agency of the third mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from the inception no intention whatever on the part of the assessee to re-sell the shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them. Naturally when the third mill was not erected and the object of securing the managing agency became impossible of fulfilment, the assessee withdrew the shares and sold them at a profit. After conceding that the taking up of the shares by the assessee in the sugar company was an essential part of the arrangement arrived at, the only reasonable conclusion to which the High Court should have come was that the investment of the money in the purchase of shares was of a capital nature and the profits arising out of the sale of the shares in the circumstances of this case were accretions to capital and were not liable to tax.

Accordingly, the decision of the High Court was to be reversed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.
