The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and added the entire sum of Rs. 2.80 crores received by the assessee to his unexplained income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the assessment order.

On second appeal : HELD: It was apparent from records that the consideration received by the assessee, if any, was to be bifurcated into two parts—one for relinquishment of right over the property and another for facilitating the peaceful possession to the vendee. However, the Assessing Officer considered the entire consideration received as income of the assessee without mentioning the head of income under which he assessed it, which was not proper. [Para 7.5]

Further, there were two agreements of sale—one for 3 acres and another for 7 acres dated 6-1-2006. As per these agreements of sale-cum -general power of attorney, the vendor had delivered the vacant possession of the scheduled property to the vendee. As per the provision of section 2(47 ) transfer takes place as soon as the possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of property Act, 1882. Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was allowed, in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of the managed company as a consequence of its take over by the State Government. For the assessment year 1960-61, the ITO taxed the compensation amount, treated it as a capital receipt.

On appeal, the AAC while upholding the assessment, held that only the amount actually received during the previous year should be the amount of income taxable.

On Second Appeal, the Tribunal held that entire receipt to which the provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted, was a taxable income assessable during the year in question as the assessee itself having credited the entire sum to its profit and loss account in keeping with the system of its accounting, which was mercantile, no justification vested with the AAC to change it.

On reference :

HELD: Since a managing agency is a creature of contract and since its formation, operation and termination are all to be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act, in so far as they apply, there was no force in the contention that a managing agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other manner. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the compensation amount was taxable profit within the meaning of section 10(5A).

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: II. Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether when assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to carrying on of business in agencies - Held, yes - Assessee-company had income from contracts and commission from various parties - It was also distributor of products of a foreign company for 22 years - A joint venture - company HTIPL was formed to manufacture and market products of said foreign company in India - Under an agreement, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets such as trained manpower, personal dealings, list of customers, etc., and in turn it had received certain amount by way of compensation, which was claimed by the assessee as consideration for ‘goodwill’, being capital receipt not taxable - Whether since assessee continued to do same line of business, i.e., distributorship of other companies with same name, fame, place and approach even after formation of joint venture, it could not be said that assessee had received compensation for sale of ‘goodwill’ - Held, yes - Whether what assessee had got in terms of compensation was a normal incidence of business arising due to its re-organisation and formation of a joint venture and, thus, what assessee had received was of revenue character and was taxable accordingly - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was a distributor of products of foreign company for last 22 years. A joint venture company HTIPL, consisting of the assessee and the foreign company, was formed to manufacture the products of foreign company in India and also to market products of the foreign company manufactured abroad. Under an agreement entered into between the assessee and company HTIPL, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets like trained manpower personnel dealing with said products in India and detailed list of customers of said products and introduce HTIPL to all the customers both in public and private sectors for sale of said products. In view of transfer of above intangible assets, the assessee received certain compensation from HTIPL. The assessee treated that sum as a consideration for transfer of goodwill and offered same for taxation as long term capital gains. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had income from service contracts and commission from various parties; that it was a compensation received on termination of managing agency; that the assessee was carrying on several managing agencies and it gave up only one and continued with other; that the business structure of the assessee did not suffer and it was free to carry on the trade with other agencies; that the cancellation and compensation, therefore, was merely a normal incidence of business; and that the income of the assessee had increased in the subsequent years. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the amount received by the assessee was revenue receipt taxable in its hands. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had parted with a part of its apparatus to a joint venture and for the loss so suffered it had received compensation. He directed the Assessing Officer to tax the receipt as capital receipt.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: A careful consideration of the case laws indicated following principles :

1. When a payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of contract which does not affect the trading structure of the recipient’s business nor deprive the assessee from source of income, then termination of contract is only a normal incidence of business.

2. Where trading structure of the assessee is impaired or cancellation results in loss of sources of income, payment to compensate such loss of source is capital.

3. A source of income may be a capital structure of one assessee. But where the assessee is dealing in several such sources/assets, then it becomes a stock in trade. Loss of one such source/asset will be a loss of capital if the assessee is dealing only in one but will be revenue if it is dealing in many such sources/assets as stock in trade.

4. When assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to the carrying on of the business in agencies. Where there is a modification in the terms of any one of such agencies, it will again be a normal incidence of business.

5. There is no immutable principle that compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital.

6. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated for loss of goodwill, is prima facie of the nature of capital receipt.

7. Manner of payment of compensation is not material. Whether capital is repaid in instalments or is paid in lump sum, it will not affect the basic nature of receipt in the hands of the recipient.

8. When assessee is not disposed of any asset, then amount received cannot be regarded as compensation in respect of loss of an enduring asset.

FACT: The assessee-company was appointed as sales agent and distributor for certain silicon products produced by the GE group. Later on the said agency and its distributorship were terminated by the GE group and the assessee paid certain sum as compensation was for said termination. The assessee claimed said receipt as a capital receipt. The Assessing Officer rejected its claim and treated the same as its business receipt/income on the ground that the GE group had control and management of the assessee-group and that the assessee was non-exclusive agent and distributor of the GE group. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The agency and distributorship agreements were entered into on 1-5-1991 and 31-10-1995, respectively, and were terminated vide agreements dated 1-7-1996 with retrospective effect from 31-10-1995 and 3-12-1995, respectively. As on the date of the termination of the agreement the GE group was holding 50 per cent shareholding of the company, while the other 50 per cent of the shares were held by 'F' Company, and, hence, it could not be presumed that the GE group had the control over the management of the assessee-company. [Para 14]

A perusal of the agency as well as distributorship agreements showed that the assessee was the non-exclusive agent and distributor of the GE group, but was not an agent simplicitor. It was not merely an intermediary between the principal and its customers but was expected to employ staff; promote the sale and also to maintain warehousing facility. Thus, it was carrying on the business of GE by creating its own infrastructure and for the said purpose it had made huge financial commitments; the assessee was not entitled to act on its own behalf and for itself in respect of the goods entrusted to it. Thus, there was a relationship of agency with GE and not on principal-to-principal basis, as contended by the assessee. As regards the assessee's contentions that since it had to make huge financial commitments, it was acting as a principal, it was found that all the expenses incurred by the agent in connection with the fulfilment of its obligations [like travel, correspondence, telephone, telecopy and the like] had been taken into account while fixing the rate of commission at 6 per cent on all the sales of the products initiated by the agent. Thus, it could not be said that the assessee was acting as the principal agent of GE. [Para 15]

Thus, it could be seen that the amount received for termination of agency was a taxable receipt. However, the nature of the receipt is to be seen before bringing it to tax under section 28(ii)(c ). If the receipt is on termination of the agreements of agency and distributorship simplicitor, the compensation received is for the loss of revenue and, hence, a revenue receipt. In such a case, the agent/distributor can carry on business of a similar nature with any other principal. But if there is a restrictive covenant to deal with similar business, then all the agreements have to be considered in unison and not in isolation. By the restrictive covenant the assessee is not only losing the revenue but is also losing the revenue-generating source. As held by the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Ambadi Enterprises Ltd. [2004] 267 ITR 702/139 Taxman 96, one test for ascertaining as to whether what had received was a capital receipt or a revenue receipt is to find out whether the assessee had snapped its link with the profit making apparatus that had been transferred. [Para 16]

on the business of managing agency, but it was clear that the source of the receipt was the managing agency business itself. It could not, therefore, be said that the receipt was income from a new and independent source. The High Court was right in holding that in enacting sub-section (5A) the legislature was concerned only with providing a head under which the receipt which has been deemed to be income could be brought to tax and was not concerned with creating a new source for that deemed income. The Bombay High Court, in CIT v. Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Private Ltd. [1967] 65 ITR 50 and the Madras High Court in R.V. Lakshmiah Naidu and Co. v. CIT [1963] 48 ITR 661 have both held that the compensation paid for termination of a managing agency business is a payment in relation to said business and, therefore, the previous year relevant to that receipt would be the same as the previous year for the managing agency business itself. These two decisions state the law on the point correctly.

Thus, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The transfer of right or relinquishment of part and parcel of business undertaking of the assessee is nothing but transfer of capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14). Any profit arising from the transfer of capital asset must be chargeable under the head 'capital gain'. The word 'transfer' has been defined in section 2(47). [Para 33] From the definition under section 2(47), it is clear that the word 'transfer' is inclusive of definition, which inter alia provides 6 situations under which there can be transfer in relation to the capital asset. Relinquishment of any rights in the capital asset is one of the situation enumerated in section 2(47). The word 'relinquishment' denotes that relinquishment should be only in the case of capital asset with reference to which the word 'transfer' has been defined. The right of the assessee over the landed property which was part and parcel of the business undertaking of the assessee is a capital asset. The moment assessee losses the right attached to a part of the business undertaking of the assessee, there is relinquishment of right over the said property. The relinquishment of assets or extinguishment of any right in it which may not amount to a sale can also be considered as a transfer. Therefore, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are not acceptable that there is no transfer under section 45 and the assessee has done only business transaction. Accordingly, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue are reversed and it is held that the income accrued to the assessee out of relinquishment of right over the property is to be chargeable under section 45 and computation of capital gain has to be done in accordance with section 48. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to compute the income under the head capital gain on relinquishment of right over the impugned landed property. [Para 34]

In the result, assessee's appeal is partly allowed. [Para 35]

Section 28(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee, who was one of partners of managing agency firm and was director of managed company, received his share of compensation from managed company in terms of arbitration award for premature termination of managing agency agreement - Assessee claimed amount so received to be capital receipt and hence not liable to tax - Whether amount in question was capital receipt and not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee company was managing agents of various companies including one 'G', in which assessee held a large block of shares - In 1951, board of directors of 'G' decided to terminate agency against payment of certain amount to assessee - Whether termination of managing agency in question had resulted in destruction of source of in come of assessee and, thus, amount received by assessee was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as – Assessment year 1952-53 – Assessee was acting as managing agents for 'N' - Subsequently, agreement was terminated when Government of State of Madras in exercise of powers conferred upon it by Electrical Undertakings Acquisition Act, 1949, compulsorily acquired undertaking of that company, and assessee was paid as compensation for premature termination of its agency - The ITO observed that assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end, assessee still continued as 'managing agents of other companies' and therefore receipt was to be considered as revenue - Whether such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of assessee, was a capital receipt, therefore, same was not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

Section 28(i)  of the Income-tax Act 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee firm was agent of ‘HML’ - It assigned its agency rights to ‘P’ which agreed to pay part of its profits subject to minimum sum per annum - Subsequently, by another agreement, assessee transferred its rights under assignments to ‘O’ for lump sum consideration - Whether by second agreement assessee had parted with its profits making apparatus and, therefore, amount recived by it from ‘O’ was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business Income - Compensation (Applicability of) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee company had joined hands with company DE to form a new venture in name and style of AMPL vide agreement - Assessee’s stake in said joint venture reached at 49 per cent - Balance 51 per cent equity in said joint venture remained with DE - Assessee and DE entered into an agreement wherein latter entity transferred its shareholding in AMPL to a wholly owned assessee’s subsidiary for US $ 1 and further agreed to pay it an amount of US $ 10 million as compensation for erosion in value of its investment in AMPL - Compensation received by assessee from DE was assessed under head business income under section 28(ii)(b) - It was noted that neither agreement clause between assessee and DE nor assessment order had proved assessee to be a managing agency in foregoing terms - Whether once assessee was not managing agency in foregoing terms, impugned compensation was not assessable under section 28(ii)(b) - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipts - Assessment year 1944-45 - By an agreement assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent of a company - During relevant accounting year managed company received offer from another company, company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as managing agents - Said offer was accepted by managed company and it asked assessee to retire - Assessee received certain amount by way of compensation towards termination of managing agency - Majority of shareholders of company ‘J’ were members of assessee-firm - Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was not casual receipt and it did arise out of business of assessee and, therefore, was not exempted under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was managing agent of a company receiving commission at rate of 20 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Subsequently, by a resolution managed company resolved that as per agreement between parties assessee, in consideration of managed company paying a lump sum amount as compensation for releasing it from obligation to pay commission at rate of 20 percent, should accept as remuneration for rest of period of managing agency agreement 10 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Whether lump sum amount in question was received by assessee as compensation for deterioration or injury to managing agency by reason of release of its rights to get higher remuneration and therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 28(ii)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether amount received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreement are capital in nature - Held, yes - ‘ITF’ was managing agent of a company - Under an agreement, it transferred managing agency to assessee firm - Due to some disputes arose subsequently between assessee and ‘ITF’, assessee had to resign from office of managing agency and in arbitration proceedings, received damages towards compensation for loss of managing agency commission - Whether compensation received by assessee was capital receipt and not revenue receipt - Held, yes - Whether, however, said amount would be treated as ‘profits and gains of business’ under section 28(ii) of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and compensation was awarded to assessee on basis of remuneration as having accrued to it during earlier five assessment years, compensation must be deemed to have accrued to assessee during said years - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipt - Assessment year 1942-43 and 1944-45 - Assessee-company was incorporated with an object of carrying on business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, etc. - Assessee invested certain amount with a newly incorporated sugar company with a condition that assessee was to be given managing agency in a company to be erected in future - That company, however, could not be erected - During relevant accounting years assessee sold shares acquired by it and made certain profit - Whether object of assessee in buying shares in sugar company was purely to obtain managing agency of new mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from inception no intention whatever on part of assessee to re-sell shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them - Held, yes - Whether therefore investment of money in purchase of shares was of a capital nature and profits arising out of sale of shares were of a capital nature and were not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 28(i) sections 45 and 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation (Termination of agency) - Assessment year 2001-02 - 'Sea Land-India' was clearing and forwarding agent of 'Sea Land-USA' - Assessee was sub-agent of 'Sea Land-India' - As business of 'Sea Land-USA' was taken over by 'AP mollar', 'Sea Land-USA' terminated agency agreement with 'Sea Land-India' and 'Sea land-India' terminated sub-agency agreement with assessee - 'AP mollar' appointed 'Maersk' and 'Maersk' purchased shipping sub-agency business of assessee - Assessee offered consideration received by it on transfer of same as capital gains and claimed exemption under section 54EC - Assessing Officer completed assessment - Commissioner sought to revise assessment order on ground that amount was received in connection with termination of agency as stipulated in section 28(ii)(c) and exemption under section 54EC could not be claimed - Whether assessee was a recipient of impugned amount for holding an agency in India for activities relating to business of 'Sea Land-India' and it was received only in connection with termination of agency, and, therefore, Commissioner was justified in invoking section 263 - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where consideration received by assessee was only towards termination of agency, income received by assessee was to be treated as business income and not as capital gain

Section 28(ii), read with sections 45 and 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee received certain amount from a company which he claimed as professional goodwill - Assessing Officer held that said amount was received by assessee on account of relinquishment of his rights in management of a company and, therefore, was to be taxed under section 28(ii)(a) - Whether since Assessing Officer had not established that assessee was person who was managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of company, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed - Held, yes - Whether even, assuming that amount received by assessee was relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, cost of any such managerial right being indeterminate, provisions relating to computation of capital gain were not workable and, consequently, amount could not be taxed under section 45 also - Held, yes [Para 7.4] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : For invoking section 28(ii)(a) it has to be established whether amount due or received is against termination of any right which an assessee was enjoying by managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of an Indian company; where Assessing Officer did not record such finding, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed

Section 28(ii)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee-company under an agreement with an English company was appointed as a sole agent in regard to management of estates of English company in India - During relevant assessment year, that agency was terminated and certain sum was paid by way of compensation to assessee - Whether compensation amount was taxable in view of provisions of section 28(ii)(e) - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee was appointed administrator of certain temples and its properties on certain land - Assessee sold some portion of leasehold land and claimed that as according to lease deed an obligation was created on him for proper maintenance and upkeep of temple including conduct of pooja, etc., and since entire sale amount was utilised for purpose of temple, no capital gains was exigible -Whether Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting assessee’s claim - Held, yes

Section 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Transfer (AOP, in case of) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee entered into a MOU with one 'PK', for jointly developing property, whereby assessee agreed to provide land as capital contribution - It was observed that at time of MOU, assessee was yet to acquire land from original vendor, hence it was not a case of pure development agreement - Further, it was observed that intention of assessee was to reap and share in profit on eventual sale of flats to be constructed and not to transfer of property as such - However, owing to certain disputes, a settlement was arrived at amongst parties according to which assessee was to receive Rs. 14 crores for foregoing their rights and Rs. 6 crores for conveying property - While filing return, assessee declared long-term capital gain only on sum of Rs. 6 crores - However, Assessing Officer considered entire sum of Rs. 20 crores as taxable under head capital gains - Whether since two parties had voluntarily combined for a common purpose and their main objectives were to produce profit, essential conditions for forming an AOP were satisfied - Held, yes - Whether settlement deed practically put an end to AOP and transfer of title in land was nothing but distribution of capital assets of AOP on its dissolution - Held, yes - Whether thus addition of Rs. 14 crores made under head capital gain was incorrect - Held, yes [Paras 25, 27  32] [In favour of assessee]IT: Settlement amount received by assessee for foregoing its rights upon termination of AOP entered into by assessee for jointly developing property, whereby assessee agreed to provide land as capital contribution, was not taxable as settlement deed practically put an end to AOP and transfer of title in land was distribution of capital assets of AOP on its dissolution

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1944-45 - Appellant company appointed a firm as its managing agent for 20 years at 2½ per cent commission - Though firm was not guilty of negligence, laches, fraud or inefficience, appellant terminated managing agency after two years and for this paid certain amount to said firm as compensation - Appellant, however, appointed another managing agent at 2 per cent commission - Whether disbursement of compensation to outgoing managing agent was of capital nature and was, therefore, not deductible expenditure - Held, yes

SECTION 28(ii)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BUSINESS INCOME-COM-
PENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF AGENCY-ASSESSEE-COMPANY WAS SELLING PRODUCTS OF AND LOOKING AFTER INTERESTS OF AN AMERICAN COMPANY FOR ABOUT 19 YEARS-AMERICAN COMPANY FLOATED A NEW COMPANY TO WHICH ASSESSEE-COMPANY WAS ASKED BY AMERICAN COMPANY TO ASSIGN ALL RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES AND IN CONSIDERATION OF SUCH ASSIGNMENT, ASSESSEE WAS PAID A CERTAIN SUM BY AMERICAN COMPANY-ASSESSEE CLAIMED THAT 
PART OF SUCH SUM WAS ON ACCOUNT OF GOODWILL AND NOT TAXABLE-
WHETHER PAYMENT CLAIMED BY ASSESSEE TO HAVE BEEN RECEIVED ON 
ACCOUNT OF GOODWILL WAS IN FACT COMPENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF 
AGENCY AND WAS TAXABLE UNDER SECTION 28(ii)(c)-HELD, YES

Section 12B(1) of the indian income-tax act, 1922 [corresponding to section 45 of the income-tax act, 1961]-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessment year 1962-63-Assessee retired from firm and as per terms of settlement received his sharb in value of firm's net assets representing difference between their book value and market value-Whether impugned receipt was not assessable as capital gains since the transaction did not involve any element of sale or extinguishment of rights-Held, on facts, yes

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B of the Indian  Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was partner in a firm - Said firm sold shares of a company together with its managing agency rights at an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share though market value of share was Rs. 46 only - Whether full value must be true value and not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset and, hence, for purposes of section 12B of 1922 Act sale price of shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. at 65 per share - Held, yes

u Section 4 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Compensation received for destruction or sterilisation of capital asset which produced income would be capital receipt
ITO v. Oberoi Hotels (I) Ltd. [1989] 33 TTJ (Cal.) 420
The assessee, a limited company, had acquired certain skills and experience in managing big hotels in different countries of the world. Its Memorandum of Association authorised it not only to purchase and run hotels on its own account but also to operate, manage or administer hotels belonging to others for a fee. During the relevant previous year, the assessee was operating hotels belonging to others for a fee in several places. By an agreement dated 2-11-1970, the assessee agreed to operate a hotel at Singapore. Later, however, due to change of management of the hotel it gave up its right to operate the said hotel and received certain amount as compensation.
Held that these rights constituted the profit-earning apparatus of the assessee and so the compensation was received for the destruction or sterilisation of that capital asset. Hence the compensation received by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1987-88 - Whether amount received by assessee-lessee to give vacant possession of premises as per agreement with lessor, could be charged to tax as capital gains under section 45 - Held, no

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as (General) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee holding GPA for certain persons sold certain immovable property belonging to them during relevant assessment year - He did not offer capital gains tax on said transaction contending that he had executed sale deed as a GPA holder only, and that he had not received any amount from transaction - Whether since assessee was not owner of property, capital gain could not be brought to tax in his hand - Held, yes [Para 6][In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Capital gain would arise in hands of owners of property and not GPA holder

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Where the assessee contributed certain land as capital in a firm and the Tribunal held that there was no transfer in the absence of registration of conveyance in that regard and no capital gain arose from the transaction, it was held that no question of law arose from Tribunal's order

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1948-49 to 1950-51 - Assessee had acted as agents and distributors of explosives manufactured by principal company but without a written agreement - Subsequently, principal company terminated agency and paid Compensation to assessee - Assessee claimed exemption contending that said amount was compensation for termination of agency and for agreeing to refrain from carrying on in future substantive business in explosives - Whether circumstances that agency was determinable at will of principal company which maintained a large staff at their expense justified inference that upon cancellation of agency, assessee's business organization was not substantially impaired - Held, yes - Whether since cancellation of contract of agency did not affect profit-making structure of assessee, nor did it involve a loss of an enduring trading asset, rather it merely deprived assessee of a trading avenue, leaving it free to devote its energies after cancellation to carry on rest of business, compensation in question did not represent price paid for loss of a capital asset - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee's claim was to be disallowed - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation for termination of agency, etc. - Assessment year 1970-71 - Assessee was working as consultant of a company on 10 years contract and receiving annual remuneration - When its services were terminated after 5 years, it received lump sum payment as compensation as per mutual agreement - Revenue contended that amount received was revenue receipt and even if held to be capital, it was assessable under section 28(ii)(c) - Whether since cancellation of contract had impaired profit-making trading structure/asset of assessee which had resulted in loss of source of income to assessee and also considering unexpired period which was quite long, payment made was a capital asset/receipt - Held, yes - Whether pre-requisite for applicability of section 28(ii)(c) is that it must be an agency agreement - Held, yes - In instant case, Tribunal recorded a finding that agreement was purely one of consultancy service and what was contemplated in agreement was between principal and principal and there was no agency agreement - Whether, therefore, compensation received by assessee on termination of agreement was not taxable even under provisions of section 28(ii)(c) - Held, yes

Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business loss - Allowable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee was a dealer in shares and also carried on business of acquiring managing agencies - It purchased shares of a company to acquire managing agency of that company - Assessee incurred loss when it sold part of the shares and claimed it as revenue loss - Tribunal found as a fact that share purchased by assessee-company, although it was dealer in shares did not become its stock-in-trade - Whether acquisition of managing agency was an acquisition of a capital asset - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, loss incurred on sale of shares was of capital nature - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable (Capital receipt v. revenue receipt) - Whether where, assessee had left institution after new members were elected as managing committee and it was not a case of life time appointment of assessee, sum received by assessee for relinquishing secretaryship of an educational society could not be treated as capital receipt since in forgoing secretaryship, there was no capital asset which had been transferred by assessee - Held, yes [Paras 4 and 5][In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX: Sum received by assessee for relinquishing secretaryship of an educational society could not be treated as capital receipt since in forgoing life membership or secretaryship, there was no capital asset which had been transferred by assessee

Section  45,  read with section  147,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Capital gains  -  Chargeable as  (Reassessment) - Assessment year  2016-17  - Assessee filed her return of income for relevant year - Assessing Officer reopened case of assessee on ground that she had not declared capital gain arising from an alleged Joint Development Agreement (JDA) - Accordingly, he made addition to income of assessee - It was noted that addition sustained by Commissioner (Appeals) was premised entirely on a document presumed to be a JDA - However, on perusal of said document, it was found that it was merely a General Power of Attorney (GPA), executed by four joint owners of a house property in favour of assessee - It did not evidence transfer of any capital asset within meaning of section 45 resulting in any capital gain in hands of assessee - Further, it was undisputed that assessee was not owner of land - Whether, in absence of ownership of a capital asset, no capital gain could arise in hands of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, a GPA issued in favour of assessee did not constitute transfer, nor could it be treated as a JDA and thus, very foundation of addition failed - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Assessing Officer was to be directed to delete addition sustained by Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Casual and non-recurring receipts -  Whether where any amount of capital gain is not taxable as capital gain for any reason, that amount cannot be treated as a casual and non-recurring receipt under section 10(3) - Held, yes

facts.text:
The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

The assessee-company had held two-third shares of company A and was also its managing agent. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold all these shares to company B at a profit of Rs. 3,14,519 and claimed that the surplus realised was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains. The ITO took the view that the assessee had acquired these shares to procure the managing agency and it had, in fact, carried on multifarious activities in various lines including banking, financing of various companies as well as managing agency. He, accordingly, held that the entire profit from the sale of these shares represented business profit. On appeal, the AAC held that a major portion of the sale proceeds was relatable to the assessee's right to the managing agency which passed along with the shares. He further held that in view of the numerous agencies which the assessee carried on, this transaction involving the giving up of the managing agency was of a revenue nature. Consequently, the AAC upheld the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the assessee had parted with an asset of enduring nature and observed that nothing had been received by the assessee as price for its foregoing managing agency rights. What it had legally received was the value of the shares though it could not be denied that it received a higher value because the shares carried with it the managing agency rights. Further, the Tribunal was of the view that it was concerned with the true and legal realisation resulting from the transaction which appeared to be that of the sale of shares and that the shares were not the assessee's stock-in- trade It, accordingly, held that the impugned profit was liable to be taxed as capital gains and not as revenue gains.

On reference:

The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee was a managing agent of a company F. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company and to procure that principal company 'M' also agreed to compensate the assessee for loss of office after it submitted its resignation.

Subsequently, the assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of the company. Accordingly, the assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office. In the proceedings for the relevant assessment year the ITO, included this amount in the assessee's taxable income. On appeal the AAC modified the assessment holding that the sum received by the assessee as compensation for surrendering the managing agency, which was to enure for five years more, and which in normal course might have continued for another term of twenty years, was a capital receipt. On further appeals Tribunal confirmed the order of the AAC. On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee-company entered into an agreement with a firm. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to manufacture ‘bidies’ as per the specifications, such as shape, size, quality and standard, of the firm. The assessee was also free to manufacture bidies for any person, firm or company. It was also provided that the assessee should purchase its own raw materials at its own discretion but, however, the wrapping paper and printed label bearing firm’s trade-mark were to be supplied by the firm. The price was to be fixed mutually from time to time but in no case it was to exceed the manufacturing cost plus 10 per cent profit thereon. Thereafter, another agreement was entered into between the assessee and the firm by which both the parties agreed to terminate mutually the earlier agreement. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to sell and the firm agreed to purchase running business of the assessee. As a consideration for the purchase of the bidi manufacturing business the firm was to pay to the assessee as ‘slump price’ of Rs. 5 lakhs. The IAC held that the assessee was holding an agency and the aforesaid amount received by the assessee was an amount towards termination of this agency, and, therefore, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held it as capital gain and directed the IAC to work out the taxable capital gains in accordance with the relevant provisions.

On appeal:

An incorporated limited liability company 'L' had a subscribed capital consisting of preference shares, ordinary shares and deferred shares. The assessee-company became the managing agents of said company under an agreement. Subsequently, the assessee acquired its ordinary shares and preference shares. On 10-10-1947, the assessee made a further acquisition of some deferred shares. Thereafter, the assessee agreed to make over its managing agency to 'K'. The terms included that 'K' should take over the deferred shares and also pay the assessee a further sum of certain amount as compensation for loss of future remuneration to the assessee as managing agent. The assessee sold during the relevant assessment year, the ordinary and preference shares which resulted in a loss. After adjusting this loss on the extra amount received on the sale of deferred shares, there was a net profit. The assessee did not return the amount as its income for the year on the ground that it was a capital receipt. The revenue disagreed and brought the amount to tax treating it as income. The Tribunal concurred with that view. It also declined to a make a reference.

On application under section 66(2):

There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

The assessees were engaged in business as merchants and agents of various companies having branch officer in different parts of India. Assessees’ agency with two of the Companies was terminated in the end of previous assessment year. During the assessment year under consideration i.e. 1929-30, assessee received from one of the companies whose agency had been terminated a sum as full compensation for cessation of the agency. However another company also panel certain sum as compensation for the loss of officer as agent to the Company. The quotations were accepted on both sides as correctly expressing the nature of the transactions. While computing the assessable income of assessee, ITO took abovementioned receipts as profits and gains from business and also allowed certain deductions thereform in respect of compensation paid to various employees. Consequently the balances were included in the total income. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner and Commissioner confirmed the assessment. On further appeal, High Court held that sums in question were not incomes, profits or gains with in meaning of Act at all. In one part of its judgment the High Court seemed to hold that "compensation for loss of these agencies is a receipt in respect of a capital asset in the nature of goodwill. In another part of the judgment the payment seemed to be regarded as in the nature of compensation in lieu of notice.

On revenue’s appeal to the Privy Council :

The assessee-company had entered into an Agreement for Distribution, Manufacturing and Agency of products (ADMA 1997) with one BM Germany in 1997, by virtue of which the assessee acquired right to carry on above business, earlier carried out by BM Germany and its subsidiary. In 2004 RDG had acquired BM group all over the world and in the same year RDG unilaterally terminated certain obligations under 1997 agreement, which was challenged by the assessee in UK court and thereafter assessee and RDG entered into out of court settlement as per which the assessee and RDG mutually agreed to terminate the (ADMA 1997) and RDG paid compensation to assessee.

Said compensation was offered to tax under head 'Capital gain' by assessee contending that as it had transferred entire business and its rights under the agreement had been terminated, the amount received in consideration thereof was assessable as capital gain.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to hold that the proceeds received by the assessee company from RDG on account of termination of agency and distribution of products in India fell under the provisions of section 28(ii)(c) read with section 28(va)(a).

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was a distributor of products of foreign company for last 22 years. A joint venture company HTIPL, consisting of the assessee and the foreign company, was formed to manufacture the products of foreign company in India and also to market products of the foreign company manufactured abroad. Under an agreement entered into between the assessee and company HTIPL, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets like trained manpower personnel dealing with said products in India and detailed list of customers of said products and introduce HTIPL to all the customers both in public and private sectors for sale of said products. In view of transfer of above intangible assets, the assessee received certain compensation from HTIPL. The assessee treated that sum as a consideration for transfer of goodwill and offered same for taxation as long term capital gains. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had income from service contracts and commission from various parties; that it was a compensation received on termination of managing agency; that the assessee was carrying on several managing agencies and it gave up only one and continued with other; that the business structure of the assessee did not suffer and it was free to carry on the trade with other agencies; that the cancellation and compensation, therefore, was merely a normal incidence of business; and that the income of the assessee had increased in the subsequent years. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the amount received by the assessee was revenue receipt taxable in its hands. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had parted with a part of its apparatus to a joint venture and for the loss so suffered it had received compensation. He directed the Assessing Officer to tax the receipt as capital receipt.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee owned coal mines. Later, he along with other family members incorporated a company. By an agreement, the assessee transferred the management of entire business of working his collieries and mines to the company for consideration of royalty. The company also agreed to take over all the business liability of the assessee by allotting shares of the equivalent net value. The ITO was of the opinion that by the transfer of the management of the mines to the company the assessee made a capital gain.

On appeal, the Appellate Commissioner upheld the order of ITO but reduced the amount of capital gain.

On further appeal, though the Tribunal held that the company would have been required to pay higher amount of royalty if it had not paid certain amount on account of goodwill. The Tribunal, thus, opined that the assessee had capitalised a part of his income. It accordingly, concluded that the amount paid to assessee was liable to be taxed at the rates appropriate to 'income' and not at the rates appropriate to capital gain.

On reference:

The assessee vacated its business premises and received Rs. 38,300 from the vendee of the landlord as consideration for vacating the premises. The ITO treated the receipt as a trading receipt. The assessee also filed an appeal questioning the correctness of the restoration of the matter to the ITO for making the assessment of possible capital gains. On reference:

On reference :

On reference :

During the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company was operating, managing or administering many hotels belonging to others for a fee, as it had acquired certain skills and experience in managing big hotels in different countries of the world. The memorandum of association of the assessee-company authorised it not only to purchase and run hotels on its own account, but also to operate, manage or administer hotels belonging to others for a fee. The assessee-company agreed to operate the ‘S' hotel in Singapore in terms of an agreement and also provided supervisory services in the form of providing technical staff. In return, the assessee-company was to receive certain fee called 'management fee' which was calculated on the basis of gross operating profits as laid down in the agreement. This agreement was to run for an initial period of 10 years, but the assessee had option to ask for renewal of the said agreement for two further periods of 10 years each by mutual agreement. In 1975, however, the 'S' hotel/company went into liquidation and a receiver was appointed to take charge of its undertaking and properties. As the receiver wanted to sell the hotel to a third party, it entered into a supplemental agreement with the assessee in pursuance of which the assessee-company gave up its valuable rights to operate, manage or administer the 'S' hotel in consideration of a lump-sum payment.

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company received the aforesaid consideration amount and claimed it to be a capital receipt because the assessee received the same in consideration of giving up a capital asset.

The ITO held that in the case of the assessee-company, the contract to manage and administer 'S' hotel was entered into in the ordinary course of business and, therefore, the compensation received for termination of such agreement was nothing but a revenue receipt. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) was of the view that the assessee's business was not to buy and sell hotel operation agreements and as long as the agreements to manage and administer hotels which were long-term agreements were in force, the assessee-company could expect such agreements to yield income year after year and so each of the agreements constituted a source of the assessee-company's income. Therefore, he held that the receipt of compensation from the receiver of the 'S' hotel/company was nothing but a capital receipt. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference:

The assessee was carrying on sub-broking business with 'S' and had about 1800 clients. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer taxed the sum of Rs. 1.11 crores under section 28(ii)(c) by treating the same as compensation for termination of agency.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that relationship between 'S' and the assessee was on principal to principal basis and the termination of the agreement between 'S' and the assessee was termination of agreement of two principals. He held that the amount in question was paid by 'S' as compensation for trading infrastructure of business of the assessee, and accordingly, same was to be treated as capital receipt. Accordingly, he directed the Assessing Officer to assess income under the head 'Income from capital gain' and allow exemption under section 54EC to the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee claimed that sum as a receipt of casual non-recurring nature not arising from business or the exercise of a profession, vocation or occupation and so exempt under section 4(3)(vii)of the 1922 Act. On reference, the Commissioner also took the same view which was taken by the ITO.

The managing partner ‘AP’ of the assessee-firm was granted on lease a piece of land. He constructed certain buildings on this land and leased out the same to ‘V’ (Voltas Ltd.) on monthly rent. Therefore, the Tribunal held that capital gains would also have to be assessed to tax as transfer of capital asset took place.

On reference :

The assessee owned ten fully-paid shares of the said society, by virtue of which it owned the first floor of said properly admeasuring 3,200 sq. ft. Sometime during the relevant previous year, i.e., calendar year 1983 corresponding to the assessment year 1984-85, the assessee thought of transferring the first floor to the trustees of eight trusts. The trustees of these trusts insisted on having vacant possession of the first floor and agreed to pay Rs. 55 lakhs in this regard. B y an agreement dated 10-5-1983, entered into between the assessee and CPC, it was agreed that CPC would vacate 2,200 sq. ft. of the first floor allotted to it under the agreement dated 1-11-1974 in consideration of Rs. 37 lakhs by way of compensation. On second appeal:

The assessee-company carrying on business In a rented premises agreed to surrender the leasehold rights under an agreement under which it was to be provided with an alternative accommodation. On reference :

The assessee-firm was appointed as the managing agents of the K Mills Ltd. under a managing agency agreement entered into in 1935. It was common ground that the terms of the agreement were fulfilled and that the resignation of the assessee-firm was also accepted by the board of directors of the K Mills Ltd. In the return of the assessee for the calendar year relevant to the assessment year 1955-56, the above receipt of Rs. 2,24,000 was not returned as part of the income. These objections were overruled. On the first question, the departmental authorities and the Tribunal came to the conclusion that section 10(5A) applied and that the amount was taxable. On the second question, the ITO was of the view that the previous year for a business "which had no books of account which were not made up to profit and loss account for any particular period" should be the financial year. On reference :

The assessee had taken a factory premises on lease from the lessor as per lease agreement and was paying rent thereof from year to year. The lessor sold the said premises to another person. During the Assessment year 1987-88, the assessee claimed that the amount received from the lessor was not chargeable to tax, as the same was to be treated as capital receipt in its hands.
