On second appeal:

The assessee was one of the two managing directors of a private limited company T. Ltd. The other managing director was one 'P'. Out of the total of 20 shares of Rs. 100 each, the assessee held nine shares and his son one share, the remaining shares being held by 'P', his wife and cousin. This company was the managing agent of a public limited company A Ltd. Both these companies had been incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The public limited company had issued 11,986 shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each, out of which the assessee held, 1,674 shares. The assessee and his son transferred ten shares in T. Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin or their nominees for Rs. 3,50,000 as also 4,165 shares in the A Ltd.

By the transfer two sets of shares the assessee made a profit of Rs. 3,14,100 in respect of nine shares and another sum of Rs. 72,515 in respect of 1,674 shares. These two amounts were brought to tax for the assessment year 1956-57 treating them as income and liable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act. Both the ITO as well as the AAC repelled the assessee's contention that the receipts were in the nature of capital assets by sale of the shares. The AAC accepted the view that the amounts in excess of the book value of the shares transferred by the assesses were in the nature of inducement to him or compensation for giving up the management.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was neither a manager nor a managing agent of an Indian company within the meaning of section 2(9A) of the Indian Companies Act and that the provisions of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act were, therefore, not applicable to the two amounts.

The Tribunal also considered the further question whether the two amounts could be regarded as compensation for loss of management rights in A. Ltd. and came to the conclusion that there was no material to hold that the profit represented such compensation.

On reference:

The assessee was appointed as business consultant of a company and as per agreement, it was entitled to a monthly remuneration for 10 years contract period. After 5 years its services were terminated. As per mutual agreement, the assessee agreed for a compensation of Rs. 60,000 in lieu of Rs. 1,45,500 which was payable otherwise. The Assessing Officer held that it was a capital receipt and at the same time taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. Before the Tribunal, the revenue argued that the amount was a revenue receipt. At the same time, it was also contended that even if it was assessed as a capital receipt, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). The Tribunal held that the termination of the agreement affected the business structure of the assessee’s business and the unexpired period of the agreement was sufficiently long and so, it could be inferred that the compensation amount paid was a capital receipt. The Tribunal further held that the agreement originally entered into was not an agency agreement at all but an agreement entered into purely for rendering consultancy services and the agreement was between principal and principal. Therefore, the amount was not taxable even under section 28(ii)( c).

On reference:

The assessee entered into a MOU with others, for jointly developing property, whereby assessee agreed to provide land as capital contribution. It was observed that at time of MOU, the assessee was yet to acquire land from original vendor; hence it was not a case of pure development agreement. On account of dispute, settlement was entered into between members of AOP and properties were distributed according to which assessee was to receive Rs. 14 crores for foregoing their rights and Rs. 6 crores conveying property.

While filing return, the assessee declared long-term gain only on Rs. 6 crores. However, the Assessing Officer considered entire amount of Rs. 20 crores was taxable under head 'capital gains'.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

It was further held by the Tribunal that when distribution of assets took place the same was not transfer of assets. Further, the Tribunal had taken note of the fact that the assessment at Rs. 14 crore was on the basis of 20 per cent, share of the profit which the assessee would have earned in future. It was also contended that the share of the income was not taxable in the hands of the members. Ultimately, the Tribunal found that the addition of Rs. 14 crore made under the head of capital gain was incorrect and the said addition was to be deleted.

The department contended that if such mode was permitted by formation of AOP and thereafter to transfer the property under the head of distribution, the property would be transferred and the department would not be able to recover any tax on capital gain and therefore, the question would arise for consideration in the present appeal.

The family members of the assessee were holding apart from personal properties, the family properties and shares in different business concerns. However, disputes arose between the assessee and the other family members. The dispute was referred to an arbitrator. The arbitrator suggested a settlement, which the assessee and the other family members agreed. Thereupon a family arrangement was made between the assessee and the other family members; whereby the assessee had resigned from a partnership firm and transferred his share of profit/loss in the firm to a family member for a consideration of Rs. 35,000 being the capital balance of the firm. The assessee claimed that in the instant case there was no transfer, which gives rise to any capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that there was a transfer in the instant case and consequently there was a capital gain in the hands of the assessee. He, therefore, held that the assessee was liable to pay capital gain tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner(Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that admittedly there were lot of disputes between the family members of the assessee, who were none other than the relatives of one other, and in that event the family arrangement and settlement entered into between the parties on the suggestion made by the arbitrator could not be termed as a transfer either in respect of movable or immovable properties or in respect of commercial properties. Therefore, there was no transfer and it was only a family arrangement. Therefore, the assessee was not liable to pay capital gain tax. Accordingly, it set aside the orders passed by the lower authorities.

Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

The agency agreement entered into by the assessee with ‘HML’ in the year 1955 was a capital asset; the whole of it was not destroyed, lost or parted when the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ in the year 1960. It was merely an exploitation of the commercial assets in a different form. Till then, the recurring amount which the assessee was getting from ‘P’ was income. But by the arrangement arrived at on the basis of the second agreement, the whole of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee was parted with and lost. The question has presented some difficulty when the assessee gets some amount of compensation on termination of agency agreement from the principal itself. Sometimes, in a given case, such compensation, and especially with regard to the managing agency business, has been treated as revenue receipts. But, in the instant case, the type of agreement which the assessee entered into with ‘O’ even if it would have entered into with ‘P’ on payment of Rs. 50,000, would not have clothed the receipt with the chartered of a revenue receipt; still it would have been a capital receipt. This was clearly so, without presenting any difficulty, when the agreement was with another company. After having parted with all its rights of profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960, by a subsequent agreement executed in the year 1962, the assessee was left with no business activity in connection with the agency agreement with ‘HML’. The amount, therefore, received by it was not in lieu of compounded profit but surely in lieu of loss of profit-making apparatus.

What is received by way of price or compensation on disposing of circulating capital or stock-in-trade, namely, the trading asset, is ordinarily and generally revenue receipt. What, however, comes in the hands of the assessee on disposal of the capital assets referable to fixed capital is generally a capital receipt. What is capital asset in the hands of one may be a trading asset in the hands of another.

In the instant case the assessee was not parting with the benefits of a trading contract, rather it parted with its profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960; by utilising that apparatus it was earning profit from the agency business, and the whole of it was lost when he decided to retire on the receipt of Rs. 50,000. It was a sum paid to the assessee, truly a compensation for parting with its business, and the agreement entered into deprived the assessee of the benefit of its agreement entered in 1960, with ‘P’ which constituted the framework or whole structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus. For the reasons stated above, the receipt of Rs. 50,000 by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. The former only is treated as income, but not so with regard to the latter. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the firm itself was formed solely for the purpose of managing the company by entering into the agreement in question with the I.T.F. and there was no other business for it. If that was so, when on account of the loss of the managing agency the assessee-firm lost its business itself, the compensation received by it for that loss would be capital in nature. It is also generally held by the courts that lump sum amounts received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreements are capital in nature.

In the possible case, it was not possible to say that the agreement entered into between the assessee-firm and the I.T.F. under which the assessee-firm acquired the managing agency of the company was a contract, entered into in the ordinary course of business or a trading contract. It followed from the above discussion that the amount of compensation awarded to the assessee-firm was capital receipt and not a revenue receipt liable to tax. Though the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was capital in nature, none the less it was to be treated as "profits and gains of business" as provided under section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act and section 28(ii ) of the 1961 Act.

It was true that the assessee-firm did not enter into any agreement directly with the managed company. It was only the ‘I.T.F.’ which entered into the managing agency agreement with the managed company. But as per the terms of the agreement entered into between the ‘I.T.F.’ and the assessee-firm, the ‘I.T.F.’ assigned its rights under the managing agency agreement to the assessee-firm. The managed company also passed a resolution ratifying the assignment. The umpire awarded damages to the assessee-firm for its loss of managing agency commission, which the assessee-firm would have otherwise been entitled to, but for the breach of the agreement. It was only on the basis of the managing agency commission which the assessee-firm, would have received and estimating it, the umpire awarded the damages to the assessee-firm. What was relevant was whether the amount received was towards compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement or not. It mattered little who paid the amount. Therefore, the amount awarded to the assessee-firm must be deemed as profits and gains of business carried on by it and, therefore, it was income liable to tax.

In the instant case, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum monthly remuneration. Though some quantification was also involved in arriving at the actual damages, the compensation was awarded to the assessee-firm on the basis of the remuneration of so much per year as having accrued to it during the relevant years 1955-56 to 1959-60 (up to 14-8-1960). It was on that basis estimation of the damages was made by the umpire in the arbitration proceedings in awarding the compensation. As the assessee-firm employed the mercantile system of accountancy the relevant amounts as estimated by the umpire in the award must be deemed to have accrued to the assessee-firm during the relevant years.

Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of the revenue.

There was no dispute that the portion of the compensation which represented past profits was a revenue receipt. The only question was whether the remaining portion was a revenue receipt or capital receipt. The remaining portion purported to be compensation given to the three partners for giving up: (i) the managing agency rights, (ii) the selling agency rights, and (iii) the goodwill. The managing agency rights vested with new firm (BJ). Similar was the case of the goodwill assuming that any goodwill had been built up by that time. 'BJ' continued to be in existence. It had not parted with managing agency rights nor its goodwill taken away. What had happened was that the partners representing the assessee firm in 'BJ' had surrendered their rights in partnership to the remaining partners and obtained certain payments for such surrender. This was not a case of parting with any agency rights. This was really a case of cancellation of a contract which had been entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such contracts are liable, in the ordinary course of business, to be altered or terminated on terms and any payment received in settlement of the rights as a result of the termination of the contract really represents the profits which the assessee would have made had the contract been performed. In the instant case, no deed of partnership had been entered into. Therefore, the same was terminable at will. Any of the partners of the firm could have brought the partnership to an end. Consequently, the possibility of termination of a partnership was inherent in the very course of business. Further the assessee-firm had various business activities; one of which was to join 'BJ' to carry on certain business activities. The assessee's representatives by entering into that agreement were merely carrying on a trading activity. Such being the case, it could not be held that the compensation paid for the termination of the contract was a capital receipt. It was not the case of the assessee that its only trading activity had come to an end. It had several activities. Just one of its trading had been put an end to. Hence, the amount received could not be considered as compensation for stopping its business.

As regards the transfer of the selling agency to 'BJ', this was not a right transferred under agreement as that right had been transferred to 'BJ' even at the time the partnership was formed. Further the trading structure of the assessee-firm was not affected. It merely replaced one trading activity by another with the aid of Rs. 35,01,000. In such circumstances, the amount received from the cancellation of agency did not represent the price paid for the loss of capital; it was of the nature of income. Therefore, the entire sum of Rs. 35,01,000 received by the assessee was a revenue receipt assessable under section 10 of 1922 Act.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

Since a managing agency is a creature of contract and since its formation, operation and termination are all to be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act, in so far as they apply, there was no force in the contention that a managing agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other manner. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the compensation amount was taxable profit within the meaning of section 10(5A).

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

On principle also it was difficult to understand why a distinction should be made between the destruction of the whole of the capital asset or a part of the capital asset. In either case, it was clear that the amount received as solatium for that destruction could not be profits arising out of the business of the assessee. The assessee was sought to be taxed under section 10 and the department had to satisfy that the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was profit made by the assessee in the course of its business or profit earned out of its business. Surely when Rs. 25,00,000 had been paid to the assessee for the cessation of its particular business, it could not be urged that this very sum of Rs. 25,00,000 were profits earned by the assessee in the course of its business.

Inasmuch as the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was received by the assessee in consideration of the termination of its managing agency, it was a solatium for the cessation of one of the several activities which the assessee company was entitled to carry on under the agreement, and if it was a solatium then it could not be looked upon as income but must be looked upon as representing the capital asset which had ceased to exist.

The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

It was not the case of the Department and it had never been their case that the capital asset in respect of which capital gain was made by the assessee and which was sought to be taxed was the shares and the managing agency. The whole of the reference was based upon the fact that the only capital asset concerned with was the shares and not the managing agency. Therefore, one must separate the managing agency from the shares in considering what was the value to be put upon the shares. The parties had put upon the shares a value which was much higher than the market value. Admittedly, it was an artificial value and it was artificial because the value put upon the shares was not the value of the shares alone but it was the composite consideration paid by the purchasers for obtaining the shares and also acquiring the managing agency. Under the circumstances, for the purposes of section 12B(2) the sale price of the shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. 65 per share.

In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

The assessee in the instant case was not acting as agent of the principal company, but was distributing the goods of the companies on principal-to-principal basis. The Tribunal recorded a finding that the agreement was not an agency agreement, which finding was not disputed by the revenue. [Para 11] Applying the above ratio decidendi, the assessee had acquired an advantage of enduring nature by way of distribution rights from three companies since 1964. The advantage was continuing to the assessee for more than 20 years by virtue of periodical renewal of the distribution agreement, till it was terminated in the year 1984 and by virtue of the agreement the assessee had developed a pucca establishment and a large marketing network and had been earning very good profit in all these years, till the date of the termination agreement. Under the termination agreement, the entire establishment, the man-power along with the distributorship network which earned profits to the assessee had been transferred to the companies and thereby the assessee was deprived of its source of income and profit-earning apparatus. Further, the assessee was also impaired from doing any distribution business as done earlier because of the prohibitive covenant in the termination agreement. All these factors would clearly indicate that by virtue of the termination agreement, the structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus had been considerably crippled. The reasoning of the authorities below the Tribunal that the compensation had been quantified on three counts, i.e., the cost of trained manpower, compensation for cost of dealers and compensation for loss of profits and, thus, the payment received by the assessee was only reimbursement of such cost factors, was not correct. That was only a method to quantify the lump sum to be paid. Such method adopted could not be stretched to the extent of concluding that the assessee had only recouped or reimbursed the expenses incurred in the past nor could it be said that the assessee had been reimbursed the profit that was not available to it, as a result of the termination of the agreement. The Tribunal was, therefore, right in its approach in treating the amount received by the assessee as a capital receipt. [Para 12]

From the finding of the Tribunal, the following inferences seemed to be derivable : (1) That the receipt was compensation. (2) The compensation was for loss of anticipated profits. (3) The profits were to accrue by the operation of the Hind Roadways Corporation. (4) The loss was suffered by the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation at the instance of the Government.

On this premises which was clearly implied in the finding of the Tribunal, it appeared to be plain that the compensation was not for loss of profit of any business of the assessee but was to accrue out of a profit-making structure, viz., the corporation, of which the assessee was to be appointed the managing agent. With the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation, the prospect of the assessee becoming the managing agent of the corporation also vanished. Compensation was paid to him in lieu of the benefit which he might have derived by becoming the managing agent of the corporation. The corporation or the profit-making structure or the managing agency were only an asset of a capital nature. Compensation paid for the loss of a capital asset is not and cannot be taxable income. It followed that on the finding recorded by the Tribunal, the conclusion in law which it arrived at, namely, that "the amount was clearly taxable" was entirely erroneous.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

It has been laid down in a number of decision that when an expenditure is made with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, there is good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to the opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as property attributable not to revenue but to capital.

From the facts found in the instant case it was clear that the managing agency was terminated on business considerations and as a matter of commercial expediency. There was no basis for holding that by terminating the managing agency, the company acquired any enduring benefit or any income yielding asset. It is true that by terminating the services of the managing agents, the company not only saved the expense that it would have had to incur in the relevant previous year but also for few more years to come. It would not be correct to say that by avoiding certain business expenditure, the company could be said to have acquired enduring benefits or acquired any income yielding asset. Thus, the compensation paid for termination of the services of the managing agents was a revenue expenditure.

Note : The decision was in favour of the assessee.

In view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spg. & Wvg. Co. Ltd. [1954] 24 Comp. Cas. 103, 110; AIR 1954 SC 119, 123, it could be said that the right of management being property had to be equated to a capital asset as being a part of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee and, for that reason, compensation paid for divesting the assessee of its management was compensation for acquisition of part of its profit-making apparatus and must be of a capital receipt rather than a revenue receipt or income.

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Senairam Doongarmall v. CIT [1961] 42 ITR 392 : (1962) 1 SCR 257 (SC), in the instant case, the assessee having been divested of its management did not and could not carry on business in the sense of carrying on an activity with the object of earning profit by a process of production. The divesting of its management was really divesting the assessee of its property. The compensation paid was, therefore, for the loss of a capital asset. The mere fact that the compensation paid to the assessee-company was measured by its past profits did not make the compensation paid the income of the assessee, as a result of business done by it. The compensation paid to the assessee was not income.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

In the instant case, there was no dispute as to the fact that the managing agency agreement with the assessees was in fact terminated by the managed company in connection with which the managed company had paid and the assessees had received the impugned sums of Rs. 81,000 and Rs. 2,00,000. In the order of the Tribunal in the managed company's assessment, the Tribunal had, on various circumstances mentioned by it therein, found that the termination of the managing agency agreement by the managed company was not bona ride, i.e., being brought about for some ulterior purpose. The said conclusion presupposed that factually the agency agreement was terminated. Nowhere in the order the Tribunal had held that factually there was no termination or that the termination was sham or without consideration or that the amounts said to have been paid by the managed company to the assessee towards the compensation for the termination of the agency agreement were in fact not paid but merely book entries. The transaction which is not bona fide does not necessarily become a sham transaction or a transaction without consideration. Thus, the compensation received by the assessee from the managed company for the termination of the managing agency agreement was taxable in their hands under section 10(5A )(a) of the 1922 Act.

It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

the assessee for the year under consideration and the subsequent years go to prove that there was no loss of business and at the same time terms and conditions of the agreement and settlement agreement apparently shows that the assessee by virtue of the agreement has worked as an agent for all intent purposes and as such received a compensation for loss of agency business, which is taxable as business income under section 28(ii)(c) read with section 28(va)(a) of the Act. [Para 35]

The contentions raised by the assessee inter alia qua the provisions contained under section 28(va) that the existing provisions of clause (ii) of section 28(a) is restrictive in its scope as far as taxation of compensation is concerned; a large segment of compensation received in connection with business and employment is within the purview of taxation, is not sustainable because it is nowhere case of the assessee before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that because of settlement agreement qua the termination of agency and distribution business the compensation is in respect of business loss and employment. Rather in the preceding para it is discussed that after termination of the agency and distribution assessee's business has been increased considerably. [Para 36]

Moreover, when the assessee and the RDG were entered into agreement to do business and any settlement arrived at between them for termination of the business would be business income. The assessee has also raised one additional ground to supplement ground No. 1 to the effect that compensation received on termination of agreement is a capital receipt. When it is nowhere case of the assessee that it has lost its livelihood on account of termination of the business agreement compensation received by it by virtue of the termination agreement is business income. [Para 37]

So in view of what has been discussed above, "compensation received by the assessee from RDG to the tune of Rs. 92,76,62,688/- in out of court settlement is a business income and not an income assessed to capital gains as claimed by the assessee" and as such provisions contained under section 28(ii)(c) read with section 28(va)(a) of the Act are attracted. Hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) has rightly confirmed the addition of Rs. 92,76,62,688/- as business income. [Para 38]

The Supreme Court in the case of Karam Chand Thapar & Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1971] 80 ITR 167 had held that ordinarily compensation for loss of an office or agency is regarded as capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and that its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. The Court further held that it was difficult to lay down a precise principle of universal application but various workable rules have been evolved for guidance.

Applying the aforesaid test laid down, in the present case, it was to be held that the Tribunal was right in arriving at a conclusion that it was a capital receipt. Reason is that as provided in article XVIII of the first agreement, assessee was having an option or right or lien, if owner desired to transfer the hotel or lease all or part of the hotel to any other person, the same was required to be offered first to the assessee (operator) or its nominee. This right to exercise its option was given up by a supplementary agreement which was executed between the receiver and the assessee. It was agreed that the receiver would be at liberty to sell or otherwise dispose of the said property at such price and on such terms as he may deem fit and was not under any obligation requiring the purchaser thereof to enter into any agreement with the operator (assessee) for the purpose of operating and managing the hotel or otherwise and in its return, agreed consideration was as stated above in clause X. On the basis of the said agreement, the assessee had received the amount in question. The amount was received because the assessee had given up its right to purchase and/or to operate the property. Further, it was loss of source of income to the assessee and that right was determined for consideration. Obviously, therefore, it was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt.

After analysing number of cases, the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 had observed that the following satisfactory measure of consistency in the principle was disclosed : 'where on a consideration of the circumstances, payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business, nor deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated), the receipt is revenue : Whereby the cancellation of an agency, the trading structure of the assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss of what may be regarded as the source of the assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipts'.

Considering the aforesaid principles laid down, as per article XVIII of the principal agreement, the amount received by the assessee was for the consideration for giving up his right to purchase and/or to operate the property or for getting it on lease before it was transferred or let out to other persons. It was not for settlement of rights under trading contract, but the injury was inflicted on the capital asset of the assessee and giving up the contractual right on the basis of principal agreement had resulted in loss of source of the assessee's income. Therefore, the amount received was a capital receipt.

There could be no doubt that by paying the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 the managed company had secured for itself a release from the obligation to pay a higher remuneration to the assessee for the rest of the period of managing agency covered by the principal agreement. Prima facie, that release from liability to pay a higher remuneration for over 17 years must be an advantage gained by the managed company for the benefit of its business and the immunity thus obtained by the managed company might well be regarded as the acquisition of an asset of enduring value by means of a capital outlay which would be a capital expenditure.

In the resolution adopted by the managed company as well as in the recitals set out in the supplementary agreement that sum had been stated to be a payment "as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous term as to remuneration contained" in the principal agreement. It was true that the language used in the document was not decisive and the question had to be determined by a consideration of all the attending circumstances; nevertheless, the language could not be ignored altogether but must be taken into consideration along with other relevant circumstances.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued.

A managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at the rate of 20 per cent of the profits was not the same thing as a managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at 10 per cent of the profits. There was a distinct deterioration in the character and quality of the managing agency viewed as a profit-making apparatus and this deterioration was of an enduring kind. The reduced remuneration having been separately provided, the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 must be regarded as having been paid as compensation for that injury to or deterioration of the managing agency.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid and received not to make up the difference between the higher remuneration and the reduced remuneration but was in reality paid and received as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous terms as to remuneration as it was in terms expressed to be. In other words, so far as the managed company was concerned, it was paid for securing immunity from the liability to pay higher remuneration to the assessee firm for the rest of the term of the managing agency and, therefore, a capital expenditure and so far as the assessee firm was concerned, it was received as compensation for the deterioration or injury to the managing agency by reason of the release of its rights to get higher remuneration and, therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax.

In identical situation in the case of South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Madras High Court held that in the absence of inadequacy of the profit, under the agreement, the managing agent was entitled to the minimum remuneration payable at such rate for each year and insofar as the additional remuneration was concerned, there was no provision in the agreement as to when it accrued. The High Court held that in the absence of any provision in the agreement as to when it accrued, it accrued at the time when it became payable to the assessee. Similarly, on the facts of the case, the contract was silent as to when the amount became due and in the absence of any material, it was to be held that it was not possible to treat the amount as being due on the last date of the accounting year. The finding of the Tribunal was that the additional remuneration became due only after the audited balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company were laid before the company’s General Body Meeting and approved by the same. Since the additional remuneration was based on the profit and unless the amount of profit was known, it was not possible to hold that the additional remuneration accrued at the end of the relevant accounting year. The department was not able to show that under provision of the agreement, the additional remuneration became due prior to the approval in the General Body Meeting. Therefore, it was to be held that the view of the Tribunal that the income did not accrue to the assessee on or before 31-03-1970 and the additional remuneration received by the assessee was not liable to be included for the assessment year 1970-71 appeared to be in order.

In the case the assessee, taking up managing agency along with secretary ship to the plantation company and other trading rights was part of the assessee's normal trading activities. The assessee dealt with, among other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other rights from the plantation companies certainly facilitated that trade in tea. The managing agencies, the assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event the assessee received the compensation it was entitled to by agreement. The agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for T. It was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to the assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea. The assessee was in a position to obtain such contracts with plantation companies because of its large experience in handling tea for export and also in managing plantations in India. Even confining to the managing agency the loss of one of several such managing agencies could have little effect on the structure of the assessee's business even in tea or on its profit earning apparatus as a whole. They endured virtually unimpaired by the termination of the managing agency for the T even as the business of the assessee remained unimpaired when other managing agencies were terminated in the past. The assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding the termination of such agreements. The termination of the agreement with the T could well be said to have been brought about in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and the money paid to the assessee as a result of or in connection with the termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and that therefore, it was a trading receipt.

The head under which income would be chargeable under section 176(3A) need not necessarily be ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’ and the head under which such income would be chargeable would depend on the circumstances in which recipient received the amount. In the instant case, the firm was, no doubt ‘ carrying on business of builders and contractors and it was in the course of that business that the agreement dated 9-11-1963 was entered into. However, the fact remained that the firm never obtained possession of the land. It had not paid full price of the land. It had paid only earnest money. The firm did not acquire any right, title or interest in said land. The only right it had, at the time of agreement, was right of obtaining specific performance from the vendor. Even that right came to an end when the land was acquired by the Government by notification. The right that survived was thereafter right to obtain appropriate share in the compensation that would be paid by the Government to the vendor as a result of compulsory acquisition. In these circumstances, it could not be said that land in question was stock-in-trade of the firm at any moment of time.

It is now well-settled that the property allotted to a partner on dissolution of the firm is capital asset in his hands. In the instant case, therefore, one-fifth share in the interest under agreement dated 9-11-1963 was a capital asset in the hands of the assessee on the date of dissolution and the gains received by him on receipt of his share of compensation would, therefore, be capital gains chargeable under section 45.

Accordingly, the matter was restored to the ITO with direction to compute the capital gains and bring them to tax in accordance with law after giving exemption under section 54E, if the assessee was so entitled.

It was apparent from records that the consideration received by the assessee, if any, was to be bifurcated into two parts—one for relinquishment of right over the property and another for facilitating the peaceful possession to the vendee. However, the Assessing Officer considered the entire consideration received as income of the assessee without mentioning the head of income under which he assessed it, which was not proper. [Para 7.5]

Further, there were two agreements of sale—one for 3 acres and another for 7 acres dated 6-1-2006. As per these agreements of sale-cum -general power of attorney, the vendor had delivered the vacant possession of the scheduled property to the vendee. As per the provision of section 2(47 ) transfer takes place as soon as the possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of property Act, 1882. Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

The issue was concluded by the decision in the case of CIT v. Mangtu Ram Jaipuria [1991] 192 ITR 533 (Cal.) where it had been held that where there was no cost of acquisition for the tenancy right, there could be no changeability in respect of the consideration received for transfer or surrender of tenancy rights, to tax as capital gains.

Hence, the Tribunal was justified in holding that extinguishment of tenancy right was not exigible to capital gains.

Section 50(2) refers to block of assets ceasing to exist as such by reason of transfer of the entire ‘block of assets’. The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. Even if it was taken as a capital asset, in view of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Ambica Chemical Production v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal No. 238/V/2002, dated 26-5-2005] no tax was leviable in terms of section 45 on the amount received by the assessee. [Para 30]

Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld. [Para 32]

An agency contract cannot always be considered as a profit earning apparatus, so as to render any compensation for an injury caused to that contract to be treated as a capital receipt. Where the work of an agent is to bring about the business between his principal and his customers, the agency would be the apparatus which leads to the business and, therefore, so far as the agent is concerned, a capital asset. But where, however, the assessee has a business in taking up agency on behalf of others, i.e., the agency is one of the business which the assessee has, such business could be held to be a circulating capital or stock-in-trade, and the compensation received in respect of injury thereto would be a revenue receipt.

Where a partnership is entered into for the purpose of doing one of the items of the business, it cannot be said that the partnership is a structure of the business, but on the other hand it would be one entered into in the ordinary course of its business.

The assessee was a firm engaged in the production of films. Tamil film was not its only venture; it was only a part of its business activity. It had already started production of another picture. It had also engaged artists for the production of said Tamil film. It was only during the course of its production that it entered into partnership with BP. Such contracts are but a normal feature in the business relating to a film production; it facilitates the coming in of the necessary finance, and brings together varied talents whose combined effort would go to make a better or more successful picture. That such combinations were common is shown by the fact that the assessee itself entered into a financial arrangement with R, agreeing to give him one-half share of its proceeds. A partnership, as in the present case, for the production of the film, should be held, therefore, to be one entered into in the ordinary course of trade.

The question then was whether the termination of the agreement was made in the course of its business. It was evident from the terms of the agreement of partnership that the parties did contemplate a sale of the picture to an outsider or even inter se the partners even before the completion of the picture. It was, no doubt, true that the partnership agreement evidenced a joint venture, but the joint venture was only for obtaining a commercial asset, that was, to secure a stock-in-trade. If that venture failed, it was only an incident in the assessee's business. It was not such a fundamental asset like a managing agency agreement, which, if terminated, would put an end to the entire profit earning structure.

agents of a company can be carried on by a servant as well as a business by a person working as managing agent. 27. In Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC) the Appellant, Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. ('KBCL') was a managing agent of six companies including Fort Williams Jute Co. (FWJC). KBCL entered into an agreement with Mugneeram Bangur & Co. (MBC), whereunder MBC agreed to purchase the entire shareholding of KBCL in FWJC; procure repayment of all the loans advanced by KBCL to FWJC and to procure that FWJC will compensate KBCL for the loss of office in the sum of Rs. 3,50,000 after KBCL resigned as its managing agent. KBCL tendered its resignation as managing agent and received Rs. 3,50,000 from FWJC. The question was whether the amount received by KBCL to relinquish the managing agency was a revenue receipt liable to tax. It was held that by relinquishing the managing agency, KBCL parted with an asset of an enduring nature. It mattered little that the KBCL did continue to conduct the remaining managing agency of other companies even after the termination of its agency with FWJC. It was held that it cannot be said as general rule that what is determinative of the nature of a receipt on the cancellation of a contract of agency or office is the extinction or compulsory cessation of the agency or office. Where payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business or deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business, and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated), the receipt is revenue; where by the cancellation of an agency the trading structure of the Assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss or what may be regarded as the source of the Assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipt. This test was followed in Oberoi Hotel (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 903/103 Taxman 236 (SC).

The original contract was with regard to the benefits under those agreements and no other benefit. The assessee company received Rs. 1 crore because they lost those benefits and the Dalmia Co. was prepared to pay Rs. 1 crore because it wanted those benefits. But when the transaction ultimately went through and the assessee company resigned, those benefits had been extinguished or destroyed and they never vested in the Dalmia Co. If the two companies had appointed the Dalmia Co. as managing agents, that would have been a fresh appointment and a fresh agreement would have to be entered into between the companies and the Dalmia Co. That managing agency would have been entirely different from the managing agency which vested in the assessee company. Therefore it is clear that as a result of the transaction by which the assessee company obtained Rs. 1 crore the assessee company ceased to be the managing agents of the two companies; but no one else obtained the benefits of those two agreements. In other words, the property which was vested in the assessee company in the shape of the managing agency was destroyed and ceased to exist. That property was never transferred in favour of any one else, nor did it ever vest in any one else. Even if Sir Nusserwanji was right that the Dalmia Co. brought about the same result by a different transaction, it was open to the parties to select one transaction rather than another, to select a transaction which avoided tax rather than a transaction which attracted tax. But if the two transactions were in essence different, if they created different legal rights and obligations, it is not open to the taxing authorities to say, "Treat one transaction as if it was the same as the other transaction". As we have just pointed out on the authorities, what we have to consider is whether the transaction which would have resulted if the first contract had not been modified, and the transaction which was ultimately carried out by result of the modification, are the same or are they different, different in the sense that they give rise to different legal positions and different legal rights and obligations. In our opinion, it seems to be fairly clear that these two transactions are not identical. In the one case the result would be the sale or the transfer of property in favour of Dalmia Co.; in the other case there is no sale or transfer, there is only the relinquishment of rights by the assessee company or destruction of property by the assessee company at the instance of Dalmia Co.

It may be a lacuna, but the Legislature, for reasons best known to it, has not chosen to tax such a transaction, and Sir Nusserwanji also concedes that if we take the view that Rs. 1 crore which the assessee company received was received by it for resigning the managing agency and not for selling the managing agency, and if resignation means relinquishment of the assessee company's rights as managing agents, then the assessee company would not be liable to tax. Shorn of extraneous and irrelevant matters, the position really narrows itself down to this. Originally, the assessee company agreed to sell or transfer its managing agency to Dalmia Co. for a consideration of Rs. 1 crore. That agreement was altered and for the same consideration the assessee company agreed to relinquish its rights in the managing agency commission by resigning as managing agents. The consideration remained the same, the result as far as the assessee company was concerned was the same, but the legal position that emerged was entirely different from the legal position that would have arisen if the first contract had stood. We are unable to accept the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee company transferred the managing agency to the managed companies and that therefore there was a transfer which resulted in capital gains to the assessee company. It is difficult to understand how by resigning the managing agency the assessee company transferred the agency of the two companies. Sir Nusserwanji himself has not attempted to support this view which has been given expression to by the Tribunal in its order.
