6. In all cases of agency agreement, generally the ownership of goods or services is not transferred to the agents; the ownership remains with the principal. According to Concise Oxford Dictionary (9th edition), agent means "a person who acts for another in business, politics, etc." Some of the other dictionaries also provide the similar meaning. Simply an agent is a representative who acts on behalf of other persons or organizations. Thus, when ownership of goods or services is transferred to an agent, he cannot be treated as agent, because in that case he will be doing work for himself. In case of Pratap Singh & Sons v. CCE, Mumbai [2007] 6 STT 390 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee was purchasing and reselling the products of several manufacturers. The agreements with the assessee and respective manufacturers stipulated that the assessee should improve marketing conditions and sell the products. For said purpose the assessee was required to establish facilities and to deploy sufficiently trained and suitable labour, to advertise and to display the products of these manufacturers. The department taking the view that the above activities of the assessee were of clearing and forwarding agent, demanded service tax. Further, the department took the view that special discount given by the manufacturers should be treated as service charges and, accordingly, confirmed service tax on the discount. The Tribunal held that the assessee had purchased and sold products from the principals as their distributor. On purchase of the goods, the assessee became the owner and as owner, dealer or transferee of the goods, it was in his own interest to promote the sale activities and to make advertisement and keep the trained salesman and, hence, they were part of the dealers’ job. That could not be treated as service rendered to the principals, namely, the manufacturers. If there was any special relationship or additional consideration leading to charging of lower price to the assessee, at the most, it could become an issue relating to valuation of the goods. The discount given by the manufacturer could not be taken as service charges. Thus, the Tribunal held the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals), in treating the assessee as provider of clearing and forwarding service, as erroneous and the service provided by the assessee as non-taxable.

A caterer supplying tea and biscuits during the production of advertising film will also become a person connected with preparation of advertisement and became an advertising agency. Such absurdities, from an interpretation have to be avoided. The term ‘service connected with used in the definition of "Advertising agency" is to be understood in context of and in a restrictive manner.

The astrological or marriage bureau only carries out the function of match making or assisting in the same. It does not in any way engage in planning, promotion, organizing or presentation of any event.

No. The Government in its Master Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated August 23, 2007 has clarified that the nature of service provided by ‘Express cargo service’ provider falls within the scope and definition of courier agency.

Whether fee collected by institution falls under Commercial training or coaching services?

No. The Tribunal held that education has a larger scope and may include coaching or training and not vice versa. Coaching or training is a very narrow activity, imparting skill in a particular discipline. But, education is a broader term, which is a process of development of personality of body, mind and intellect. Just because institution collects fees from students, one cannot come to conclusion that it imparts commercial training or coaching. Institutions preparing students for entrance exams to universities are covered under commercial training or coaching services and not institutions offering degrees recognized by law.

Magnus Society v. CC & CE [2009] 18 STT 193 (Bang. - CESTAT)

Whether computer engineering firm falls under ‘Consulting engineer services’?

Yes. The Finance Act, 2008 with effect from May 16, 2008 has amended the definition of ‘taxable service’ to bring back the computer software engineering consultancy service under the service tax net and to provide that services provided by a consulting engineer in relation to advice, consultancy or technical assistance in the disciplines of both computer hardware engineering and computer software engineering shall also fall under ‘Consulting engineer service’.

Whether an organization formed for charitable purpose is liable for service tax?

Yes. The CESTAT in its judgment held that an organization may be charitable organization established for some purpose, but may still be engaged in commercial activities, as without any commercial activities, the income required for charitable purpose cannot be generated. For levy of service tax, it is the activity of an organization, which is relevant and not objective.

Punjab Ex-Servicemen Corpn. v. CCE [2009] 18 STT 21 (New Delhi - CESTAT)

Whether the person manufacturing the signboards falls under advertising services?

No. The Tribunal in its judgment held that the person who is only writing or preparing the signboards at the behest of their customer cannot be called as advertising agency. There was no evidence on record to show that the relationship between the customers and the appellant is of advertising agent which is necessary for imposition of service tax.

Star Neon Signs v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 223 (New Delhi - CEGAT)

Whether assisting a person in acquiring share in a company falls under management consultant services?

No. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not carrying out activity of management but it was manufacturer. Incidental help in acquisition of shares does not fall under ‘Management consultant service’.

K.R. Alloys Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 10 STT 510 (Bang. - CESTAT)

Whether receiving, storing and distributing the products on behalf of client will attract service tax?

No. The High Court relied upon the case of Medpro Pharma (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 341 (New Delhi - CESTAT) (LB) and held that the activities undertaken by the respondent would not fall under C&F agency services.

in trade by a partner from a firm [Section 9B]

Section 9B provides that where a partner receives during the previous year any capital asset or stock-in-trade or both from a firm in connection with the dissolution or reconstitution of such firm, then the firm shall be deemed to have transferred such capital asset or stock-in-trade or both, as the case may be, to the partner in the year in which such capital asset or stock in trade or both are received by that partner. Further, it provides that any profits and gains arising from such deemed transfer of capital asset or stock in trade or both, as the case may be, by the firm shall be deemed to be the income of the firm of the previous year in which stock or capital asset were received by the partner and chargeable to income-tax under the head 'business or profession' or 'capital gain' in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

Furthermore, the fair market value of the capital asset or stock on the date of its receipt by the partner shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration while computing profit and gains arising from deemed transfer of such stock or capital asset by the firm.

Section 9B also defines the expression "reconstitution of specified entity". It means where:

(a)

One or more of its partners or members ceases to be partners or members;

(b)

One or more new partners or members are admitted. However, at least one existing partner or member should continue to be partner or member of the specified entity after admission of the new partner(s) or member(s); or

(c)

All the partners or members continue with change in their respective share or in share of some of them.

Further, the CBDT is empowered to issue guidelines, with prior approval of the Central Government, for removing difficulties arising in giving effect to the provisions of this section. Every such guidelines shall be laid before each house of Parliament and shall be binding on the Income-tax authorities and assessee.

Section 9B deals with the following three aspects.

1.2-1. Distribution of stock or capital asset by a firm to its partner is deemed as transfer

This provision creates a deeming fiction that the distribution of stock or capital asset by a firm to its partner is a transfer. This is done to overrule various judicial rulings which held that the distribution, division or allotment of assets by a partnership firm upon dissolution or reconstitution is nothing but a mutual adjustment of rights between the partners.

The Apex Court in the case of Malabar Fisheries Co. v. CIT [1979] 2 Taxman 409/120 ITR 49 has held that a partnership firm, under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, is not a distinct legal entity, apart from the partners constituting it. The firm, as such, has no separate rights of its own in the partnership assets and when one talks of the firm's property or firm's assets, all that is meant is property or assets in which all partners have a joint or common interest. If that be the position, it is difficult to accord the contention that upon dissolution the firm's rights in the partnership assets are extinguished. The firm, as such, has no separate rights of its own in the partnership assets but it is the partners who own jointly in common its assets. Therefore, the consequence of the distribution, division or allotment of assets to the partnership, which flows upon dissolution after discharge of liabilities, is nothing but a mutual adjustment of rights between the partners and there is no question of any extinguishment of the firm's rights in the partnership assets amounting to a transfer of assets within the meaning of section 2(47).

Now, Section 9B has created a deeming fiction for treating such flow of stock or capital asset at the time of dissolution or reconstitution as transfer.

1.2-2. How to compute the gains arising from deemed transfer of stock-in-trade?

Sub-section (2) of Section 9B provides that any profit and gains arising from deemed transfer of stock-in-trade shall be deemed to be income of the firm of the year in which such stock is received by the partner and, accordingly, it shall be charged to tax under the head "Profit and gains from business or profession".

For such computation, it provides that the fair market value of the stock on the date of its receipt by the partner shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration while computing profit and gains arising from deemed transfer of such stock by the firm. The income arising from the transfer of stock shall be taxable as business income under Section 28. In simple words, the fair market value of stock transferred to the partner shall be recorded as sale by the firm as the same shall form part of the business of the firm.

1.2-3. How to compute the gains arising from deemed transfer of capital asset?

Sub-section (2) of Section 9B provides that any profit and gains arising from deemed transfer of capital asset shall be deemed to be income of the firm of the year in which such capital asset is received by the partner. It shall be charged to tax under the head "Capital Gains".

Further, it provides that fair market value of capital asset on the date of its receipt by the partner shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration while computing capital gain arising from deemed transfer of such capital asset by the firm.

Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 2 STT 258 (New Delhi - CESTAT) - The appellant was a selling agent of certain companies. The authorities noticed that the appellant had rendered certain services which according to them fell in the category of clearing and forwarding agents but failed to register with the department as a service tax assessee. Thus, the service tax was demanded from the appellant with interest and penalty. On appeal, the Dy. Commissioner upheld the demand and penalties. In this case it was held that the selling agency agreement, which was on record, clearly threw light on the nature of the services provided by the appellant. The appellant was appointed as a selling agent ‘for the sale and distribution, in the area, of the products of the principals’. Though under clause (6), the deliveries to the customers were to be effected by the manufacturers directly, there were other clauses which connected the appellant with the deliveries which were required to be made to the customers. Under clause (18) of the agreement, even where all firm orders were placed with the appellant till the date of expiry or termination of the agreement, the appellant was entitled to be paid a commission of 1 per cent of the price indicated in the invoice for machines and spares delivered within six months from the date of expiry of the agreement. The commission payable to the appellant under clause (16) of the agreement was 4 per cent of the contract price. If there was no other service to be provided under the agreement by the appellant except procuring firm orders, there was no reason for reducing the commission from 4 per cent to 1 per cent in case of firm orders already procured by the appellant for the manufacturer prior to the date of the expiry or termination of the agreement. In view of the above clauses of the agreement, it appeared that the applicant had failed to make out any case for waiver of pre-deposit of service tax and penalty amount, as prayed for in the application. It, however, appeared from the impugned order that the service tax was calculated on the entire amount of the commission and no effort had been made to apportion the commission having regard to the nature of the agency which involved in procuring of firm purchase orders as well as assisting the customers in getting the delivery, and indemnifying the manufacturer in case of delay in deliveries. No effort had been made either on behalf of the appellant to bifurcate the nature of services under the agreement and to claim that the service tax could have been imposed only on a portion of the commission, which was attributable to clearing and forwarding activity. However, having regard to the fact that in clause of the agreement, there was an indication that so far as firm orders were concerned commission of only 1 per cent was to be paid, the rest of the commission out of 4 per cent payable under clause (16) could be attributed to the other services rendered by the appellant including those connected with the delivery to the buyers. The interest of justice would be served if the appellant would deposit 50 per cent of the service tax payable under the impugned order under section 83, read with section 35F, of the Central Excise Act by way of pre-deposit.

Religious place (temple) as a mandap

10. We are a religious trust having a big temple and this temple has a big open ground, which we are giving regularly for organizing marriages and marriage receptions and also for other functions. We have received a notice from the Central Excise office of our city to get register under the ‘Mandap keeper service’ and pay service tax. Please advice us.

Service tax is not leviable if service provided to any person for the use of precincts of a religious place as Mandap. This has been provided in Notification No. 14/2003 - ST, dated June 20, 2003. As per this Notification the religious place means a place, which is meant for conduct of prayers or worship pertaining to a religion.

Since the service in the form of Mandap is being provided for the use of precincts of a temple or other religious place, no service tax is payable.

Transfer of land development right through JDA is not a lease transaction because it is a right to develop a land. Lease is a right to enjoy the immovable property. Moreover, the transfer of land development right is permanent and irrevocable subject to agreed terms and conditions. It grants right to developer to sell the property. Non-cash consideration like securities issued by SPV should be recorded at the lowest of : (a) fair value of such consideration; (b) carrying value (net) of securitized assets; and (c) net realizable value of securitized assets. In case of a mix of cash and non-cash consideration, the non-cash consideration will be recorded as aforesaid subject to the cash component being reduced from the value of securitized assets. All costs like legal expenses, etc., incurred on a ‘true-sale’ securitisation transaction should be fully and immediately recognized in the profit and loss statement. Obligations accepted by the originator (for example, recourse obligation) should be valued and expected losses, if any, should be provided in the profit and loss statement.

If, however, the securitisation transaction is not a ‘true-sale’, the securitized asset should continue to be carried in the balance sheet of the originator and the consideration received should be shown as ‘borrowings’ with appropriate disclosure about security, i.e., assets securitised. Costs like legal fees, etc., incurred on such transaction could be either recognized fully and immediately in the profit and loss statement or amortized over the life of such borrowing.

4.4 Income-tax treatment - The income-tax treatment primarily depends on the nature of the assets of the originator. In a true sale transaction, if the securitised asset is a trade receivable (‘trading portfolio’), then the ‘securitised result’ should be considered as the ‘business income’. As a corollary, if the securitised asset is an investment, i.e., a capital asset for the originator, then the ‘securitised result’ should be considered as ‘capital gains’. Classification of ‘securitisation result’ is important as capital loss can be recouped only against capital gains and not against any other income. So, in absence of sufficient taxable ‘capital gains’ accruing to the originator either in the year of securitisation or eight succeeding tax years thereafter, the un-recouped ‘capital loss’ arising on securitisation will be a dead tax loss for the originator. Such loss will increase the cost of securitisation.

An alternate view, on securitisation of a ‘trading portfolio’, could be that since the originator severs his income-generating asset, the ‘securitisation result’ should be considered as being on ‘capital’ account. However, the better view appears to be that since securitisation is akin to realisation of a trading asset, any resultant gains or loss should be considered as ‘business income’ and not ‘capital gains’.

The servicing fee received by the originator (in case he services the assets) should be treated as ‘business income’ where it relates to securitisation of ‘trading portfolio’. Similarly, interest on cash collateral and/or subordinate securities should be considered as ‘business income’ of the originator. Legal fees and related securitisation costs should, therefore, be considered as tax-deductible business expenditure.

In case of securitisation of ‘capital asset’, the service fee/interest income from cash collateral/subordinate securities could be classified as ‘income from other sources’. The legal fees and related costs may be deductible against capital gains on the basis that they are wholly and exclusively incurred for transfering the ‘capital asset’. However, dispute with the tax authorities on this count cannot be fully ruled out.

FAQ 16. Whether the out-of-pocket expenses received by professionals shall form part of gross receipts? The expression "gross receipts" in the profession would include all receipts arising from carrying on of such profession. Generally, professionals like solicitors, advocates or chartered accountants receive out-of-pocket expenses in advance and credit it in a separate client's account to utilise them for making payments for stamp duties, registration fees, travelling expenses, etc., on behalf of the clients. These amounts, if collected separately in advance or otherwise, should not form part of the "gross receipts". If, however, such out-of-pocket expenses are collected by way of a consolidated fee, the whole of the amount so collected shall form part of gross receipts, and no adjustment shall be made in respect of actual expenses paid on behalf of his clients out of the gross fees so collected.

Furthermore, the advance fees received for which services are yet to be rendered will not form part of the receipts, as such advances are the liabilities of the assessee and cannot be treated as his receipts till the services are rendered.

FAQ 17. How to calculate the turnover of the commission agent?

Turnover of a commission agent or a person selling goods on a consignment basis is determined concerning the transfer of significant risk or reward of ownership. Where the property in goods or all significant risks and rewards of ownership of goods continue to belong to the principal, the relevant sale price shall not form part of the turnover of the commission agent. In this case, the turnover shall be the amount of commission earned by the agent. However, if the property in the goods, significant risk, and reward of ownership belong to the commission agent, the sale price received/receivable shall form part of his turnover.

ICDS-IV (Revenue Recognition) also provides that in the case of an agency relationship, the revenue of an agent shall be the amount of commission and not the gross inflow of cash, receivables or other consideration. The CBDT6 has also clarified that while determining the turnover in the case of Kachha Arahtias, the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of the principals, and only the gross commission has to be considered. However, in the case of Pucca Arahtias, the total sales/turnover of the business should be taken into consideration.

FAQ 18. How to calculate the turnover of a share broker?

When a share broker purchases securities on behalf of his customers, he does not get them transferred in his name, but they are delivered in the name of the customer. The same is true in the case of sales. The share broker holds the delivery merely on behalf of his customer. The property in securities does not get transferred to the share-brokers. Only brokerage, which is being accounted for in the books of share brokers, should be considered for calculating the turnover. However, in the case of transactions entered into by a share broker on his personal account, the sale value should be considered while calculating the sales turnover. The case of a sub-broker is not different from that of a share broker.

FAQ 19. How to calculate the turnover in case of a speculative transaction?

A 'speculative transaction' means a transaction in which a contract for the purchase or sale of any commodity or securities is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery or transfer of commodity or scrips. Thus, in speculative transactions, both positive and negative differences can arise from the settlement of contracts. Each transaction, whether resulting in a positive or negative difference, is an independent transaction. In such transactions, though the contract notes are issued for the full value of the purchased or sold asset, the entries in the books of account are made only for the differences. Accordingly, the aggregate of both positive and negative differences is considered as the turnover.

Sale deed executed by a general power of attorney holder after the death of the original owner was invalid: SC

M. S. Ananthamurthy v. J. Manjula [2025] 172 taxmann.com 7 (SC)

The suit property was originally part of 1 acre 8 guntas of land in Chunchaghatta Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bangalore South Taluk, owned by the original owner, M @ R. He developed the land into individual plots and sold them to various buyers.

The original owner executed a General Power of Attorney (GPA) and an Agreement to Sell in favour of the holder of the GPA. After the owner's death, the holder, in her capacity as a GPA holder, executed a registered sale deed in favour of her son, appellant No. 2.

The respondents contended that the sale deed was executed after the original owner's death and was, therefore, invalid. On the other hand, the respondents claimed that after the death of the original owner, his legal heirs sold the suit property to a person through a registered sale deed.

Later, the person sold the property to another person via another registered sale deed. Finally, the person gifted the suit property to her daughter, the answering respondent, through a registered gift deed.

The High Court ruled in favour of the respondents, and the matter reached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that a power of attorney derives its basic principles from Chapter X of the Contract Act, which provides for 'Agency' along with sections 1A and 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882. The relationship between the executant of a general power of attorney and the holder of the power is one of principal and agent.

A principal is bound by the acts done by an agent or the contracts made by him on behalf of the principal. Likewise, the power of attorney in the nature of the contract of the agency authorizes the holder to do acts specified by the executant or represent the executant in dealings with third persons.

In the present case, it is evident from the contents of the GPA executed by the original owner in favour of the holder that the holder was authorized to manage the property. However, the import of the word 'general' in a POA refers to the power granted concerning the subject matter. The test to determine the nature of POA is the subject matter for which it has been executed. The nomenclature of the POA does not determine its nature. Even a POA termed as a 'general power of attorney' may confer powers that are special in relation to the subject matter. Likewise, a 'special power of attorney' may confer powers that are general in nature concerning the subject matter. The essence lies in the power and not in the subject matter.

The holder of the POA did not choose to register the agreement to sell executed by the original owner in her favour. Even if such an argument were to persuade the Court, the document must have been registered as per section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act. In the absence of such registration, it would not be open for the holder of the POA to contend that she had a valid right, title and interest in the immovable property to execute the registered sale deed in favour of the appellant.

Whether charging rent for displaying advertisement falls under advertising services?

No. The CESTAT in its judgment in the case of CCE v. Azad Publications [2007] 8 STT 242 (Delhi - CESTAT) held that permitting display of advertisement on its site and raising bills for realising rental charge is mere sub-letting to an advertising agency without providing services of the nature defined for advertising services and, hence, the activity of the respondent will not bring it under the definition of ‘advertising agency’.

Whether technical know-how generated for internal consumption sold out later falls under consulting engineer services?

No. In the case of Aksh Optifibers Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 252 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the appellants had developed certain technical know-how for themselves for the purpose of providing e-governance and rural governance in India and had named the project Gramdoot. Since the appellants could not implement the project themselves, they sold the technical know-how by agreement. It was held that since the agreement was for technology transfer and not for providing any technical know-how service and even the ownership of the technical know-how was transferred to the buyer, the demand of service tax was not sustainable.

Whether services provided by express cargo service transporters are different from courier agency services?

No. The Government in its Master Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated 23-8-2007 has clarified that "the nature of service provided by ‘Express Cargo Service’ provider falls within the scope and definition of courier agency".

Whether fee collected by an institution falls under commercial training or coaching services?

No. In the case of Magnus Society v. CC&CE [2009] 18 STT 193 (Bang. - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that education has a larger scope. Education may include coaching or training and not vice versa. Coaching or training is a very narrow activity, imparting skill in a particular discipline. But, education is a broader term, which is a process of development of personality of body, mind and intellect. Just because an institution collects fees from students, one cannot come to conclusion that it imparts commercial training or coaching. Institutions preparing students for entrance exams to universities are covered under commercial training or coaching services and not institutions offering degrees recognized by law.

Whether a computer engineering firm falls under consulting engineer services?

Yes. The Finance Act, 2008, with effect from May 16, 2008, has amended the definition of ‘taxable service’ to bring back the computer software engineering consultancy service under the service tax net and to provide that services provided by a consulting engineer in relation to advice, consultancy or technical assistance in the disciplines of both computer hardware engineering and computer software engineering shall also fall under consulting engineer service.

Whether an organization formed for charitable purposes is liable for service tax?

Yes. The CESTAT in its judgment in the case of Punjab Ex-Servicemen Corpn. v. CCE [2009] 18 STT 121 (New Delhi - CESTAT) held that an organization may be charitable organization established for some purpose, but may still engage in commercial activities, as without any commercial activities, the income required for charitable purpose cannot be generated. For levy of service tax it is the activity of an organization, which is relevant and not objective.

Whether the person manufacturing the sign boards falls under advertising services?

No. In the case of Star Neon Sign v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 223 (New Delhi - CESTAT), it was held that the person who is only writing or preparing the sign boards at the behest of his customers cannot be called as advertising agency. There was no evidence on record to show that the relationship between the customers and the appellant was of advertising agent, which is necessary for imposition of service tax.

Whether assisting a person in acquiring shares in a company falls under management consultant services?

No. In the case of K.R. Alloys Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 20 STT 392 (Bang.- CESTAT), the Tribunal held that the appellants were not carrying out activity of management but they were manufacturers. Incidental help in acquisition of shares does not fall under ‘management consultant service’.

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent services - Wholesale business of Indian made foreign liquor 5.2 The assessee-corporation was established by the State Government with a view to undertake wholesale business of Indian made foreign liquor to ensure good quality at fair price, and to end certain undesirable practices. There was an agreement between the assessee and the various manufacturers/suppliers of liquor under which the manufacturers/suppliers were to supply the liquor on FOR (destination) basis to various depots maintained by the assessee. The assessee was required to sell liquor only to dealers who were licensed by the State Excise Commissioner. The Commissioner had held that ownership of liquor had never been transferred to the assessee; that the invoices were prepared by the assessee on behalf of principal; that it collected the landing price and the commission from the retailers; that it was a consignment agent and the commission paid to the assessee shall be subject to service tax under the heading ‘C&F agent’. Accordingly, he confirmed service tax demand along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner had held that the assessee-corporation was a procurement agent for the State Government.

According to the Tribunal, if that view was accepted, then the assessee would be rendering the services to the State Government and the State Government would become the recipient of services. It had not been shown that the State Government was required to pay any charges to the assessee for the so-called services rendered. In view of the above, the assessee could not be considered as an agent rendering services to the State Government for consideration, in spite of the fact that the agreement between the assessee-corporation and the supplier of liquor referred to the assessee as a procurement agent.

The Tribunal held that as regards the relationship between the assessee and the supplier of the liquor, it was found that transfers were in the nature of sale and purchase. The licence granted to the assessee-corporation was also for purchase and sale of liquor and the agreement clearly referred to prices on F.O.R. destination basis. Overlooking all these evidences, it would not be proper to conclude that there was no sale by the assessee and that it was acting as procurement agent. At any rate, it was not undertaking any agent’s function for the supplier of liquor or the manufacturer supplier of liquor. Notwithstanding the fact that the assessee had chosen to describe its income from sale of liquor as commission in the balance sheet, it was to be viewed that the assessee-corporation was engaged in purchase/sale of liquor and could not be considered as C&F agent.

In CIT v. Anglo India Jute Mills Co. Ltd. [1981] 6 Taxman 54/129 ITR 352 (Cal.) the assessee wanted to purchase certain machinery from abroad. For this purpose, the assessee did all that was necessary for obtaining the permission and getting the import licence. In order to protect itself from fluctuations in the exchange rate, the assessee entered into a forward contract with a bank entitling it to obtain the requisite amount of sterling at the time when the contract came to an end or was required to be performed. The assessee could not get this machinery because the licence expired and, therefore the question of enforcing payment in dollars did not arise. Therefore, the State Bank, pursuant to their commitment, credited the assessee minus the necessary costs, charges and expenses, with the difference between the exchange rate and the assessee got a credit of Rs. 3,13,651. The Court held that the amount was obtained not because the assessee surrendered any licence and not because the assessee gave up its own right under a contract but because the assessee realised its dues or, in other words, the assessee transformed its rights under the contract into money. Therefore, neither was there any transfer nor was there any profit arising therefrom. In that background of facts there was no cost of acquisition and, therefore, there could not be any capital gains in respect of such an asset. Accordingly, the sum of Rs. 3,13,651 could not be considered to be capital gains in terms of section 45. However, it appears that the chargeability to tax under the head 'business' could not be disputed.

There was a difference between a payment made as compensation for the termination of an agency contract and an amount paid as solatium for the cancellation of a contract entered into by a businessman in the ordinary course of business. In an agency contract, the actual business consists in the dealings between the principal and his customers, and the work of the agent is only to bring about that business. What he does is not the business itself but something which is intimately and directly linked up with it. The agency may, therefore, be viewed as the apparatus which leads to the business rather than the business itself. Considered in this light, the agency can be held to be of the nature of a capital asset invested in business. But this cannot be said of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business. 'Performing specific services', meaning of - The words 'performing specific service' mean conferring particular benefits on the members. With reference to a trade, professional or similar association, the performing of specific services must mean conferring on its members some tangible benefit which otherwise would not be available to them as such except for payment received by the association in respect of those services. Thus, amount received in the nature of entrance fee and other subscription fees from its members for allowing their application for enlisting names of companies not already on quotations list so that shares and stocks of said companies might be placed on the stock market chargeable to tax u/s 28(iii) [CIT v. 2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : “An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

2.2-12 Sale and lease back - It may be noted that if an intangible asset is sold and then taken for use from the transferee, Explanation 4A to section 43(1) may apply if the transferor has already obtained depreciation on the asset. Under this Explanation, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on the written down value of the transferor at time of transfer of the intangible asset, although he may have acquired the intangible asset for a higher sum. To illustrate, if the written down value of an intangible asset is Rs. 20 lakhs in the hands of the transferor and if he sells the asset for Rs. 50 lakhs, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on Rs. 20 lakhs by virtue of the provisions of Explanation 4A.

It may be noted that the aforesaid Explanation does not apply if the transferor has not claimed any depreciation on the intangible asset. In such an event, the actual cost for the transferee shall not be restricted to the written down value of the transferor and he will get depreciation on his cost of acquisition.

CIT [2024] 165 taxmann.com 271 (Delhi) through an interesting and illuminating judgment dated 7th August, 2024 by reversing the order passed by the ITAT Delhi Bench, has held that where assessee received a lump sum amount from company towards full and final settlement of all disputes and differences with it and in terms of settlement agreement, assessee unconditionally and irrevocably relinquished all his rights in respect of registration of shares held by him and to consequently handover share certificates in original to company, the said settlement amount was not liable to be construed as payment connected to termination of assessee's employment and, thus, was liable to be recognized as capital gain.

The assessee, an individual, derived income from salary and capital gains during the assessment year 2014-15. It was submitted before the Assessing Officer that the assessee was offered 50,000 equity shares of TTPL as on 8th June, 2010, in which he was employed with effect from 1st December, 2007 at a purchase cost of NIL and the assessee relinquished the same shares on 23rd January, 2014 for a sum of Rs. 303.75 lakhs thus earning a long-term capital gain of same amount.

The Assessing Officer called for the details of Grant date, Vesting date, Exercise date and Exercise price with reference to the said shares sold. These shares were offered in instalments of 7,500 shares each over a period of four years with 7,500 shares options maturing on completion of each year of service of the company starting from 1st December, 2007. These shares represented 3% of the paid-up capital of the company. The appointment of the assessee was terminated in the month of August 2010 and the assessee approached the Company Law Board against this termination and the Company Law Board vide order dated 29th March, 2012 ordered 'status quo'.

However, an agreement styled as "Settlement Agreement" dated 23rd January, 2014 was entered into between the assessee and TTP Ltd. as a result of which 50,000 shares were allotted to the assessee as on 8th June, 2010.

The Assessing Officer treated the entire money realised by the assessee "as profits in lieu of salary" as defined in Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act.

CIT [2000] 243 ITR 158, held that cancellation of sale of assets cannot be such a subsequent event so as to change the nature of the receipt of the forfeited amount. 6.15-2e WHETHER A RECEIPT IS CAPITAL OR REVENUE - The principles that can be deduced from various decisions of the Indian and the foreign courts for determining whether a particular amount received by an assessee is capital or revenue in nature are as under :

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

■ Profit motive is not decisive of the question, whether a particular receipt is capital or income.7

■ The question whether the payer is compelled to pay has no relevance in the determination of the character of the receipt. It may be that the payee has no legal claim for payment and the payment is made voluntarily, yet the receipt may be of revenue character.8

A voluntary payment is a profit of employment if it accrues by virtue of the employment notwithstanding that there may not be any legal obligation to make the payment. If, however, the payment is in the nature of a personal gift to him, it is not regarded as a payment for services but as a mere present.8

■ The voluntary payment to a lawyer by a person who is not a client but who has benefited by the lawyer’s professional services to another is taxable.1

■ The fund out of which the money came is not material.2

■ General payments made by way of donation to a company out of benevolence or feeling of charity would not entail income in the hands of the recipient.3

■ Amounts received in settlement of a right under trading contract are trading receipts.4

6.15-2f COMPENSATION - WHETHER REVENUE OR CAPITAL - About the receipt of compensation the law is that as discussed below :

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

■ Compensation for surrender of industrial licence - In CIT v. Automobile Products of India Ltd.1, the Bombay High Court held that where the termination of the activity is not a necessary incident of the business of the assessee and the extinction and surrender of the industrial licence and the collaboration agreement have impaired the profit-making structure of the assessee, the amount received by it as compensation will be a capital receipt.

Extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset

The booklet "How to compute capital gains published by the Income Tax Department" explains 'extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset' as under:

"This covers every possible transaction which results in destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation of all or any bundle of rights in a capital asset."

For example, termination of a lease or of a mortgagee interest in a property. In the case of CIT v. Grace Collis [2001] 115 taxmann 326 (SC) the Supreme Court held that the definition of 'transfer' in section 2(47) also contemplates the extinguishment consequent upon the transfer thereof.

Therefore, the expression 'transfer' does include the extinguishment of rights in a capital asset independent of and otherwise than on account of transfer.

Tracing the history of "extinguishment of rights"

If legislative history is traced, the Indian Income-tax Act 1922(the 1922 Act) did not contain any specific provision corresponding to section 2(47) of the Act defining 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset, though section 12B of the 1922 Act relating to capital gains spoke of "sale, exchange or transfer", as attracting capital gains. The "transfer" was mentioned in juxtaposition of "sale and exchange"- The term juxtaposition means the fact of two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect.

Reference to relinquishment was not mentioned in the said provision. Section 12B of the 1922 Act was recast by the Finance (No.3) Act,1956 wherein it was mentioned that ".the tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head "Capital Gains" in respect of any profits or gains arising from the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer of a capital asset effected after the 31st day of March, 1956, and such profits and gains shall be deemed to be income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place" In other words, the phrase " relinquishment" was added but the other phrase "extinguishment of any rights (therein)" about which this discussion centers around was placed in a separate clause by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1984 with effect from 01-04-1985 when the section 2(47) of the Act was recast apparently with the object of avoiding any ambiguity and repetition of the expression in the charging section though the phrase " extinguishment of any rights (therein)" had also been in the statute book since the inception of the 1961 Act itself.

This clause gives an artificially extended meaning to the expression 'transfer' and expands the same to include the cases of extinguishment of any rights and the compulsory acquisition which were conspicuous by their absence in the 1922 Act.

The Supreme Court as early as 21st February 1978 in the case of Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 803/2 SCC 50 (a Bench consisting of 7 Hon'ble Judges) with regard to transfer of a right in a property by extinguishment observed as under-

His right to receive the sum of Rs. 1,50,000 was only going to arise or accrue either on retirement or on death in the manner provided in the indenture. 6.1-2 Contracts 'relating' to business

The amended section 28(ii)(e) covers any contract "relating" to the business. Hence, it would cover contracts relating to purchases, sales or services or any other aspect of a business including joint venture agreements, distribution, etc.

6.1-3 Contracts 'relating' to acquisition of capital assets

Since the amended section is very widely worded it would cover contracts relating to acquisition of capital assets and hence on a literal reading, the compensation or other payment at or in connection with termination of such contract would be taxable as business income under section 28(ii)(e). On the other hand, Courts have held that giving up the right to obtain conveyance of immovable property or to claim specific performance is a transfer, assessable as capital gains [CIT v. Smt. Laxmidevi Ratani [2005] 147 Taxman 642 (MP); CIT v. Vijay Flexible Container [1990] 48 Taxman 86 (Bom.); Asian PPG Industries Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 38 SOT 114 (Mum. - Trib.); Asstt. CIT v. United Motors (I) Ltd. [2009] 32 SOT 399 (Mum. - Trib.)]

Thus, it is possible that a receipt is taxable as capital gains as well as under section 28(ii)(e) on its literal reading, if such receipt is in connection with the termination of the contract. In such circumstances, it could be argued that the provision may be so construed as being applicable to cases other than those relating to transfer of a capital asset. See for instance a case such as Patel Brass Works v. CIT [2007] 163 Taxman 279 (Guj.). In CIT v. T. P. Sidhwa [1981] 6 Taxman 91 (Bom.), the Bombay High Court explained the Supreme Court judgment in Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v. CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 and stated that "whether an income falls under one head or the other has to be decided according to the common notion of practical men, for the Act does not provide any guidance in the matter. In other words, the heads of income must be decided on the nature of the income by applying practical common notion and not by reference to the assessee's treatment of income". Now, under the common notion, gains of the type mentioned above should fall under capital gains and not profits and gains of business which is ordinarily not meant to cover capital receipts.

Further, the Explanatory Memorandum reads as follows:

"Under the existing provisions of the Act, certain types of compensation receipts are taxable as business income under section 28. However, the existing provisions of clause (ii) of section 28 is restrictive in its scope as far as taxation of compensation is concerned; a large segment of compensation receipts in connection with business and employment is out of the purview of taxation leading to base erosion and revenue loss."

Thus, the intent is to bring within the scope of the law cases that presently fall outside resulting in base erosion and revenue loss and not cases which are already covered under the head capital gains.

Therefore, the purpose of clause 16(e) is that the In-come-tax Department can examine the receipts that are not recorded in the profit and loss account based on the argument that they are capital receipts to deter-mine their classification as either capital or not.

It is well settled that capital receipts are not liable to income tax unless specifically made taxable by the Income-tax Act. The capital receipts that are taxable under section 28 of the Act, if not recorded, are to be reported under clause 16(a). The capital receipts other than these are reported under clause 16(e).

Redemption of preference shares is relinquishment and transfer

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 509 (SC) the Court held that redemption of preference shares is clearly 'sale' by the shareholder to the company and would come within the purview of 'transfer' in view of the following:

A reading of sections 77, 80 and 85 of the Companies Act, 1956 [now sections 67, 55 and 43 of the Companies Act, 2013] makes it clear that when a preference share is redeemed by a company, what a shareholder does is, to sell the shares to the company. Such a transaction is nothing but sale of the preference shares by the shareholder to the company.

That is why after specifically laying down in section 77(1) of the said Act [now section 67(1) of the 2013 Act] that no company shall have the power to buy its own shares, it was necessary to specify in sub-section (5) thereof [sub-section (4) of section 67 of the 2013 Act] that this provision shall not affect the rights of a company to redeem any preference shares issued by it.

If redemption of preference shares did not amount to sale, it would not have been necessary to specifically provide that the restriction imposed upon a company in respect of buying its own shares will not apply to redemption of preference shares issued by the company.

The Court held that the assessee had purchased the preference shares at less than face value. When the shares were redeemed by the company, she received more than what she had paid for the shares. In order to get this amount the assessee had to give up or abandon or surrender the shares held by her. The meaning of the word 'relinquish' as given in Webster's Comprehensive Dictionary International Edition 1984, is: (1) to give up; abandon; surrender, (2) to cease to demand; renounce; to relinquish a claim, (3) to let go (a hold or something held).

The assessee in this case gave up the shares and received in lieu thereof a sum of money. This came clearly within the mischief of section 2(47)(i). That apart, the transaction amounted to sale.

In the instant case, the preference shares were held as capital assets. The excess amount received by the shareholder on redemption of these shares would have to be treated as capital gain in view of section 2(47), read with section 4. Accordingly, the assessee's case squarely came within section 2(47)(i).

6.15-5D Capital gains - Profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset are chargeable to income-tax under the head ‘Capital gains’. The charging section envisages transfer of capital asset and the profits and gains arising on account of such transfer.

The expression ‘transfer’ has been defined in section 2(47) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 as including sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any rights therein, or compulsory acquisition thereof; or conversion of a capital asset into stock-in-trade, or transaction involving the allowance of the possession which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of an immovable property, etc.

Since the transfer as contemplated is one as a result whereof consideration has passed to the assessee or has accrued to him, extinguishment or relinquishment of rights must relate to that ‘capital asset’ corporeal or incorporeal. It is, therefore, obvious that transfer of a capital asset in order to attract liability to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ must be a ‘transfer’ as a result whereof some consideration is received by or accrues to the assessee. If the transfer does not yield any consideration, there can be no question of capital gains. If the transfer takes effect on extinguishment of a right in the capital asset, there must be receipt of consideration for such extinguishment to attract liability to tax.1

The word ‘transfer’ also covers cases which result in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise of all or any of the bundle of rights which a person has in the capital assets.1 It is only when consideration is received in respect thereof.

The word ‘transfer’ is comprehensive and is regarded generally as comprehending within its scope transfers both voluntary and involuntary. In the absence of a distinct genus or category, no presumption can arise that the word ‘transfer’ in section 2(47) must be construed in the sense of a voluntary transfer, because the words ‘sale’, ‘exchange’ and ‘relinquishment’ are in the normal acceptation of those terms voluntary acts, and, therefore, if an existing title of a capital asset is extinguished and a new one created, there is within the meaning of section 2(47) a ‘transfer’ of capital asset, and the fact that the divestiture of title takes place under a law relating to compulsory acquisition of property would make no difference. The compulsory acquisition of capital asset may be a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 2(47), but is not sale. These expressions are not synonymous conveying the same meaning. Had this been so, and also the expression ‘sale’ as embracing within its scope ‘compulsory acquisition’ of an asset, there would have been no need to refer to both these expressions in the inclusive definition of ‘transfer’ in section 2(47). One of the purposes of the inclusive definition is to expand the concept defined. The meaning of the expression ‘transfer’ was extended to cover the compulsory acquisition of an asset along with sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any right therein, etc.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

Corporate veil lifting - Tax avoidance

The courts have been stepping into pierce the corporate veil when fiscal or legal obligations are sought to be bypassed by a corporate entity. The Supreme Court has upheld the right of the tax authorities to go behind the corporate façade to look at the economic realities of transactions, if the shell of the corporate entity is used for tax evasions or to circumvent tax obligations [see Juggilal Kamlapat v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 702 (SC) and CIT v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd. [1967] 63 ITR 609 (SC)]. The courts have been upholding the revenue’s right to disregard the consequences of transactions even in respect of those which are genuinely undertaken if their purpose is to avoid tax that would otherwise be payable. The taxing authority is entitled and is indeed bound to determine the true legal relations resulting from a transaction. If the parties have chosen to conceal by a device the legal relation, it is open to the taxing authority to unravel the device and determine the true character of the relationship. It is the duty of the court, in every case where ingenuity is expended to avoid and taxing legislation, to go behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs. The court is not be satisfied with form and leave well alone the substance of a transaction [Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. v. Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. [1986] 157 ITR 77 (SC)/Ess Ess Kay Engg. Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 151 ITR 636 (Punj. & Har.)]

In Juggilal Kamlapat’s case the Supreme Court exercised the right of unraveling a colourable device of tax evasion. In that case the assessee- firm was a managing agent of a company. Three brothers held majority of shares in the company as well as in the firm. The company asked the assessee to arrange for finance to pay off a loan taken from a sister-company and when the assessee regretted its inability to arrange the finances, the company decided to terminate the managing agency, by paying a compensation of Rs. 2 lakhs. The managing agency was entrusted to another sister-company which was newly floated, in which also the aforesaid three brothers held majority of shares. The Tribunal held that the reason for terminating the managing agency was not a true reason but was merely a fake one and the whole transaction was a hoax for the purpose of evading income-tax both in the hands of the payer and the payee. The Tribunal also found that that there was only a change of personnel in the managing agency and not a change in office and that the assessee had no right of compensation for any loss of office. The question for consideration was whether the compensation received by the assessee could be treated as capital receipt on the ground that it arose out of the destruction of capital asset, viz., the managing agency. The Supreme Court held that the managing agency business carried on by the assessee- firm was not destroyed or lost to the four individual partners who constituted the assessee-firm. What happened was that the individuals who constituted the assessee-firm became the directors of the newly- formed company and in this new capacity they undertook the conduct of the managing agency business and as shareholders continued to benefit from the profits of that business flowing to them in the shape of dividend instead of as a share of profits from the assessee-firm. In other words, the managing-agency asset was enjoyed by four individual partners in a different capacity with the same object of profit-making. There was, therefore, no destruction of the apparatus of the profit- making asset, i.e., the managing agency contract. It was obvious that there was an intimate connection in this case between the managing agency business of the assessee-firm and the payment of a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs and, therefore, this amount represented as a revenue receipt. While so upholding, the Supreme Court laid a proposition that the court is entitled to lift the mask of corporate entity if the corporation is used for tax evasion or to circumvent tax obligation or to perpetrate fraud.

Entries in account books - The date of sale or transfer is the date when the sale or transfer takes place, and for the purpose of determining that date, entries in the account books are irrelevant [Alapati Venkataramiah v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 185 (SC)].

Signing of agreement - Capital gains would be charged only on receipt of sale consideration after development of land; and not when agreement was signed for development of land [CIT v. Smt. Najoo Dara Deboo [2013] 38 taxmann.com 258/218 Taxman 473 (All.)].

Registration of sale deed - In order to attract section 45, it should be established that, by the transfer, the title to the property stands passed to the purchaser. If what was sold was immovable property, it should further be established that the same was conveyed by a registered deed. It is the date of execution of the registered deed, and not the date of delivery of possession, that will be relevant in such circumstances, for on that date alone the title to property passes [CIT v. F. X. Periera & Sons (Travancore) (P.) Ltd. [1991] 55 Taxman 242 (Ker.)]. Also see, R. Krishnaswamy v. CIT [2014] 43 taxmann.com 177/222 Taxman 270 (Mad.).

Receipt of part consideration - Where, on transfer of shareholding, assessee received only a part of sale consideration and balance amount was to be received in succeeding years, in such a case, whole of such sale consideration would be chargeable to tax in year of transfer of shares [Potla Nageswara Rao v. Contingent payment - Merely because the agreement provides for payment of the balance of consideration upon the happening of certain events, it cannot be said that the income has not accrued in the year of transfer [Ajay Guliya v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 24 taxmann.com 276/209 Taxman 295 (Del.)].

Possession given - Where actual possession of property was given to developer vide agreement dated 30-4-2001, transfer u/s 2(47) would be considered to take place in year of agreement, and not in year when power of attorney was executed to give access to developer to do certain jobs on said land [Dr. Joao Souza Proenca v. Receipts of Advocate-General - Amount (such as retainer fee) received by the Advocate-General of the State from the State, though styled as 'salary', is assessable under the head 'PGBP' [CIT v. Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 22/244 Taxman 188 (SC)].

Margin money - Where assessee-bank in the course of its business, purchased securities for its constituents on receiving certain percentage of face value called 'margin money in deposit' and as constituents failed to pay balance amount of purchase value of securities, on stipulated date fixed therefor, margin money was forfeited and securities became property of assessee, margin money so forfeited was to be assessed as business income of assessee [CIT v. Lakshmi Vilas Bank Ltd. [1996] 86 Taxman 231 (SC)].

Brokerage income - In case of a broker, the activities are carried on either under a written agreement or even verbal agreement in respect of different constituents and since the activities would amount to business, therefore, income from brokerage held to be business income [CIT v. Bhagwan Broker Agency [1993] 70 Taxman 453 (Raj.)].

Management/advisory fees - Management and advisory fee received by assessee engaged in dealing in shares, investments, loan, finance and related activities, is business income of the assessee, irrespective of the fact as to whether assessee has not substantiated sum incurred to earn same [CIT v. Ashok Mittal [2014] 41 taxmann.com 115/221 Taxman 233 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

Futures and options transactions - Income from futures and options transactions and daily trading in shares carried with business motive mainly through stockbroker registered with NSE and BSE was taxable as business income [CIT v. Om Prakash Suri (No. 1) [2014] 46 taxmann.com 242/225 Taxman 123 (Mag.) (MP)].

Dharmada or charity - Since the dharmada amount was clearly not a part of the price but a payment for the specific purpose of being spent on charitable purposes, therefore, it could not be regarded as the assessee's income chargeable to income-tax [CIT v. Bijli Cotton Mills (P.) Ltd. [1979] 116 ITR 60 (SC)].

Subsidies - Subsidies for reimbursement of cost incurred in production of goods are includible under the head "PGBP" [CIT v. Meghalaya Steels Ltd. [2016] 67 taxmann.com 158/238 Taxman 559 (SC)].

Compensation for loss/damage to stock-in-trade - Where payment is made by insurance company to compensate for loss of use of any goods in which the assessee does not carry on any business or the payment is a just equivalent of the cost incurred by the assessee, but excess accrues due to fortuitous circumstances or is windfall, then the accrual may be a receipt, but it would not be income arising from business [Universal Radiators v. CIT [1993] 68 Taxman 45 (SC)].

If any amount is received as compensation for an injury which affects a capital asset of the assessee or the capital structure of the assessee's business, such amount may normally be considered to be a capital receipt. If, however, any amount is received by an assessee as compensation or damages for any wrong done which does not affect any capital asset or the capital structure of the assessee's business but causes injury to the assessee in its trade, such amount will normally constitute a trading receipt of the assessee [CIT v. Siewart & Dholakia (P.) Ltd. [1974] 95 ITR 573 (Cal.)].

Where on account of damage to assessee-company's stock-in-trade pledged with bank to obtain overdraft, bank agreed to adjust overdraft amount against assessee's claim for damages, since amount so received represented compensation for loss or damage to stock-in-trade, it constituted a trading receipt and was assessable to tax irrespective of fact whether assessee had or had not claimed loss or damage to stock-in-trade, as and when it occurred [Ramesh Narain Saxena v. CIT [1996] 86 Taxman 65 (SC)].

Damages for non-performance - Where assessee received payment on settlement of damages for non-performance of contract by sellers and that non-performance was for reasons beyond control of assessee, said payment was to be treated as business income and not income by way of speculative transaction [CIT v. Premier Vegetable Products Ltd. [2014] 50 taxmann.com 418/227 Taxman 259 (Raj.)].

FACT: The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

27. In Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC) the Appellant, Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. ('KBCL') was a managing agent of six companies including Fort Williams Jute Co. (FWJC). KBCL entered into an agreement with Mugneeram Bangur & Co. The question was whether the amount received by KBCL to relinquish the managing agency was a revenue receipt liable to tax. It was held that by relinquishing the managing agency, KBCL parted with an asset of an enduring nature. It mattered little that the KBCL did continue to conduct the remaining managing agency of other companies even after the termination of its agency with FWJC. It was held that it cannot be said as general rule that what is determinative of the nature of a receipt on the cancellation of a contract of agency or office is the extinction or compulsory cessation of the agency or office. Where payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business or deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business, and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated), the receipt is revenue; where by the cancellation of an agency the trading structure of the Assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss or what may be regarded as the source of the Assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipt. This test was followed in Oberoi Hotel (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 903/103 Taxman 236 (SC).
