Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee was managing agent of company F - It entered into agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company - 'M' also agreed to compensate assessee for loss of office - Subsequently, assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of company - Accordingly, assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation received by assessee to relinquish managing agency could not be regarded as revenue receipt and, thus, it was not liable to tax - Held, yes

It has been laid down in a number of decision that when an expenditure is made with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, there is good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to the opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as property attributable not to revenue but to capital.

From the facts found in the instant case it was clear that the managing agency was terminated on business considerations and as a matter of commercial expediency. There was no basis for holding that by terminating the managing agency, the company acquired any enduring benefit or any income yielding asset. It is true that by terminating the services of the managing agents, the company not only saved the expense that it would have had to incur in the relevant previous year but also for few more years to come. It would not be correct to say that by avoiding certain business expenditure, the company could be said to have acquired enduring benefits or acquired any income yielding asset. Thus, the compensation paid for termination of the services of the managing agents was a revenue expenditure.

Note : The decision was in favour of the assessee.

The assessee carried on business as merchants and also as managing agents and agents of a many companies and firms. They were appointed as managing agents of company 'C' but there was nothing in the articles regarding their appointment for any fixed term of years. There was no contract actually executed between the company and the assessee for their services as managing agents of the company. It was not at the option of the company to very the remuneration from time to time and the assessees were at liberty to terminate their own appointment as managing agents at their option. On 16-01-1925 company 'C' was wound up voluntarily. Certain amount was paid to the assessee as compensation for their loss of office as managing agents of the company. The assessee claimed that sum as a receipt of casual non-recurring nature not arising from business or the exercise of a profession, vocation or occupation and so exempt under section 4(3)(vii)of the 1922 Act. The ITO considered the sum as a receipt from business and included it in their income for purposes of assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessment. On reference, the Commissioner also took the same view which was taken by the ITO.

In view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spg. & Wvg. Co. Ltd. [1954] 24 Comp. Cas. 103, 110; AIR 1954 SC 119, 123, it could be said that the right of management being property had to be equated to a capital asset as being a part of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee and, for that reason, compensation paid for divesting the assessee of its management was compensation for acquisition of part of its profit-making apparatus and must be of a capital receipt rather than a revenue receipt or income.

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Senairam Doongarmall v. CIT [1961] 42 ITR 392 : (1962) 1 SCR 257 (SC), in the instant case, the assessee having been divested of its management did not and could not carry on business in the sense of carrying on an activity with the object of earning profit by a process of production. The divesting of its management was really divesting the assessee of its property. The compensation paid was, therefore, for the loss of a capital asset. The mere fact that the compensation paid to the assessee-company was measured by its past profits did not make the compensation paid the income of the assessee, as a result of business done by it. The compensation paid to the assessee was not income.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether share of a partner in partnership concern is property and, thus, a capital assest within meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Assessee and ‘G’ were partners in three partnership firms which were managing agents of three mills - Assessee’s share in one concern was transferred to ‘G’ in exchange for G’s share in other concerns and additional sum of Rs. 1,00,000 - Whether transaction in question involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets and had all elements of sale and, thus, sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was assessable to tax as capital gains - Held, yes

HELD: Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

The Supreme Court in the case of Karam Chand Thapar & Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1971] 80 ITR 167 had held that ordinarily compensation for loss of an office or agency is regarded as capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and that its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. The Court further held that it was difficult to lay down a precise principle of universal application but various workable rules have been evolved for guidance.

Applying the aforesaid test laid down, in the present case, it was to be held that the Tribunal was right in arriving at a conclusion that it was a capital receipt. Reason is that as provided in article XVIII of the first agreement, assessee was having an option or right or lien, if owner desired to transfer the hotel or lease all or part of the hotel to any other person, the same was required to be offered first to the assessee (operator) or its nominee. This right to exercise its option was given up by a supplementary agreement which was executed between the receiver and the assessee. It was agreed that the receiver would be at liberty to sell or otherwise dispose of the said property at such price and on such terms as he may deem fit and was not under any obligation requiring the purchaser thereof to enter into any agreement with the operator (assessee) for the purpose of operating and managing the hotel or otherwise and in its return, agreed consideration was as stated above in clause X. On the basis of the said agreement, the assessee had received the amount in question. The amount was received because the assessee had given up its right to purchase and/or to operate the property. Further, it was loss of source of income to the assessee and that right was determined for consideration. Obviously, therefore, it was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt.

After analysing number of cases, the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 had observed that the following satisfactory measure of consistency in the principle was disclosed : 'where on a consideration of the circumstances, payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business, nor deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated), the receipt is revenue : Whereby the cancellation of an agency, the trading structure of the assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss of what may be regarded as the source of the assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipts'.

Considering the aforesaid principles laid down, as per article XVIII of the principal agreement, the amount received by the assessee was for the consideration for giving up his right to purchase and/or to operate the property or for getting it on lease before it was transferred or let out to other persons. It was not for settlement of rights under trading contract, but the injury was inflicted on the capital asset of the assessee and giving up the contractual right on the basis of principal agreement had resulted in loss of source of the assessee's income. Therefore, the amount received was a capital receipt.

There could be no doubt that by paying the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 the managed company had secured for itself a release from the obligation to pay a higher remuneration to the assessee for the rest of the period of managing agency covered by the principal agreement. Prima facie, that release from liability to pay a higher remuneration for over 17 years must be an advantage gained by the managed company for the benefit of its business and the immunity thus obtained by the managed company might well be regarded as the acquisition of an asset of enduring value by means of a capital outlay which would be a capital expenditure.

In the resolution adopted by the managed company as well as in the recitals set out in the supplementary agreement that sum had been stated to be a payment "as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous term as to remuneration contained" in the principal agreement. It was true that the language used in the document was not decisive and the question had to be determined by a consideration of all the attending circumstances; nevertheless, the language could not be ignored altogether but must be taken into consideration along with other relevant circumstances.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued.

A managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at the rate of 20 per cent of the profits was not the same thing as a managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at 10 per cent of the profits. There was a distinct deterioration in the character and quality of the managing agency viewed as a profit-making apparatus and this deterioration was of an enduring kind. The reduced remuneration having been separately provided, the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 must be regarded as having been paid as compensation for that injury to or deterioration of the managing agency.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid and received not to make up the difference between the higher remuneration and the reduced remuneration but was in reality paid and received as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous terms as to remuneration as it was in terms expressed to be. In other words, so far as the managed company was concerned, it was paid for securing immunity from the liability to pay higher remuneration to the assessee firm for the rest of the term of the managing agency and, therefore, a capital expenditure and so far as the assessee firm was concerned, it was received as compensation for the deterioration or injury to the managing agency by reason of the release of its rights to get higher remuneration and, therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax.

Had it been a case where the move for the purchase of the shares came from other parties and the assessee as and when any offer was made to it disposed of the shares, it could have justifiably inferred that the intention of the assessee was to keep these shares as an investment, that is to say, as a capital asset, the disposal of which under such circumstances not leading to any revenue income. But that the assessee, within less than a week after the acquisition of the shares started to invite offers for the sales of these shares, necessarily drove to the conclusion that even at the time of the acquisition of the shares the assessee must have had the intention of selling the shares.

The result was that the inference reached by the Tribunal that it was an adventure in the nature of trade which yielded the profit in question was amply supported by adequate material.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The head under which income would be chargeable under section 176(3A) need not necessarily be ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’ and the head under which such income would be chargeable would depend on the circumstances in which recipient received the amount. In the instant case, the firm was, no doubt ‘ carrying on business of builders and contractors and it was in the course of that business that the agreement dated 9-11-1963 was entered into. However, the fact remained that the firm never obtained possession of the land. It had not paid full price of the land. It had paid only earnest money. The firm did not acquire any right, title or interest in said land. The only right it had, at the time of agreement, was right of obtaining specific performance from the vendor. Even that right came to an end when the land was acquired by the Government by notification. The right that survived was thereafter right to obtain appropriate share in the compensation that would be paid by the Government to the vendor as a result of compulsory acquisition. In these circumstances, it could not be said that land in question was stock-in-trade of the firm at any moment of time.

It is now well-settled that the property allotted to a partner on dissolution of the firm is capital asset in his hands. In the instant case, therefore, one-fifth share in the interest under agreement dated 9-11-1963 was a capital asset in the hands of the assessee on the date of dissolution and the gains received by him on receipt of his share of compensation would, therefore, be capital gains chargeable under section 45.

Accordingly, the matter was restored to the ITO with direction to compute the capital gains and bring them to tax in accordance with law after giving exemption under section 54E, if the assessee was so entitled.

It was apparent from records that the consideration received by the assessee, if any, was to be bifurcated into two parts—one for relinquishment of right over the property and another for facilitating the peaceful possession to the vendee. However, the Assessing Officer considered the entire consideration received as income of the assessee without mentioning the head of income under which he assessed it, which was not proper. [Para 7.5]

Further, there were two agreements of sale—one for 3 acres and another for 7 acres dated 6-1-2006. As per these agreements of sale-cum -general power of attorney, the vendor had delivered the vacant possession of the scheduled property to the vendee. As per the provision of section 2(47 ) transfer takes place as soon as the possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of property Act, 1882. Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

The issue was concluded by the decision in the case of CIT v. Mangtu Ram Jaipuria [1991] 192 ITR 533 (Cal.) where it had been held that where there was no cost of acquisition for the tenancy right, there could be no changeability in respect of the consideration received for transfer or surrender of tenancy rights, to tax as capital gains.

Hence, the Tribunal was justified in holding that extinguishment of tenancy right was not exigible to capital gains.

The perception of the Assessing Officer that there was no requirement for ‘B’ to pay consideration for goodwill to the assessee-company as it was a mere transporter and not a distributor and dealer in soft drinks was not borne out by record or evidence. On the contrary, the statistics submitted by the assessee showed that it was marketing products of ‘S’ as distributor and there was substantial improvement in the business of the assessee. Further, the agreement of goodwill showed that ‘B’ acknowledged the fact that the assessee-company had goodwill and had agreed to pay for the same. The basis on which such goodwill was to be quantified was given in the agreement itself. The Assessing Officer could not simply state that he disbelieved the agreement, as in his perception there was no goodwill whatsoever, that too without any rhyme or reason. Hence, the observation made by the Assessing Officer that the agreement in question was a make-believe agreement was without an iota of evidence. Thus, the order of the appellate authority to tax amount of goodwill under capital gain was to be upheld. [Paras 27 and 29]

Section 50(2) refers to block of assets ceasing to exist as such by reason of transfer of the entire ‘block of assets’. The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. Even if it was taken as a capital asset, in view of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Ambica Chemical Production v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal No. 238/V/2002, dated 26-5-2005] no tax was leviable in terms of section 45 on the amount received by the assessee. [Para 30]

Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld. [Para 32]

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

The very fact that the board was prepared to go to such lengths and offer a much higher price than the ruling market price for the share showed their anxiety to buy the shares even at a considerable premium only with an eye to some other advantage, namely, the acquisition of the managing agency. If it were a purely business deal, there was no reason why the board should not have ensured that the purchase was made at the prevailing market rate which on that day was much lower. The bona fides of the transactions had not been challenged and, therefore, the extra rate sanctioned and the extra rate per share actually offered would, in court's opinion, clearly indicated an object other than the mere object of making profit in the way of business from the shares. To commence with, therefore, it was clear that the intention of the company was to buy the shares only with a view to acquiring the controlling interest in the NGME Ltd. and, thereby acquiring its managing agency.

The shares were purchased and sold within a short time, but that they were sold within a short time might equally be compatible with the shares being sold in the ordinary course of business as being sold on capital account because the assessee-company failed to attain its main objective, namely, the acquisition of the managing agency of the company whose shares they had been purchased. It all depended upon the circumstances established. Therefore, not much could be made of the fact that the shares were sold away within a short time after their purchase. The intention of the assessee-company in purchasing the shares. The dealings of the company with those shares after the purchase clearly indicated that their whole intention was to purchase the shares with a view to acquiring the managing agency and not with a view to dealing with those shares in the way of business. At the time of sale also, that in the case of the first lot of shares of NGME Ltd. as well as the second lot of the ACE Ltd., appropriate resolutions were passed by the board of directors and each resolution clearly explains the reason why those shares were being sold so abruptly. In the case of NGME shares it was clear that the objective failed because the then managing agents already had held more than 50 per cent of the shares of the company and it was impossible for the assessee-company to get hold of the managing agency. The main objective having failed, those shares were naturally sold off. So far as the ACE shares were concerned, it was clear not only from the resolution authorising their sale, but also from the correspondence and the alarming reports that the company was in a very bad way and acquiring the managing agency of such a company would not only reflect adversely upon the assessee, but cause them difficulty at the time of resale. Collectively, the assessee would also be involved in the misfeasance or misconduct of the erstwhile managing agents.

It is now settled law that where shares in a company are purchased as a part of the transaction of acquiring the managing agency of the company, the shares purchased for that purpose would themselves be of a capital nature and any profit or loss resulting from the purchase or sale of such shares cannot be treated as a revenue loss or profit, but must be treated as a profit or loss on capital account. The sole object and intention of the dealings in shares of the assessee in question before the Court was the acquisition of the managing agencies of the companies whose shares they had purchased and the managing agency itself would undoubtedly be a capital asset. Therefore, whatever gain accrued as a result would be on capital account.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. [1979] 120 ITR 913 held that the additional remuneration was approved only after the audited balance sheet and the profit and loss account were placed before the General Body Meeting of the managing companies and approved in the said General Body Meeting; therefore, the additional remuneration would be assessable in the year in which it was approved.

On reference : HELD: In identical situation in the case of South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Madras High Court held that in the absence of inadequacy of the profit, under the agreement, the managing agent was entitled to the minimum remuneration payable at such rate for each year and insofar as the additional remuneration was concerned, there was no provision in the agreement as to when it accrued. The High Court held that in the absence of any provision in the agreement as to when it accrued, it accrued at the time when it became payable to the assessee. Similarly, on the facts of the case, the contract was silent as to when the amount became due and in the absence of any material, it was to be held that it was not possible to treat the amount as being due on the last date of the accounting year. An agency contract cannot always be considered as a profit earning apparatus, so as to render any compensation for an injury caused to that contract to be treated as a capital receipt. Where the work of an agent is to bring about the business between his principal and his customers, the agency would be the apparatus which leads to the business and, therefore, so far as the agent is concerned, a capital asset. But where, however, the assessee has a business in taking up agency on behalf of others, i.e., the agency is one of the business which the assessee has, such business could be held to be a circulating capital or stock-in-trade, and the compensation received in respect of injury thereto would be a revenue receipt.

Where a partnership is entered into for the purpose of doing one of the items of the business, it cannot be said that the partnership is a structure of the business, but on the other hand it would be one entered into in the ordinary course of its business.

The assessee was a firm engaged in the production of films. Tamil film was not its only venture; it was only a part of its business activity. It had already started production of another picture. It had also engaged artists for the production of said Tamil film. It was only during the course of its production that it entered into partnership with BP. Such contracts are but a normal feature in the business relating to a film production; it facilitates the coming in of the necessary finance, and brings together varied talents whose combined effort would go to make a better or more successful picture. That such combinations were common is shown by the fact that the assessee itself entered into a financial arrangement with R, agreeing to give him one-half share of its proceeds. A partnership, as in the present case, for the production of the film, should be held, therefore, to be one entered into in the ordinary course of trade.

The question then was whether the termination of the agreement was made in the course of its business. It was evident from the terms of the agreement of partnership that the parties did contemplate a sale of the picture to an outsider or even inter se the partners even before the completion of the picture. It was, no doubt, true that the partnership agreement evidenced a joint venture, but the joint venture was only for obtaining a commercial asset, that was, to secure a stock-in-trade. If that venture failed, it was only an incident in the assessee's business. It was not such a fundamental asset like a managing agency agreement, which, if terminated, would put an end to the entire profit earning structure.

Considering the above principles, in the instant case, the compensation received by the assessee from HTIPL was revenue in nature and was taxable accordingly. The reasons were (i ) the assessee was carrying on business of agencies/distributorship. It had lost only one. This business apparatus was not impaired. It was its business to deal in agencies. The impugned agency was not the sole bread earner for the assessee. It lost one trading item and continued with others, (ii ) what had been done with HTIPL was only a business arrangement. A legal structure had been erected wherein the same business of distributorship of products in question would continue but under different banner and in partnership with HTIPL in a joint venture. This was no stoppage of business as such. In place of deriving income from foreign company directly, it would derive income for the same job from HTIPL as a share in joint venture. The business apparatus, if any, had been remodelled in a different form to suit the principal i.e., the foreign company. The income flow had not been stopped from this source. So, what had been done through this resource transfer agreement was only a business arrangement or business re-organisation whereby the assessee’s income or source of income was not affected (iii) what was transferred to HTIPL was not an asset, as no such asset had been acquired by the assessee. It did not figure in the balance sheet. It was claimed by the assessee that intangible asset had been transferred. In fact, it was found that the customer data base as such was not transferred on an absolute ownership basis. The assessee was not prevented from using the same. What was done was that HTIPL would use the same database henceforth after the termination date. No legal ownership or intellectual copyright was claimed over this database. At least no evidence was placed in support of the claim that customer database was a copyright protected or intellectual property right protected asset. The transfer of employees/staff also was merely a transfer of a resource, which could have been otherwise also built up. This was again a normal business arrangement and was only a condition of joint venture. Further, arrangement with foreign company was only modified vis-a-vis the assessee. Earlier there was an arrangement of foreign company directly with assessee. Now it was again with assessee but in a joint venture. In commercial parlance, nothing had changed except form of relationship which was only a more suitable and convenient trade arrangement. Hence, transfer of employees and staff was not helpful to support the argument that there was a transfer of asset and, hence, the compensation so received was capital in nature; (iv) in fact HTIPL only received certain benefits in terms of resource transfer which would help the joint venture in running the business. [Para 12]

Those resources (employees and customer database) were not the part of balance sheet. They were also not a part of definition of ‘asset’ as given in section 2(14), ‘property’ of any kind held by an assessee. [Para 13]

As held in CIT v. National Insurance Co. Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 37 (Cal.), a property is a bundle of rights, which the owner can lawfully exercise to the exclusion of all others. He is entitled to use and enjoy it as he wishes. The property can be either corporeal or incorporeal. Though it does not always mean physical property but it does mean the right, title, interest in a property. Property also includes rights such as trade marks, copyrights, patents and even intellectual rights capable of transfer or transmission. They also include beneficial rights to a thing considered as having money value especially with reference to transfer/succession and their capacity to be injured. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the revenue had sought to make employees and customer database as same sort of right. For it to be right, there should be (i) possession (ii ) ownership to the exclusion of others; (iii ) transferability/succession (iv) some money value; (v) or created by statute. Employee could not fall under the definition of capital asset as they did not fit under the concept of ‘property’. Though the customer database had been formed over the years but had not been actually transferred to HTIPL. It had been only allowed to be used by it. [Para 15]

So far as the argument of the assessee that what had been received by the assessee was for ‘goodwill’ was concerned, those two items alone did not form goodwill. [Para 16]

[Chandrashekar Naganagouda Patil v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax, Circle 6(2)(1), Bangalore [2020] 117 taxmann.com 520/183 ITD 457 (Bang. - Trib.)]

2.3-8 Route permits are capital assets Route permits for plying buses issued by authorities under the Motor Vehicles Act are property for the deprivation of which compensation is payable to the permit holder and, hence, such route permits are capital assets in the hands of the assessee-transport company - Addl. CIT v. Ganapathi Raju Jegi, Sanyasi Raju [1979] 119 ITR 715 (AP)/S. Vaidyanathaswami v. CIT [1979] 119 ITR 369 (Mad.).

2.3-9 Running business is a capital asset

A business as a going concern would constitute a capital asset - CIT v. F.X. Periera & Sons (Travancore)(P.) Ltd. [1990] 184 ITR 461/[1991] 55 Taxman 242 (Ker.).

2.3-10 Share in firm is a capital asset

Share of a partner is a partnership concern is a capital asset and its transfer will give rise to capital gains - V. Rangaswami Naidu v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 711 (Mad.).

The Apex Court in Sunil Siddharthbhai v. CIT [1985] 23 Taxman 14W/156 ITR 509 (SC) has observed that when a partner contributes a capital asset into the firm, he gives up his exclusive interest and enters the partnership and it is reduced on such entry into a shared interest. Thereafter he possesses no exclusive or excessive interest in the asset contributed to the firm. Similarly, during the subsistence of partnership no extra ownership/interest could be held by a partner or partners and it is held jointly by all the partners. Hence, partners hold shared interest in all the assets of the firm and there could be no transfer on the change in constitution of the firm. Similar view was expressed in B.T. Patil & Sons v. CGT [2001] 114 Taxman 301/247 ITR 588 (SC).

2.3-11 Tenancy right is property

A tenancy right is a capital asset - Asstt. CIT v. G.C. Shah & Co. [2015] 58 taxmann.com 49 (Guj.).

2.3-12 An undertaking is a capital asset

'Capital asset' will definitely include an 'undertaking' - Indian Bank Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 22 Taxman 479/153 ITR 282 (Mad.).

2.3-13 Stock exchange membership card is a 'capital asset'

Where on account of chronic default, stock exchange declared assessee, its member, as defaulter, terminated his membership and sold his stock exchange membership card in an auction, stock exchange card of assessee sold by stock exchange was 'capital asset' attracting tax on profit arising out of sale of same under section 45 - CDR. P.J. Mathew v. ITO [2010] 188 Taxman 376 (Ker.).

2.3-14 Indira Vikas Patra is not a capital asset

Indira Vikas Patra is not a capital asset and repayment of deposited amount with interest on maturity by Post Office cannot be treated as consideration for transfer of IVP by holder - Dr. R.P. Patel v. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 305 (Ker.).

2.3-14.1 NSS is a not a capital asset

It is clear from a combined reading of section 80CCA (now extinct) of the Act and National Savings Scheme Rules, 1987, it is abundantly clear that deposit in NSS account does not amount to purchase of capital asset and similarly withdrawal from NSS account is not money received on transfer of capital asset and since no specific section is provided under which money withdrawn from NSS account is to be taxed, withdrawals are to be taxed as income from other sources and not as capital gain- Mrs. Uma Borkar v. ITO [2002] 83 ITD 453 (Mum. - Trib.)

2.3-15 Right to sue is not a capital asset

Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act which uses the same expression 'property of any kind' in the context of transferability makes an exception in the case of a mere right to sue. The decisions thereunder make it abundantly clear that the right to sue for damages is not an actionable claim. It cannot be assigned. Transfer of such a right is as much opposed to public policy as is gambling in litigation. As such, it will not be quite correct to say that such a right constitutes a 'capital asset' which in turn has to be 'an interest in property of any kind' - CIT v. Abhasbhoy A. Dehgamwalla [1991] 59 Taxman 498/[1992] 195 ITR 28 (Bom.).

If the managing agent happens to be an individual, he can take up the work of a managing agent in either of the two capacities of a servant or as a personal business of his own. In the case of a firm, which can be constituted only for the purpose of sharing profits of a business, the work of managing agency must be held to be the business of the firm. The profits of a business using the word "business" as defined in the Indian Partnership Act would all be profits of a business, profession or vocation falling within section 10. Consequently, the profits, which the assessee-firm earned from their business of working as managing agents of company S must be held to be their profits or gains from business, profession or vocation assessable to income-tax under section 10.

In the instant case also, a single venture of floating the company S, securing its managing agency and subsequently managing its affairs was clearly intended by the partners of the assessee-firm to be an adventure in the nature of a business by them.

The question as to the capacity in which, in any particular case, the sole agent happens to be working, will depend on the facts of that case. In the instant case, there was nothing at all to indicate that the assessee-firm, in taking over the sole agency of company S, entered into any contract which created the relationship of master and servant. On the other hand, the considerations which weighed in holding that the work of managing agency of company S was being carried on by the assessee-firm as their own business equally apply to their sole agency business also and it must be held that the income gained by the assessee-firm as sole agents was income or profit from their business.

Acting under these powers the company bought and sold shares of two companies—NGM and ACE Ltd. and subsequently sold them resulting in income to the assessee-company. The ITO rejected the assessee's contention that the gains were in the nature of capital gains and on the other hand held that they were profits from business pure and simple. The facts in the case of Gangadhar Baijnath (supra) were entirely different as that was a case of cancellation of contract which had been entered into in the ordinary course of business and the ratio of that decision could not be applied to the facts of the instant case.

The amount received towards goodwill by the assessee was nothing but a capital receipt because it related to the assessee’s share in the goodwill of the firm which was a capital asset, vide section 14 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. Srinivasa Setty’s case (supra) therefore, applied to the facts of the instant case and there could be no capital gains on transfer of such an asset.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipt - Assessment year 1942-43 and 1944-45 - Assessee-company was incorporated with an object of carrying on business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, etc. - Assessee invested certain amount with a newly incorporated sugar company with a condition that assessee was to be given managing agency in a company to be erected in future - That company, however, could not be erected - During relevant accounting years assessee sold shares acquired by it and made certain profit - Whether object of assessee in buying shares in sugar company was purely to obtain managing agency of new mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from inception no intention whatever on part of assessee to re-sell shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them - Held, yes - Whether therefore investment of money in purchase of shares was of a capital nature and profits arising out of sale of shares were of a capital nature and were not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with an object to undertake and carry on the general business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, export and import agents, clearing and forwarding or house or land agents. In 1933 another sugar company was incorporated. Managing director of the assessee entered into an agreement with the sugar company in March 1933, whereby the assessee-company was to invest Rs. 5,00,000 in the sugar company in lieu of which it was to be given the managing agency of the third mill of the sugar company not in existence at the time.

The third mill was, however, not erected and the agreement about acquiring the managing agency fell through. The managing director died in December 1940, and the assessee decided to sell all the shares in 1941. The excess amount realized on sale of these shares was taxed by the ITO, as revenue receipts, the first in the assessment year 1942-43 and the second in 1944-45. The assessee-company's contention that the excess was in the nature of capital appreciation was not accepted. This order was confirmed by the AAC and the Tribunal.

On reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The exact nature of the business which the assessee was doing was admittedly not clear from the record but it was not denied that the memorandum of association of the assessee did not authorise it to purchase and/or sell shares as dealers nor was it denied that beyond this isolated transaction of purchase and sale the assessee did not deal in shares. It seemed that the object of the assessee in buying shares was purely to obtain the managing agency of the third mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from the inception no intention whatever on the part of the assessee to re-sell the shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them. Naturally when the third mill was not erected and the object of securing the managing agency became impossible of fulfilment, the assessee withdrew the shares and sold them at a profit. After conceding that the taking up of the shares by the assessee in the sugar company was an essential part of the arrangement arrived at, the only reasonable conclusion to which the High Court should have come was that the investment of the money in the purchase of shares was of a capital nature and the profits arising out of the sale of the shares in the circumstances of this case were accretions to capital and were not liable to tax.

Accordingly, the decision of the High Court was to be reversed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

Thereupon a family arrangement was made between the assessee and the other family members; whereby the assessee had resigned from a partnership firm and transferred his share of profit/loss in the firm to a family member for a consideration of Rs. 35,000 being the capital balance of the firm. The assessee claimed that in the instant case there was no transfer, which gives rise to any capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that there was a transfer in the instant case and consequently there was a capital gain in the hands of the assessee. He, therefore, held that the assessee was liable to pay capital gain tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner(Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that admittedly there were lot of disputes between the family members of the assessee, who were none other than the relatives of one other, and in that event the family arrangement and settlement entered into between the parties on the suggestion made by the arbitrator could not be termed as a transfer either in respect of movable or immovable properties or in respect of commercial properties. Therefore, there was no transfer and it was only a family arrangement. Therefore, the assessee was not liable to pay capital gain tax. Accordingly, it set aside the orders passed by the lower authorities.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was allowed, in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of the managed company as a consequence of its take over by the State Government. For the assessment year 1960-61, the ITO taxed the compensation amount, treated it as a capital receipt.

On appeal, the AAC while upholding the assessment, held that only the amount actually received during the previous year should be the amount of income taxable.

On Second Appeal, the Tribunal held that entire receipt to which the provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted, was a taxable income assessable during the year in question as the assessee itself having credited the entire sum to its profit and loss account in keeping with the system of its accounting, which was mercantile, no justification vested with the AAC to change it.

On reference :

HELD: Since a managing agency is a creature of contract and since its formation, operation and termination are all to be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act, in so far as they apply, there was no force in the contention that a managing agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other manner. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the compensation amount was taxable profit within the meaning of section 10(5A).

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether when assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to carrying on of business in agencies - Held, yes - Assessee-company had income from contracts and commission from various parties - It was also distributor of products of a foreign company for 22 years - A joint venture - company HTIPL was formed to manufacture and market products of said foreign company in India - Under an agreement, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets such as trained manpower, personal dealings, list of customers, etc., and in turn it had received certain amount by way of compensation, which was claimed by the assessee as consideration for ‘goodwill’, being capital receipt not taxable - Whether since assessee continued to do same line of business, i.e., distributorship of other companies with same name, fame, place and approach even after formation of joint venture, it could not be said that assessee had received compensation for sale of ‘goodwill’ - Held, yes - Whether what assessee had got in terms of compensation was a normal incidence of business arising due to its re-organisation and formation of a joint venture and, thus, what assessee had received was of revenue character and was taxable accordingly - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was a distributor of products of foreign company for last 22 years. A joint venture company HTIPL, consisting of the assessee and the foreign company, was formed to manufacture the products of foreign company in India and also to market products of the foreign company manufactured abroad. Under an agreement entered into between the assessee and company HTIPL, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets like trained manpower personnel dealing with said products in India and detailed list of customers of said products and introduce HTIPL to all the customers both in public and private sectors for sale of said products. In view of transfer of above intangible assets, the assessee received certain compensation from HTIPL. The assessee treated that sum as a consideration for transfer of goodwill and offered same for taxation as long term capital gains. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had income from service contracts and commission from various parties; that it was a compensation received on termination of managing agency; that the assessee was carrying on several managing agencies and it gave up only one and continued with other; that the business structure of the assessee did not suffer and it was free to carry on the trade with other agencies; that the cancellation and compensation, therefore, was merely a normal incidence of business; and that the income of the assessee had increased in the subsequent years. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the amount received by the assessee was revenue receipt taxable in its hands. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had parted with a part of its apparatus to a joint venture and for the loss so suffered it had received compensation. He directed the Assessing Officer to tax the receipt as capital receipt.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: A careful consideration of the case laws indicated following principles :

1. When a payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of contract which does not affect the trading structure of the recipient’s business nor deprive the assessee from source of income, then termination of contract is only a normal incidence of business.

2. Where trading structure of the assessee is impaired or cancellation results in loss of sources of income, payment to compensate such loss of source is capital.

3. A source of income may be a capital structure of one assessee. But where the assessee is dealing in several such sources/assets, then it becomes a stock in trade. Loss of one such source/asset will be a loss of capital if the assessee is dealing only in one but will be revenue if it is dealing in many such sources/assets as stock in trade.

4. When assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to the carrying on of the business in agencies. Where there is a modification in the terms of any one of such agencies, it will again be a normal incidence of business.

5. There is no immutable principle that compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital.

6. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated for loss of goodwill, is prima facie of the nature of capital receipt.

7. Manner of payment of compensation is not material. Whether capital is repaid in instalments or is paid in lump sum, it will not affect the basic nature of receipt in the hands of the recipient.

8. When assessee is not disposed of any asset, then amount received cannot be regarded as compensation in respect of loss of an enduring asset.

ITO [2020] 82 ITR (Trib.) 15 (Mum.). The assessee's mother-in-law occupied a flat on the second floor of a building on "licence basis". She had two sons. An out-of-court settlement was entered into under which the assessee received Rs. 25 lakhs for not interfering with the possession of HME. The Assessing Officer held that the amount of Rs. 25 lakhs was consideration in respect of giving up the claim, vacating the premises and handing over possession of the premises, that it was capital gains, which had accrued to the assessee in lieu of relinquishment of rights in the premises. He brought to tax Rs. 25 lakhs as long-term capital gains. The Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the amounts received by the assessee as consideration for transfer of "possessory rights" was not chargeable to tax as capital gains and no transfer of "tenancy rights" was involved. HEADNOTE: I. Section 28(i), read with section 4 , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company had received certain sum as compensation on account of termination of its agency and distributorship by GE group - It claimed said receipt as capital receipt - Assessing Officer, however, treated said sum as its business receipt and brought same to tax under section 28 on ground that GE group had control and management of assessee and that assessee was non-exclusive agent and distributor of GE group - Whether since on date of termination of agreement GE group was holding 50 per cent shareholding of assessee while other 50 per cent of shares were held by 'F', it could not be presumed that GE group had control over management of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, since further entire trained staff and customer network were taken over by GE and there was a restrictive covenant not to indulge in or to be associated with a similar business compensation received on account of termination of agency and distributorship agreements was a capital receipt which was not taxable as income from business or profession- Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was appointed as sales agent and distributor for certain silicon products produced by the GE group. Later on the said agency and its distributorship were terminated by the GE group and the assessee paid certain sum as compensation was for said termination. The assessee claimed said receipt as a capital receipt. The Assessing Officer rejected its claim and treated the same as its business receipt/income on the ground that the GE group had control and management of the assessee-group and that the assessee was non-exclusive agent and distributor of the GE group. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The agency and distributorship agreements were entered into on 1-5-1991 and 31-10-1995, respectively, and were terminated vide agreements dated 1-7-1996 with retrospective effect from 31-10-1995 and 3-12-1995, respectively. As on the date of the termination of the agreement the GE group was holding 50 per cent shareholding of the company, while the other 50 per cent of the shares were held by 'F' Company, and, hence, it could not be presumed that the GE group had the control over the management of the assessee-company. [Para 14]

A perusal of the agency as well as distributorship agreements showed that the assessee was the non-exclusive agent and distributor of the GE group, but was not an agent simplicitor. It was not merely an intermediary between the principal and its customers but was expected to employ staff; promote the sale and also to maintain warehousing facility. Thus, it was carrying on the business of GE by creating its own infrastructure and for the said purpose it had made huge financial commitments; the assessee was not entitled to act on its own behalf and for itself in respect of the goods entrusted to it. Thus, there was a relationship of agency with GE and not on principal-to-principal basis, as contended by the assessee. As regards the assessee's contentions that since it had to make huge financial commitments, it was acting as a principal, it was found that all the expenses incurred by the agent in connection with the fulfilment of its obligations [like travel, correspondence, telephone, telecopy and the like] had been taken into account while fixing the rate of commission at 6 per cent on all the sales of the products initiated by the agent. Thus, it could not be said that the assessee was acting as the principal agent of GE. [Para 15]

Thus, it could be seen that the amount received for termination of agency was a taxable receipt. However, the nature of the receipt is to be seen before bringing it to tax under section 28(ii)(c ). If the receipt is on termination of the agreements of agency and distributorship simplicitor, the compensation received is for the loss of revenue and, hence, a revenue receipt. In such a case, the agent/distributor can carry on business of a similar nature with any other principal. But if there is a restrictive covenant to deal with similar business, then all the agreements have to be considered in unison and not in isolation. By the restrictive covenant the assessee is not only losing the revenue but is also losing the revenue-generating source. As held by the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Ambadi Enterprises Ltd. [2004] 267 ITR 702/139 Taxman 96, one test for ascertaining as to whether what had received was a capital receipt or a revenue receipt is to find out whether the assessee had snapped its link with the profit making apparatus that had been transferred. [Para 16]

ITO v. Oberoi Hotels (I) Ltd. [1989] 33 TTJ (Cal.) 420
The assessee, a limited company, had acquired certain skills and experience in managing big hotels in different countries of the world. Its Memorandum of Association authorised it not only to purchase and run hotels on its own account but also to operate, manage or administer hotels belonging to others for a fee. During the relevant previous year, the assessee was operating hotels belonging to others for a fee in several places. By an agreement dated 2-11-1970, the assessee agreed to operate a hotel at Singapore. Later, however, due to change of management of the hotel it gave up its right to operate the said hotel and received certain amount as compensation.
Held that these rights constituted the profit-earning apparatus of the assessee and so the compensation was received for the destruction or sterilisation of that capital asset. Hence the compensation received by the assessee was a capital receipt.

The transfer of right or relinquishment of part and parcel of business undertaking of the assessee is nothing but transfer of capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14). Any profit arising from the transfer of capital asset must be chargeable under the head 'capital gain'. The word 'transfer' has been defined in section 2(47). [Para 33] From the definition under section 2(47), it is clear that the word 'transfer' is inclusive of definition, which inter alia provides 6 situations under which there can be transfer in relation to the capital asset. Relinquishment of any rights in the capital asset is one of the situation enumerated in section 2(47). The word 'relinquishment' denotes that relinquishment should be only in the case of capital asset with reference to which the word 'transfer' has been defined. The right of the assessee over the landed property which was part and parcel of the business undertaking of the assessee is a capital asset. The moment assessee losses the right attached to a part of the business undertaking of the assessee, there is relinquishment of right over the said property. The relinquishment of assets or extinguishment of any right in it which may not amount to a sale can also be considered as a transfer. Therefore, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are not acceptable that there is no transfer under section 45 and the assessee has done only business transaction. Accordingly, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue are reversed and it is held that the income accrued to the assessee out of relinquishment of right over the property is to be chargeable under section 45 and computation of capital gain has to be done in accordance with section 48.
