This decision of the Delhi High Court has been followed by the ITAT Mumbai Bench in the case of Chheda Housing Development Corporation v. Addl. CIT [2019] 110 taxmann.com 56/179 ITD 154 (Mum. - Trib.) wherein the facts were as under-

The assessee was a partnership firm engaged in business of financing, construction and development and it entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with one 'M' for developing saleable right of floor surface index on a plot of land. On execution of MOU, the assessee paid certain advance to owner of the said land and subsequently the assessee came to know that the owner of the said land had already transferred development rights to 'S' Ltd. which was a company consisting of family members of land owners. The assessee thus filed a civil suit for seeking relief for specific performance of MOU and to execute joint development agreement. The assessee also filed criminal complaint against the said land owner.

Later on, after a prolonged discussion, the assessee and owners of the land agreed to cancel the development agreement and a deed of cancellation was executed. On execution of cancellation deed, the assessee was paid Rs. 20 crores by confirming party on account of refund of advance with interest, loss of profit, liquidated damage etc. The Assessing Officer taxed the receipt in question as Long-Term Capital Gain.

The question that arose was "Whether since amount received by assessee in excess of advance was on account of compensation for extinction of its right to sue owner and said receipt was not in ordinary course of its business, the same was to be construed as capital receipt not liable to tax?"

The Tribunal answered the question in the affirmative in the sense that "the amount received by the assessee in excess of advance was on account of compensation for extinction of its right to sue the owner, the receipt is a capital receipt not chargeable to tax. Since the assessee has not received the amount in excess of advance in the course of his business it must be construed as capital receipt and not business receipt."

The assessment year concerned in this case was 2012-13.

The facts obtaining in the case which arose before the ITAT Mumbai Bench in of Asstt. CIT v. Ashwin S. Bhaliekar [2019] 74 ITR (Mum. - Trib.) 5 were that the builder who was unable to implement an agreement to construct three flats in the proposed building within the stipulated time had to pay compensation to the assessee for his inability to adhere to the contract. The assessee, therefore, got back the advance of Rs. 50 lakhs besides a compensation amount of Rs. 1.10 crores.

The assessee sought reinvestment benefit under section 54 of the Act as the investor of these moneys to acquire new flats in the same project. Since the right under the agreement had been held for more than three years, the compensation was offered as long-term capital gains, subject to deduction under section 54 of the Act. The Assessing Officer brought the compensation amount to tax under the head "Other sources" having denied relief under section 54 of the Act but the assessee succeeded on first appeal.

On appeal by the Revenue the Tribunal held that the extinguishment of the assessee's right in the flats allotted was actually extinguishment of a right in relation to a capital asset in view of the provisions of section 47 of the Act and fell within the definition of transfer and hence, resulted in capital gains chargeable under section 45 of the Act. Since right to purchase residential flats could only be a long-term capital asset, the assessee was eligible for relief under section 54 of the Act.

From the detailed discussion, it is amply clear as explained by the Madras High Court in the case of Neelamalai Agro Industries Ltd. (supra) that when a thing is destroyed by fire or when a ship sinks into sea, the capital asset is no longer available for being owned, used or enjoyed by anyone including the assessee and with destruction of the asset, right of assessee in that asset would be destroyed and destruction of such rights in an asset consequent upon assets ceasing to exist is a situation which is not contemplated either in definition of 'transfer', or in charging section 45 of the Act.

In other words, if the asset is destroyed due to natural calamity the question of "transfer of asset" by "extinguishment of rights" does not arise.

In CIT v. Anglo India Jute Mills Co. Ltd. [1981] 6 Taxman 54/129 ITR 352 (Cal.) the assessee wanted to purchase certain machinery from abroad. For this purpose, the assessee did all that was necessary for obtaining the permission and getting the import licence. In order to protect itself from fluctuations in the exchange rate, the assessee entered into a forward contract with a bank entitling it to obtain the requisite amount of sterling at the time when the contract came to an end or was required to be performed. The assessee could not get this machinery because the licence expired and, therefore the question of enforcing payment in dollars did not arise. Therefore, the State Bank, pursuant to their commitment, credited the assessee minus the necessary costs, charges and expenses, with the difference between the exchange rate and the assessee got a credit of Rs. 3,13,651. The Court held that the amount was obtained not because the assessee surrendered any licence and not because the assessee gave up its own right under a contract but because the assessee realised its dues or, in other words, the assessee transformed its rights under the contract into money. Therefore, neither was there any transfer nor was there any profit arising therefrom. In that background of facts there was no cost of acquisition and, therefore, there could not be any capital gains in respect of such an asset. Accordingly, the sum of Rs. 3,13,651 could not be considered to be capital gains in terms of section 45. However, it appears that the chargeability to tax under the head 'business' could not be disputed.

Compensation for termination of agency contract and cancellation of contract - When once it is found that the contract was entered into in the ordinary course of business, any compensation received for its termination would be a revenue receipt, irrespective of whether its performance was to consist of a single act or a series of acts spread over a period. There was a difference between a payment made as compensation for the termination of an agency contract and an amount paid as solatium for the cancellation of a contract entered into by a businessman in the ordinary course of business. In an agency contract, the actual business consists in the dealings between the principal and his customers, and the work of the agent is only to bring about that business. What he does is not the business itself but something which is intimately and directly linked up with it. The agency may, therefore, be viewed as the apparatus which leads to the business rather than the business itself. Considered in this light, the agency can be held to be of the nature of a capital asset invested in business. But this cannot be said of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such a contract is part of the business itself, not anything outside it as is the agency and any receipt on account of such a contract can only be a trading receipt [CIT v. Rai Bahadur Jairam Valji [1959] 35 ITR 148 (SC)]. Also see, Kettlewell Bullen & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC).

Compensation paid for termination of a managing agency business is a payment in relation to said business as such said receipt was obviously related to that business and was not or income from a new and independent source and, therefore, previous year relevant to that receipt would be same as previous year for managing agency business itself [Chidambaram Mulraj & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 102 ITR 7 (SC)].

INCOME DERIVED BY CERTAIN TRADE, PROFESSIONAL OR SIMILAR ASSOCIATION [SECTION 28(iii)]

'Performing specific services', meaning of - The words 'performing specific service' mean conferring particular benefits on the members. With reference to a trade, professional or similar association, the performing of specific services must mean conferring on its members some tangible benefit which otherwise would not be available to them as such except for payment received by the association in respect of those services. Thus, amount received in the nature of entrance fee and other subscription fees from its members for allowing their application for enlisting names of companies not already on quotations list so that shares and stocks of said companies might be placed on the stock market chargeable to tax u/s 28(iii) [CIT v. Calcutta Stock Exchange Association Ltd. [1959] 36 ITR 222 (SC)].

Other incomes taxable under appropriate heads of income - The plain reading of section 28(iii) suggests that the income derived by a trade association from specific services rendered by it should be brought to tax. From such a reading, no exclusion of any other type of income can be implied if such other income can otherwise be taxed under other provisions of the 1961 Act [CIT v. Shree Jari Merchants Association [1977] 106 ITR 542 (Guj.)].

GENERAL

Transfer of part asset - The words 'the transfer of a capital asset' occurring in section 45 cannot be interpreted as a transfer of the entire capital asset and not a part of the same [National Products v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 755 (Kar.)].

Capital asset on the date of transfer - It is necessary that property transferred must be a capital asset on date of transfer and not that such property should have been capital asset also on date of its acquisition by the assessee [Arun Sunny v. DCIT [2009] 184 Taxman 498 (Ker.)]. Also see, A. R. Dahiya v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 141 Taxman 449 (P&H).

CAPITAL GAINS OR NOT

Gift for tax avoidance - Where assessee transferred its shareholding, as a gift, in a company to step-down company created in a tax haven country and the said step-down company transferred stake in favour of a third-party investor for a consideration, sole intention of assessee being escape rigour of Indian tax laws, therefore, assessee was liable to tax u/s 45 [PCIT v. Redington (India) Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 136 (Mad.)].

Inherited property - Where assessee inherited certain land, leased out same on payment of ground rent and ultimately sold it after decades, profit arising from sale of land was to be taxed as 'capital gains' [CIT v. Administrator of the Estate of Shri E. F. Dinshaw [2012] 22 taxmann.com 57/208 Taxman 193 (Mag.) (Bom.)].

Intangible assets - Sale of brand names, trademark, copyright and goodwill in journals sold/transferred would clearly be a case of sale of capital asset and exigible to capital gains [CIT v. Mediworld Publications (P.) Ltd. [2011] 11 taxmann.com 374/200 Taxman 1 (Delhi); CIT v. ABB Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 338/[2022] 284 Taxman 350 (Kar.)].

Where collection of assets of undertaking transferred in slump sale included intangible assets like goodwill and intellectual property whose cost of acquisition could not be determined, said sale could not be assessable to capital gains [CIT v. AKZO Noble India Ltd. [2020] 121 taxmann.com 216/[2021] 276 Taxman 259 (Cal.)].

Malba - Proceeds of malba, i.e., material left over after demolition of a structure, would be taxable under the head 'Capital gains' and not under the head 'Income from other sources' [CIT v. Ribu Saggi [2014] 45 taxmann.com 371/223 Taxman 150 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Owelty - Amount of owelty (i.e., compensation deposited to settle inequalities in partition) represents immovable property and would not attract capital gain tax [CIT v. Ashwani Chopra [2013] 30 taxmann.com 299/213 Taxman 490 (P&H)].

Pledge of shares - No capital gains arise where there was no transfer of shares but shares have been pledged for the purposes of obtaining loan [CIT v. Reliance Communication Infrastructure Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 302/[2013] 212 Taxman 177 (Bom.)].

Sale of business as a going concern - Where business is sold as a going concern valuing plant and machinery, etc., surplus arising over and above the difference between WDV and actual cost has to be taxed u/s 45 [CIT v. Artex Mfg. Co. [1997] 93 Taxman 357 (SC)].

Shares - Where assessee-company purchased shares of a private limited company from funds received from its holding company and after some time it had sold said shares to its holding company, profit arising from sale of shares had to be taxed under head 'Capital gains' [CIT v. Renato Finance & Investment Ltd. [2013] 33 taxmann.com 262/218 Taxman 312 (Bom.)].

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : “An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

■ Profit motive is not decisive of the question, whether a particular receipt is capital or income.7

■ The question whether the payer is compelled to pay has no relevance in the determination of the character of the receipt. It may be that the payee has no legal claim for payment and the payment is made voluntarily, yet the receipt may be of revenue character.8

A voluntary payment is a profit of employment if it accrues by virtue of the employment notwithstanding that there may not be any legal obligation to make the payment. If, however, the payment is in the nature of a personal gift to him, it is not regarded as a payment for services but as a mere present.8

■ The fund out of which the money came is not material.2

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

Extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset

The booklet "How to compute capital gains published by the Income Tax Department" explains 'extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset' as under:

"This covers every possible transaction which results in destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation of all or any bundle of rights in a capital asset."

For example, termination of a lease or of a mortgagee interest in a property. In the case of CIT v. Grace Collis [2001] 115 taxmann 326 (SC) the Supreme Court held that the definition of 'transfer' in section 2(47) also contemplates the extinguishment consequent upon the transfer thereof.

Therefore, the expression 'transfer' does include the extinguishment of rights in a capital asset independent of and otherwise than on account of transfer.

Tracing the history of "extinguishment of rights"

If legislative history is traced, the Indian Income-tax Act 1922(the 1922 Act) did not contain any specific provision corresponding to section 2(47) of the Act defining 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset, though section 12B of the 1922 Act relating to capital gains spoke of "sale, exchange or transfer", as attracting capital gains. The "transfer" was mentioned in juxtaposition of "sale and exchange"- The term juxtaposition means the fact of two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect.

Reference to relinquishment was not mentioned in the said provision. Section 12B of the 1922 Act was recast by the Finance (No.3) Act,1956 wherein it was mentioned that ".the tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head "Capital Gains" in respect of any profits or gains arising from the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer of a capital asset effected after the 31st day of March, 1956, and such profits and gains shall be deemed to be income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place" In other words, the phrase " relinquishment" was added but the other phrase "extinguishment of any rights (therein)" about which this discussion centers around was placed in a separate clause by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1984 with effect from 01-04-1985 when the section 2(47) of the Act was recast apparently with the object of avoiding any ambiguity and repetition of the expression in the charging section though the phrase " extinguishment of any rights (therein)" had also been in the statute book since the inception of the 1961 Act itself.

This clause gives an artificially extended meaning to the expression 'transfer' and expands the same to include the cases of extinguishment of any rights and the compulsory acquisition which were conspicuous by their absence in the 1922 Act.

The Supreme Court as early as 21st February 1978 in the case of Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 803/2 SCC 50 (a Bench consisting of 7 Hon'ble Judges) with regard to transfer of a right in a property by extinguishment observed as under-

Redemption of preference shares is relinquishment and transfer

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 509 (SC) the Court held that redemption of preference shares is clearly 'sale' by the shareholder to the company and would come within the purview of 'transfer' in view of the following:

A reading of sections 77, 80 and 85 of the Companies Act, 1956 [now sections 67, 55 and 43 of the Companies Act, 2013] makes it clear that when a preference share is redeemed by a company, what a shareholder does is, to sell the shares to the company. Such a transaction is nothing but sale of the preference shares by the shareholder to the company.

That is why after specifically laying down in section 77(1) of the said Act [now section 67(1) of the 2013 Act] that no company shall have the power to buy its own shares, it was necessary to specify in sub-section (5) thereof [sub-section (4) of section 67 of the 2013 Act] that this provision shall not affect the rights of a company to redeem any preference shares issued by it.

If redemption of preference shares did not amount to sale, it would not have been necessary to specifically provide that the restriction imposed upon a company in respect of buying its own shares will not apply to redemption of preference shares issued by the company.

The Court held that the assessee had purchased the preference shares at less than face value. When the shares were redeemed by the company, she received more than what she had paid for the shares. In order to get this amount the assessee had to give up or abandon or surrender the shares held by her. The meaning of the word 'relinquish' as given in Webster's Comprehensive Dictionary International Edition 1984, is: (1) to give up; abandon; surrender, (2) to cease to demand; renounce; to relinquish a claim, (3) to let go (a hold or something held).

The assessee in this case gave up the shares and received in lieu thereof a sum of money. This came clearly within the mischief of section 2(47)(i). That apart, the transaction amounted to sale.

In the instant case, the preference shares were held as capital assets. The excess amount received by the shareholder on redemption of these shares would have to be treated as capital gain in view of section 2(47), read with section 4. Accordingly, the assessee's case squarely came within section 2(47)(i).

6.15-5D Capital gains - Profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset are chargeable to income-tax under the head ‘Capital gains’. The charging section envisages transfer of capital asset and the profits and gains arising on account of such transfer.

The expression ‘transfer’ has been defined in section 2(47) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 as including sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any rights therein, or compulsory acquisition thereof; or conversion of a capital asset into stock-in-trade, or transaction involving the allowance of the possession which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of an immovable property, etc.

Since the transfer as contemplated is one as a result whereof consideration has passed to the assessee or has accrued to him, extinguishment or relinquishment of rights must relate to that ‘capital asset’ corporeal or incorporeal. It is, therefore, obvious that transfer of a capital asset in order to attract liability to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ must be a ‘transfer’ as a result whereof some consideration is received by or accrues to the assessee. If the transfer does not yield any consideration, there can be no question of capital gains. If the transfer takes effect on extinguishment of a right in the capital asset, there must be receipt of consideration for such extinguishment to attract liability to tax.1

The word ‘transfer’ also covers cases which result in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise of all or any of the bundle of rights which a person has in the capital assets.1 It is only when consideration is received in respect thereof.

The word ‘transfer’ is comprehensive and is regarded generally as comprehending within its scope transfers both voluntary and involuntary. In the absence of a distinct genus or category, no presumption can arise that the word ‘transfer’ in section 2(47) must be construed in the sense of a voluntary transfer, because the words ‘sale’, ‘exchange’ and ‘relinquishment’ are in the normal acceptation of those terms voluntary acts, and, therefore, if an existing title of a capital asset is extinguished and a new one created, there is within the meaning of section 2(47) a ‘transfer’ of capital asset, and the fact that the divestiture of title takes place under a law relating to compulsory acquisition of property would make no difference. The compulsory acquisition of capital asset may be a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 2(47), but is not sale. These expressions are not synonymous conveying the same meaning. Had this been so, and also the expression ‘sale’ as embracing within its scope ‘compulsory acquisition’ of an asset, there would have been no need to refer to both these expressions in the inclusive definition of ‘transfer’ in section 2(47). One of the purposes of the inclusive definition is to expand the concept defined. The meaning of the expression ‘transfer’ was extended to cover the compulsory acquisition of an asset along with sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any right therein, etc.

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

In the present case, the wife was not claiming any right of sharing the assessee's properties as a co-sharer. Her claim was for maintenance and it was in lieu of maintenance that the properties in question were transferred by the assessee to her. Corporate veil lifting - Tax avoidance

The courts have been stepping into pierce the corporate veil when fiscal or legal obligations are sought to be bypassed by a corporate entity. The Supreme Court has upheld the right of the tax authorities to go behind the corporate façade to look at the economic realities of transactions, if the shell of the corporate entity is used for tax evasions or to circumvent tax obligations [see Juggilal Kamlapat v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 702 (SC) and CIT v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd. [1967] 63 ITR 609 (SC)]. The courts have been upholding the revenue’s right to disregard the consequences of transactions even in respect of those which are genuinely undertaken if their purpose is to avoid tax that would otherwise be payable. The taxing authority is entitled and is indeed bound to determine the true legal relations resulting from a transaction. If the parties have chosen to conceal by a device the legal relation, it is open to the taxing authority to unravel the device and determine the true character of the relationship. It is the duty of the court, in every case where ingenuity is expended to avoid and taxing legislation, to go behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs. The court is not be satisfied with form and leave well alone the substance of a transaction [Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. v. Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. [1986] 157 ITR 77 (SC)/Ess Ess Kay Engg. Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1985] 151 ITR 636 (Punj. & Har.)]

In Juggilal Kamlapat’s case the Supreme Court exercised the right of unraveling a colourable device of tax evasion. In that case the assessee- firm was a managing agent of a company. Three brothers held majority of shares in the company as well as in the firm. The company asked the assessee to arrange for finance to pay off a loan taken from a sister-company and when the assessee regretted its inability to arrange the finances, the company decided to terminate the managing agency, by paying a compensation of Rs. 2 lakhs. The managing agency was entrusted to another sister-company which was newly floated, in which also the aforesaid three brothers held majority of shares. The Tribunal held that the reason for terminating the managing agency was not a true reason but was merely a fake one and the whole transaction was a hoax for the purpose of evading income-tax both in the hands of the payer and the payee. The Tribunal also found that that there was only a change of personnel in the managing agency and not a change in office and that the assessee had no right of compensation for any loss of office. The question for consideration was whether the compensation received by the assessee could be treated as capital receipt on the ground that it arose out of the destruction of capital asset, viz., the managing agency. The Supreme Court held that the managing agency business carried on by the assessee- firm was not destroyed or lost to the four individual partners who constituted the assessee-firm. What happened was that the individuals who constituted the assessee-firm became the directors of the newly- formed company and in this new capacity they undertook the conduct of the managing agency business and as shareholders continued to benefit from the profits of that business flowing to them in the shape of dividend instead of as a share of profits from the assessee-firm. In other words, the managing-agency asset was enjoyed by four individual partners in a different capacity with the same object of profit-making. There was, therefore, no destruction of the apparatus of the profit- making asset, i.e., the managing agency contract. It was obvious that there was an intimate connection in this case between the managing agency business of the assessee-firm and the payment of a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs and, therefore, this amount represented as a revenue receipt. While so upholding, the Supreme Court laid a proposition that the court is entitled to lift the mask of corporate entity if the corporation is used for tax evasion or to circumvent tax obligation or to perpetrate fraud.

In the amalgamation, assets and liabilities of the transferor company are transferred, by a scheme of arrangement, to the transferee-company. Therefore, when assets of a partnership firm are transferred by scheme of amalgamation to a company, then capital gains may arise to the firm.

Capital gains exempted 3. List of transfers which are not considered as transfer of assets for the purposes of charging capital gain is enlisted in section 47 with conditions for exemption. Amalgamation is exempted under the provisions of section 47(vi) of the IT Act, the provision reads as "Any transfer, in a scheme of amalgamation, of a capital asset by the amalgamating company to the amalgamated company, if the amalgamated company is an Indian company."

Therefore, what is exempted, is capital gain arising on transfer of assets by a scheme of amalgamation to a amalgamating (Transferor) Company. In the present case a partnership firm, which is an unregistered company as per Companies Act, is being merged with the Private/Public Company. Therefore, advantage of section 47(vi) is not available in this case. Rather such merger of firm with the company is not regarded as amalgamation for the purposes of Income-tax Act.

Hence, question remains as when amalgamation of partnership firm with the Company happens, of course through High Court route under sections 391 & 394 of the Companies Act, whether, Capital gains arising from such transfer of capital assets are taxable? Though it is agreed that section 47(vi) of the Income-tax Act is not applicable but certainly the case falls under another listing in the same section 47, i.e., section 47 (xiii). Reasoning for the same is as follows:

Section 47(xiii) reads as follows:

(xiii) any transfer of a capital asset or intangible asset by a firm to a company as a result of succession of the firm by a company in the business carried on by the firm, or any transfer of a capital asset to a company in the course of demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India as a result of which an association of persons or body of individuals is succeeded by such company:

Provided that—

(a) all the assets and liabilities of the firm or of the association of persons or body of individuals relating to the business immediately before the succession become the assets and liabilities of the company;

(b) all the partners of the firm immediately before the succession become the shareholders of the company in the same proportion in which their capital accounts stood in the books of the firm on the date of the succession;

(c) the partners of the firm do not receive any consideration or benefit, directly or indirectly, in any form or manner, other than by way of allotment of shares in the company; and

(d) the aggregate of the shareholding in the company of the partners of the firm is not less than fifty per cent of the total voting power in the company and their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of five years from the date of the succession;

(e) the demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India is carried out in accordance with a scheme for demutualisation or corporatisation which is approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India established under section 3 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (15 of 1992);

An analysis of section 47(xiii) is as follows:

1. Business is carried on by the firm up to one date

2. Such business in a firm by succession vests in a company and, therefore, all the assets and liabilities of the firm are transferred to a Company

3. Conditions mentioned in proviso from (a) to (e) are followed,

Then such transfer of assets is not considered as transfer for charging the capital gains tax.

What section 47(xiii) contemplates is succession of business and not transfer or take over of business only. Word 'succession' has wider meaning and in its ambit, it includes transfer as well as take over. Word 'succession' is not defined in Income-tax Act. Therefore, applying rules of interpretation of statutes, general meaning of a word "succession" must be applied in this case.

As per Black's law dictionary, word 'successor' means a corporation that, through amalgamation, consolidation, or other assumptions on interests, is vested with the rights and duties (obviously properties) of the earlier corporation.

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Franchise service - Courier agency

5.10 Assessee was a courier agency with a wide network of above 45 hubs located at various stations in South India. Its agents were centered around these hubs and they collected and delivered time-sensitive letters/articles to consignees. With aid of this network, assessee acted as a courier agent and transported articles between hubs. Revenue demanded service tax from assessee in category of ‘Franchise service’ and also imposed penalty. It was found that under a standard agreement entered into with each appointed agent, the assessee and each courier agent attached to the hubs had a relation as between principal and agent. Assessee controlled and administered their activities. Those agents were not conferred with any representational right by assessee. They were entitled to use name of assessee only as an ‘authorised agent’. Registration certificates issued to those agents carried endorsement that they were agents of assessee; that they returned courier charges received from clients to assessee, while retaining their expenses and remuneration and there was no payment of fee to assessee as required by section 65(47 ).

The Tribunal held that from 16-6-2005, the franchise service involves provision of a service associated with a particular person by trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo. The registration certificates issued to the agents carried the endorsement that they were agents of the assessee. The so-called franchisees being agents who undertook the work of courier agency on behalf of the assessee, it could not be held that any other service was involved in the transactions or that there was a different person receiving the service. It was further submitted that the agents were not doing business on their own account; that they were required to use consignment notes and stationery of the assessee, with the consignment notes bearing the name of the assessee; that no fee was paid by the agents and they only made a deposit with the assessee called trade deposits; that the agents paid service tax on the charges they collected from their clients, and returned the balance after retaining their expenses and remuneration; that the assessee did not impart any skill, technical know-how or managerial expertise to the agents; and, thus, there was no service rendered by the assessee to its agents to be taxed under the category ‘Franchise service’. "Franchise means an agreement by which the franchisee is granted representational right to sell or manufacture goods or to provide service or undertake any process identified with franchisor, whether or not a trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo or any such symbol as the case may be, is involved." On the basis of facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal held that it could be said that assessee undertook only courier agency’s service, engaging several agents who did not operate as ‘principals’ and, therefore, neither those agents were franchisees nor assessee, a franchisor. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal filed by the assessee.

Till the assessment year 1987-88, section 47(ii) laid down that distribution of capital assets on the dissolution of a firm is not to be considered as a transfer for the purpose of levy of capital gains tax. Thus, on receipt of the assets by B in the assessment year 1976-77 on the dissolution of A, there is no liability to capital gains. When B contributes capital assets presumably as her share of capital in C, while it results in a transfer, capital gains tax is not exigible thereon because the consideration therefor is indeterminate under section 48 of the Act - Sunil Siddharthbhai v. CIT [1985] 156 ITR 509/23 Taxman 14W (SC). Both these transactions become taxable only with effect from April 1, 1988 by virtue of section 45(4) and section 45(3), respectively.

Conclusion

3. Thus, the Tribunal's view that there was capital gains tax liability in the hands of A, and scope for such liability in the hands of B, appears to be incorrect. More indefensible is its observation that the capital gains tax on either or both the transactions would be more than the increase in revenue by the adoption of the "written down value in the hands of the old firm even if that be permitted as the basis of cost in the hands of the assessee-firm" as being extra legal. The High Court has observed that when "there is no change in the firm, depreciation can be claimed either on the book value or the market value of the machineries ....". Amalgamation of a Partnership Firm with a Company under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956

Study of Income-tax and Accounting Aspects

Omkar V. Deosthale

CS

A Partnership firm with minimum 8 partners is considered as an unregistered company within the meaning of section 582(b) of the Companies Act, 1956; therefore, liable to be wound up under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. For the purposes of the provisions of sections 391 to 393, as per section 390, the word "Company" is defined to mean a Company liable to be wound up under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. Further, such kinds of unregistered companies can be merged with the Private or Public Companies, by the order of the High Court1. This article tries to analyse other aspects relating to such amalgamations, i.e., taxation and accounting aspect.

Taxation aspect

1. Obvious question in this case is whether any assets transferred by a Firm (Transferor) to a Transferee-Company, during the course of amalgamation, are taxable as capital gains in the hands of Transferor or not. Answer to this question is in negative. The relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act affecting the same are discussed below.

Unlike the Companies Act, in the Income-Tax Act, word "amalgamation" is defined in section 2(1B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 as follows :

"amalgamation in relation to companies, means the merger of one or more companies with another company or the merger of two or more companies to form one company (the company or companies which so merge being referred to as the amalgamating company or companies and the company with which they merge or which is formed as a result of the merger, as the amalgamated company) in such a manner that—

(i) all the property of the amalgamating company or companies immediately before the amalgamation becomes the property of the amalgamated company by virtue of the amalgamation ;

(ii) all the liabilities of the amalgamating company or companies immediately before the amalgamation become the liabilities of the amalgamated company by virtue of the amalgamation ;

(iii) shareholders holding not less than three-fourths in value of the shares in the amalgamating company or companies (other than shares already held therein immediately before the amalgamation by, or by a nominee for, the amalgamated company or its subsidiary) become shareholders of the amalgamated company by virtue of the amalgamation,

otherwise than as a result of the acquisition of the property of one company by another company pursuant to the purchase of such property by the other company or as a result of the distribution of such property to the other company after the winding up of the first-mentioned company;"

Therefore, it seems that amalgamation of one Indian Company with another Indian Company is only recognized as amalgamation for Income-tax Act. The term "Indian Company" is defined in section 2(26) of the Income-tax Act as a company formed and registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), and includes—

(i) a company formed and registered under any law relating to companies formerly in force in any part of India [other than the State of Jammu and Kashmir and the Union territories specified in sub-clause (iii) of this clause] ;

(ia) a corporation established by or under a Central, State or Provincial Act ;

(ib) any institution, association or body which is declared by the Board to be a company under clause (17) ;

(ii) in the case of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, a company formed and registered under any law for the time being in force in that State ;

(iii) in the case of any of the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Goa, Daman and Diu, and Pondicherry, a company formed and registered under any law for the time being in force in that Union territory:

Provided that the registered or, as the case may be, principal office of the company, corporation, institution, association or body in all cases is in India;

Definitely partnership with 8 or more partners is not an Indian Company for the Income-tax Act; therefore, merger of partnership firm with Indian Company is not recognised as amalgamation under the Income-tax Act.

9. 'Sachin Tendulkar' entitled to vacancy allowance as he failed to find tenant for vacant flat

[Sachin R. Tendulkar v. DCIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 253 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The Assessee, Mr. Sachin Tendulkar, owned two properties in Pune - Flat S and Flat T. Flat T was let out, however, Flat S was vacant for the whole year as suitable tenant couldn't be found. He claimed that the said flat had remained vacant throughout the year despite his reasonable effort to let out the same. In this regard, he submitted three letters written to the builder. In first letter, he thanked the builder for identifying the tenant for the flat at Flat T and also requested to identify tenant for Flat S. Subsequently, the assessee had written second letter and after that third letter being reminders for identifying the tenant to let out Flat S.

Therefore, he claimed vacancy allowance under Section 23(1)(c) for Flat S and declared nil income. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer made additions for the notional rental income from Flat S, which was also upheld by the CIT(A).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee when same builder had helped the assessee to find tenant for another flat, it couldn't be said that these letters to the same builder to help him identify one more tenant, to be considered as fake, defied logic. Therefore, if a property was held with an intention to let out in the relevant year coupled with efforts made for letting it out, the same would fall within the purview of section 23(1)(c).

10. Sum received on relinquishment of 'right to sue' is non-taxable capital receipt: ITAT

[Bhojison Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 99 taxmann.com 26 (Ahmedabad - Trib.)]

The assessee-company entered into a development agreement by virtue of which a right in land was created in its favour by owner of land. Assessee's case was that despite development agreement entered into by landlord, the landlord had decided to sell said land to other parties. The assessee filed a suit in the Courts of law for specific performance of pre-emptive right to purchase the land. Later on, it received damages from the potential purchaser for relinquishment of 'right to sue' in the Courts of law for breach of development agreement. The assessee claimed that 'right to sue' was a personal right which would not fall within sweep of definition of 'capital asset' under section 2(14). Consequently, damages received from potential purchaser were treated as non-taxable capital receipts.

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

The essence of long list of judicial pronouncements cited by assessee was that section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act which uses the same expression 'property of any kind' in the context of transferability makes an exception in the case of a mere right to sue. The decisions thereunder make it abundantly clear that the 'right to sue' for damages is not an actionable claim. It cannot be assigned. Transfer of such a right is opposed to public policy as it tantamount to gambling in litigation.

Hence, such a 'right to sue' does not constitute a 'capital asset ' which, in turn, has to be 'an interest in property of any kind'. Despite the definition of expression 'capital asset ' in the widest possible terms in Section 2(14), a right to a capital asset must fall within the expression 'property of any kind' subject to certain exclusions.

Notwithstanding widest import assigned to the term 'property' which signifies every possible interest which a person can hold and enjoy, the ' right to sue' was a right in personam and such right could certainly not be transferred. In order to attract the charge of tax on capital gains, the sine qua non is that the receipt must have originated in a 'transfer ' within the meaning of section 45, read with section 2(47) of I-T Act. In the absence of its transferability, damages received by assessee couldn't be assessed as capital gains.

FAQ 11. How to calculate the sales turnover of share brokers?

When a share broker purchases securities on behalf of his customers, he does not get them transferred in his name but they are delivered in the name of the customer. The same is true in the case of sales also. The share broker holds the delivery merely on behalf of his customer. The property in securities does not get transferred to the share-brokers. Only brokerage, which is being accounted for in the books of account of share brokers, should be taken into account for calculating the value of turnover. However, in the case of transactions entered into by a share broker on his personal account, the sale value should be taken into account while calculating the sales turnover. The case of a sub-broker is not different from that of a share broker.

When a firm ‘A' ceases to exist and its business is taken over by one of the partners who carries it on as a proprietary concern ‘B’ and then, after a brief interval, the proprietary concern again becomes a partnership firm 'C’ several complex questions arise about the assessments of A, B and C under the Income-tax Act, 1961. In this article, the author discusses some of these questions in the light of the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Bison Knitting Co. [1997] 140 CTR (Mad.) 566, in which the facts conformed to the outline given above. The main questions considered by him are:

(i )When firm A is succeeded by proprietary concern B which, after a certain interval is succeeded by another firm C; is it a case of change of constitution of firm A' under section 187(2) ?

(ii )What is the nature of the transaction when the business changes hands from A to B and then from B to C?

(iii )What is the actual cost of depreciable assets of A in the hands of B ? Likewise, what is the actual cost of such assets in the hands of C when these are taken over by it from 'B' ?

(iv )Is there profit under section 41(2) in the hands of 'A' or ‘B' ?

(v)Do chargeable capital gains arise in the hands of A or B ? - EDITOR Madras High Court's decision

1. In CIT v. Bison Knitting Co. [1997] 140 CTR (Mad.) 566, there was a firm A, in which B was the managing partner; it came to an end on March 31, 1975. Thereafter, B took over the business as a proprietary concern from April 1, 1975. On May 1, 1975, the proprietary concern became a partnership C which filed a return for the assessment year 1976-77 disclosing an income of Rs. 88,169. In arriving at this income the firm claimed depreciation of 15 per cent on Rs. 2.71 lakhs which was the cost of the machinery to the firm. The ITO allowed the claim. The Commissioner, acting under section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), took the view that the sum of Rs. 2.71 lakhs represented the book value of the machinery taken over by C from the predecessor-owner B and not their written down value, which alone should have been adopted as cost for purposes of depreciation. The Commissioner directed the ITO to make a fresh assessment keeping in view the change in the constitution of the firm, the additions stated to have been made to the machinery account, the profit under section 41(2) of the Act in the hands of A, etc.

The Tribunal held that when the earlier firm A came to an end and the business was taken over as a proprietary concern by B, it amounted to a sale and so capital gains arising out of the transfer was liable to tax. Likewise, when the proprietary business of B became once again a partnership C, there was also scope for chargeability to tax of capital gains. The tax on capital gains on either or on both of these transactions would be much more than the increase in revenue that might arise by the adoption of the written down value of the assets in the hands of A, even if that be permitted as the basis of the cost in the hands of C.

Holding that there was no prejudice to the revenue, the Tribunal cancelled the Commissioner's order under section 263.

The High Court held that Rs. 2.71 lakhs on which depreciation was claimed by C represented the book value of these assets in the hands of the firm : "If there is a change in the constitution, depreciation can be claimed only on the written down value of the assets of the firm. If there is no change in the firm, depreciation can be claimed either on the book value or on the market value of the machineries of the firm". There is no connection between the assessee C and the erstwhile firm A in which B was the managing partner: "Therefore, there is no change in the constitution of the assessee-firm. In such a case, the assessee is entitled to claim depreciation on the book value. In the present case . . . we consider that the order passed by the Tribunal in setting aside the order passed by the Commissioner under section 263 of the Act is in order".

If, however, such out-of-pocket expenses are collected by way of a consolidated fee, the whole of the amount so collected shall form part of gross receipts, and no adjustment shall be made in respect of actual expenses paid on behalf of his clients out of the gross fees so collected.

FAQ 17. How to calculate the turnover of the commission agent?

Turnover of a commission agent or a person selling goods on a consignment basis is determined concerning the transfer of significant risk or reward of ownership. Where the property in goods or all significant risks and rewards of ownership of goods continue to belong to the principal, the relevant sale price shall not form part of the turnover of the commission agent. In this case, the turnover shall be the amount of commission earned by the agent. However, if the property in the goods, significant risk, and reward of ownership belong to the commission agent, the sale price received/receivable shall form part of his turnover.

The CBDT6 has also clarified that while determining the turnover in the case of Kachha Arahtias, the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of the principals, and only the gross commission has to be considered. However, in the case of Pucca Arahtias, the total sales/turnover of the business should be taken into consideration.

FAQ 18. How to calculate the turnover of a share broker?

When a share broker purchases securities on behalf of his customers, he does not get them transferred in his name, but they are delivered in the name of the customer. The same is true in the case of sales. The share broker holds the delivery merely on behalf of his customer. The property in securities does not get transferred to the share-brokers. Only brokerage, which is being accounted for in the books of share brokers, should be considered for calculating the turnover. However, in the case of transactions entered into by a share broker on his personal account, the sale value should be considered while calculating the sales turnover. The case of a sub-broker is not different from that of a share broker.

A 'speculative transaction' means a transaction in which a contract for the purchase or sale of any commodity or securities is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery or transfer of commodity or scrips. Each transaction, whether resulting in a positive or negative difference, is an independent transaction. In such transactions, though the contract notes are issued for the full value of the purchased or sold asset, the entries in the books of account are made only for the differences. Accordingly, the aggregate of both positive and negative differences is considered as the turnover.

TAX LITERATURE/TAXATION OF CAPITAL GAINS

TAXING THE UNTAXED - INSURANCE CLAIM

Gururaj Kulkarni*

In this article, the author discusses the question of taxability of amount received as insurance claim in the light of amendment of the Income-tax Act, 1961 by insertion of sub-section (1A) in section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 by the Finance Act, 1999. The author considers both the legal and the accounting aspects of the issue - EDITOR

Background

1. All revenue receipts are taxable unless specifically exempt; all capital receipts are exempt unless specifically taxable. The profits in lieu of source is a capital receipt. Hitherto, any amount or sum received under an insurance claim was outside the ambit of section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’). With the new budget proposals, this relief is going to witness a complete change, overruling various Supreme Court decisions. A close look at the chargeability of insurance compensation is pertinent, in view of amendment of section 45. Let us cast a brief glance at the present position.

Any profit or gain arising from the transfer of a capital asset is chargeable to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ in the previous year in which the transfer took place if it is not eligible for exemption under sections 54, 54B, 54EA, 54EB, 54D, etc.

According to section 2(47) of the Act, transfer in relation to a capital asset includes :—

(a)sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset; or

(b)extinguishment of any rights therein; or

(c)the compulsory acquisition thereof under any law; or

(d)conversion of capital asset into stock-in-trade; or

(e)transaction giving possession of immovable property under part-performance of contract of the nature referred in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; or

(f)transaction which has the effect of transferring an immovable property.

The definition of transfer under section 2( 47) is merely inclusive and does not exhaust other kinds of transfer - Sunil Siddharthbhai v. CIT [1985] 156 ITR 509/23 Taxman 14 (SC).

Extinguishment of asset is not transfer

2. Transfer not only includes physical transfer of a capital asset, but also relinquishment or extinguishment of any rights therein. The existence of the asset during the process is a pre-condition to attract the provisions of section 45. If an asset is destroyed, or lost, it would be incorrect to term it as a transfer. The non-existence of the asset after such an accident entails non-application of section 45. Indeed, the right of the owner or possessor of the capital asset is lost but the extinguishment of right in the asset on account of extinguishment of the asset itself is not a transfer of right, but its destruction or loss or cessation. Extinguishment refers not to extinguishment of asset itself but to extinguishment of the holder’s right to the asset - CIT v. East India Charitable Trust [1994] 206 ITR 152/ 73 Taxman 380 (Cal.).

Judicial pronouncements

3. In Vania Silk Mills (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1991] 191 ITR 647/ 59 Taxman 3 , the Apex Court had an occasion to appraise the rationale of taxing the insurance compensation in the light of extinguishment of right. It was held that destruction of a capital asset is not a transfer and, therefore, insurance compensation received from an insurance company does not give rise to capital gains tax liability. A question normally would creep-in regarding the taxability of the sum, when salvage (damaged asset) is taken over by the insurance company. It is held that even in such a case, there is no transfer under section 2(47) and, therefore, capital gains tax liability does not arise - C. Leo Machodo v. CIT [1988] 172 ITR 744/ 38 Taxman 296 (Mad.). Followed Marybong & Kyel Tea Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 589/ 91 Taxman 11 (SC).

1.3. Tax on receipt of money or capital asset by partner in connection with reconstitution of firm [Section 45(4)]

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has substituted sub-section (4) as proposed to be substituted by the Finance Bill, 2021. This provision provides thatwhere a partner receives during the previous year any capital asset or money or both from a firm in connection with the reconstitution, then any profit and gains arising from such receipt of money by specified person shall be deemed to be the income of the specified entity under the head "Capital Gains' of the previous year in which such capital asset or money or both were received by the specified person. Further, it also prescribes the formula to compute the profit and gains arising to the partner from such receipt of money or capital asset from the firm.

The profit and gains shall be computed in accordance with the following formula:

A = B + C - D

A = Income chargeable to income-tax under this provision as income of the firm under the head 'capital gains';

B = Value of money received by partner on the date of such receipt;

C = Fair market value of the capital asset received by the partner on the date of such receipt; and

D = Balance in the capital account (represented in any manner) of the partner in the books of account of the firm at the time of reconstitution.

Where the value of A is negative, it shall be deemed to be nil.

While computing the balance in the capital account of partner in the books of account of firm, increase in capital account due to the following shall not be taken into account:

(a)

Revaluation of any asset;

(b)

Self-generated goodwill (goodwill acquired without incurring any cost for purchase or which has been generated during the course of business or profession);

(c)

Other self-generated assets.

Explanation2 to Section 45(4) clarifies that when a capital asset is received by the partner from a firm in connection with the reconstitution, the provisions of the said section shall operate in addition to the provisions of section 9B. Thus, the taxation under both the provisions shall be worked out independently.

1.3-1. Analysis of section 45(4)

Section 45(4) provides for the computation of capital gain which arises to a partner on extinguishment or relinquishment of his right in the firm in connection with reconstitution of the firm. Though the income arises to partner but it is deemed as income of the firm. Thus, the firm would be assessed under section 9B for its own income and under section 45(4) for income arising to partner thereof.

1.3-2. Section 45(4) v. Section 9B

Section 9B provides for taxability arising at the time of dissolution or reconstitution, whereas section 45(4) deals with the taxability at the time of reconstitution only. Where any asset or money is transferred to partner or member at the time of dissolution, same amounts to extinguishment or relinquishment of rights. Term "transfer" as defined under section 2(47) covers extinguishment or relinquishment of rights within its ambit. However, since such rights are not extinguished or relinquished in favour of another person in case of dissolution, no one derives any benefit from the same. Thus, section 45(4) does not apply at the time of dissolution.

1.4. Mode of computation of capital gain [Section 48]

Section 9B deals with the taxability of the income arising to the firm on transfer of capital asset to a partner in connection with dissolution or reconstitution. Section 45(4) deals with the income which arises to the partner on receipt of a capital asset in connection with the reconstitution. However, tax in respect of such receipt is charged in the hands of firm only. Thus, in case of reconstitution double taxability will arise once under section 45(1) read with section 9B and second under section 45(4). To remove the impact of such double taxation, Section 48 is amended. This section provides for reduction of cost of acquisition, improvement and expenditure incurred in connection with transfer from full value of consideration of capital asset while computing income chargeable under the head 'capital gains'.

YOUR QUERIES ON SERVICE TAX

RAJESH DHAWAN*

Whether brand owners providing right to use of their brand and technical know-how fall under intellectual property services?

Brand owners hold intellectual property rights over the brand names, whereas other persons hold license granted by the State Government to manufacture under the brand name of the brand owner. The brand owner enters into an agreement with such manufacturers/licencee to grant permission to use their brand as well as also provide technical staff/assistance to maintain required quality. Property, risk and reward of the products so manufactured rest with such manufacturer/licensee. Such manufacturer/licensee pays on the agreed sum to the brand owner for grant of permission to use the brand name and the technical know-how. The Board through instruction F.No. 249/1/2006-CX.4, dated 27-10-2008 has clarified that in such cases brand owner provides taxable service, i.e., intellectual property service to licensee/manufacturer, on which service tax is chargeable on the gross amount charged by the brand owner.

Whether amount paid for booking of space and time for advertisement falls under advertising services?

No. The Government vide its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that the amount paid by the advertising agency for space and time in getting the advertisement published in print media, i.e., news papers, periodicals, etc., or the electronic media, i.e., Doordarshan, private TV Channels, All India Radio, etc., will not be includible in the value of taxable service for the purpose of levy of service tax.

Whether ordinary transporters are different from courier services?

Yes. The Government has clarified vide its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 that the nature of business of a ‘courier agency’ is quite distinct from ordinary transporters, which carry goods from one place to another, whereas ‘courier agency’ delivers time sensitive documents, goods and articles.

Whether preservation of wasteland and bringing it into use falls under consulting engineer services?

No. In the case of CCE v. Nippon KOEI Co. Ltd. [2007] 8 STT 449 (Bang. - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that the appellants were carrying out ECO conservation works to preserve the wasteland and bringing it into use, especially for development of tribals. The said activity can’t be considered as activity coming within the ambit of ‘consulting engineer services’.

Whether facility of use of premises to the members by clubs falls under mandap keeper services?

No. In the case of Dalhousie Institute v. Asstt. Commissioner, Service Taxcell 2005 (180) ELT 18/1 STT 15 (Cal.), the High Court held that tax is recoverable from the ‘mandap keeper’ who is having a different and separate legal and physical entity, and lets out the mandap with commercial and trading object. Here the members have formed the petitioner No.1 to serve themselves mutually and for this purpose members are paying for such user and any amount of receipt alone, and not third party, therefore clubs are not liable to service tax as mandap keeper.

Whether services provided by managing director or the director of the company fall under the management or business consultant services?

The Board through Circular No. 115/09/2009-ST, dated 31-7-2009 has clarified that remuneration paid to the managing directors/directors of the companies whether whole-time or independent when being compensated for their performance as managing directors/directors would not be liable to service tax.

Whether photography service is taxable even if works contract tax is applicable?

Yes. In the case of Kerala Colour Lab Association v. Union of India 2003 (156) ELT 17/[2007] 8 STT 353 (Ker.), the High Court held that once we determine the taxable event as the service rendered, and not the sale of goods, irrespective of whether it is a works contract or contract for sale of goods, the taxable event would occur. The taxable event occurs because of the service rendered. Merely because the measure or valuation of tax is linked with gross consideration received in the transaction, it does not determine the nature of tax. The taxable event determines the true event of tax; the measure of tax does not determine the nature of tax, but the quantum of tax which can be levied and collected.

6. In all cases of agency agreement, generally the ownership of goods or services is not transferred to the agents; the ownership remains with the principal. According to Concise Oxford Dictionary (9th edition), agent means "a person who acts for another in business, politics, etc." Some of the other dictionaries also provide the similar meaning. Simply an agent is a representative who acts on behalf of other persons or organizations. Thus, when ownership of goods or services is transferred to an agent, he cannot be treated as agent, because in that case he will be doing work for himself. In case of Pratap Singh & Sons v. CCE, Mumbai [2007] 6 STT 390 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee was purchasing and reselling the products of several manufacturers. The agreements with the assessee and respective manufacturers stipulated that the assessee should improve marketing conditions and sell the products. For said purpose the assessee was required to establish facilities and to deploy sufficiently trained and suitable labour, to advertise and to display the products of these manufacturers. The department taking the view that the above activities of the assessee were of clearing and forwarding agent, demanded service tax. Further, the department took the view that special discount given by the manufacturers should be treated as service charges and, accordingly, confirmed service tax on the discount. The Tribunal held that the assessee had purchased and sold products from the principals as their distributor. On purchase of the goods, the assessee became the owner and as owner, dealer or transferee of the goods, it was in his own interest to promote the sale activities and to make advertisement and keep the trained salesman and, hence, they were part of the dealers’ job. That could not be treated as service rendered to the principals, namely, the manufacturers. The term ‘event management’ has been defined as follows :—

"‘Event management’ means any services provided in relation to planning, promotion, organizing or presentation of any arts, entertainment, business, sports or any other event and includes any consultations provided in this regard." Recently, the Tribunal in the case of Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT (Mumbai - CESTAT), has interpreted the words ‘in relation to’ appearing in the definition of advertisement agency. The words ‘advertisement agency’ are defined under section 65(2) as any commercial concern engaged in providing services connected with the making, preparation, display or exhibition or advertisement and includes advertisement consultant. The Tribunal held that the person who is engaged in providing the services relating to making or preparation of advertisement such as designing, visualising, conceptualizing, will be liable to pay service tax. Thus, the persons who are engaged in providing the services specified thereon can be liable for payment of service tax. The Tribunal further observed as follows:—

Therefore, the definition of ‘advertising agency’ cannot be read literally and out of context, if done so, every person some way connected with an advertisement will be advertising agency. That cannot be and is not the coverage of the Service Tax envisaged. In the present case, one cannot ignore term being defined i.e. ‘advertising agency’ and proceed to levy service tax on

(i )any commercial concern

(ii )providing service connected with making preparation, display or exhibition of advertisements.

If the definition is read in isolation and in an all encompassing manner out of context, then any person/company employing cameraman connected with shooting of advertisement film will become an advertising agency. A caterer supplying tea and biscuits during the production of advertising film will also become a person connected with preparation of advertisement and became an advertising agency. Similarly, a lawyer advising whether advertising film will be violating copyright law or other laws relating to obscenity etc. would be treated as advertising agent. Similarly a broadcaster (on radio or television) of an advertisement will become an advertising agency, or a cinema hall flashing an advertisement or newspaper/magazine publishing an advertisement will become an advertising agency. Such absurdities, from an interpretation have to be avoided. The term ‘service connected with used in the definition of "Advertising agency" is to be understood in context of and in a restrictive manner.

The astrological or marriage bureau only carries out the function of match making or assisting in the same. It does not in any way engage in planning, promotion, organizing or presentation of any event.

Whether charging rent for displaying advertisement falls under advertising services?

No. The CESTAT in its judgment held that permitting display of advertisement on its site and raising bills for realising rental charge is mere sub-letting to an advertising agency without providing services of the nature defined for advertising services; hence, the activity of the respondent will not bring it under the definition of advertising agency.

CCE v. Azad Publications [2007] 8 STT 242 (Delhi - CESTAT)

Whether technical know-how generated for internal consumption sold out later falls under ‘Consulting engineer services’?

No. The appellant had developed certain technical know-how for themselves for the purpose of providing e-governance and rural governance in India and had named the project Gramdoot. Since the appellant could not implement the project itself, it sold the technical know-how by agreement. It was held that since the agreement was for technology transfer and not for providing any technical know-how service and the ownership of the technical know-how was transferred to the buyer, the demand of service tax was not sustainable.

Aksh Optifibers Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 252 (New Delhi - CESTAT)

Whether express cargo service transporters are different from Courier agency services?

No. The Government in its Master Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated August 23, 2007 has clarified that the nature of service provided by ‘Express cargo service’ provider falls within the scope and definition of courier agency.

Whether fee collected by institution falls under Commercial training or coaching services?

No. The Tribunal held that education has a larger scope and may include coaching or training and not vice versa. Coaching or training is a very narrow activity, imparting skill in a particular discipline. But, education is a broader term, which is a process of development of personality of body, mind and intellect. Just because institution collects fees from students, one cannot come to conclusion that it imparts commercial training or coaching. Institutions preparing students for entrance exams to universities are covered under commercial training or coaching services and not institutions offering degrees recognized by law.

Magnus Society v. CC & CE [2009] 18 STT 193 (Bang. - CESTAT)

Whether computer engineering firm falls under ‘Consulting engineer services’?

Yes. The Finance Act, 2008 with effect from May 16, 2008 has amended the definition of ‘taxable service’ to bring back the computer software engineering consultancy service under the service tax net and to provide that services provided by a consulting engineer in relation to advice, consultancy or technical assistance in the disciplines of both computer hardware engineering and computer software engineering shall also fall under ‘Consulting engineer service’.

Whether an organization formed for charitable purpose is liable for service tax?

Yes. The CESTAT in its judgment held that an organization may be charitable organization established for some purpose, but may still be engaged in commercial activities, as without any commercial activities, the income required for charitable purpose cannot be generated. For levy of service tax, it is the activity of an organization, which is relevant and not objective.

Punjab Ex-Servicemen Corpn. v. CCE [2009] 18 STT 21 (New Delhi - CESTAT)

Whether the person manufacturing the signboards falls under advertising services?

No. The Tribunal in its judgment held that the person who is only writing or preparing the signboards at the behest of their customer cannot be called as advertising agency. There was no evidence on record to show that the relationship between the customers and the appellant is of advertising agent which is necessary for imposition of service tax.

Star Neon Signs v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 223 (New Delhi - CEGAT)

Whether assisting a person in acquiring share in a company falls under management consultant services?

No. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not carrying out activity of management but it was manufacturer. Incidental help in acquisition of shares does not fall under ‘Management consultant service’.

K.R. Alloys Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 10 STT 510 (Bang. - CESTAT)

Whether receiving, storing and distributing the products on behalf of client will attract service tax?

No. The High Court relied upon the case of Medpro Pharma (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 341 (New Delhi - CESTAT) (LB) and held that the activities undertaken by the respondent would not fall under C&F agency services.
