CIT [2000] 243 ITR 158, held that cancellation of sale of assets cannot be such a subsequent event so as to change the nature of the receipt of the forfeited amount. 6.15-2e WHETHER A RECEIPT IS CAPITAL OR REVENUE - The principles that can be deduced from various decisions of the Indian and the foreign courts for determining whether a particular amount received by an assessee is capital or revenue in nature are as under :

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

■ Profit motive is not decisive of the question, whether a particular receipt is capital or income.7

■ The question whether the payer is compelled to pay has no relevance in the determination of the character of the receipt. It may be that the payee has no legal claim for payment and the payment is made voluntarily, yet the receipt may be of revenue character.8

A voluntary payment is a profit of employment if it accrues by virtue of the employment notwithstanding that there may not be any legal obligation to make the payment. If, however, the payment is in the nature of a personal gift to him, it is not regarded as a payment for services but as a mere present.8

■ The voluntary payment to a lawyer by a person who is not a client but who has benefited by the lawyer’s professional services to another is taxable.1

■ The fund out of which the money came is not material.2

■ General payments made by way of donation to a company out of benevolence or feeling of charity would not entail income in the hands of the recipient.3

■ Amounts received in settlement of a right under trading contract are trading receipts.4

6.15-2f COMPENSATION - WHETHER REVENUE OR CAPITAL - About the receipt of compensation the law is that as discussed below :

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

6.15-2f COMPENSATION - WHETHER REVENUE OR CAPITAL - About the receipt of compensation the law is that as discussed below :

■ Compensation on termination of agency itself vis-a-vis compensation on termination of agreement which is not the source of income - If the agreement itself is the source of income from which income, profits and gains spring up and the compensation is paid to a person on account of its termination, it could be said that the compensation relates to the extinction of the source and also the profit-making apparatus and in that sense, a capital receipt, as happens normally on termination of agency contracts. In that case there is no capital asset de hors the agreement. But if the agreement is not the real source of income and the real source is something else (for example trading or commercial assets such as cinema hall, factory, which are leased out under an agreement), the compensation on termination of the agreement could be a trading receipt. The agreement is only a means to manage and exploit that asset to produce income.5

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

■ Amount paid for refraining from carrying on competitive business - There is no inimitable principle that the compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on competitive business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated or for loss of goodwill is prima facie of the nature of a capital receipt.6

■ Compensation for surrender of industrial licence - In CIT v. Automobile Products of India Ltd.1, the Bombay High Court held that where the termination of the activity is not a necessary incident of the business of the assessee and the extinction and surrender of the industrial licence and the collaboration agreement have impaired the profit-making structure of the assessee, the amount received by it as compensation will be a capital receipt.

Section 50(2) refers to block of assets ceasing to exist as such by reason of transfer of the entire ‘block of assets’. The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. Even if it was taken as a capital asset, in view of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Ambica Chemical Production v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal No. 238/V/2002, dated 26-5-2005] no tax was leviable in terms of section 45 on the amount received by the assessee. [Para 30]

Considering the above principles, in the instant case, the compensation received by the assessee from HTIPL was revenue in nature and was taxable accordingly. The reasons were (i ) the assessee was carrying on business of agencies/distributorship. It had lost only one. This business apparatus was not impaired. It was its business to deal in agencies. The impugned agency was not the sole bread earner for the assessee. It lost one trading item and continued with others, (ii ) what had been done with HTIPL was only a business arrangement. A legal structure had been erected wherein the same business of distributorship of products in question would continue but under different banner and in partnership with HTIPL in a joint venture. This was no stoppage of business as such. In place of deriving income from foreign company directly, it would derive income for the same job from HTIPL as a share in joint venture. The business apparatus, if any, had been remodelled in a different form to suit the principal i.e., the foreign company. The income flow had not been stopped from this source. So, what had been done through this resource transfer agreement was only a business arrangement or business re-organisation whereby the assessee’s income or source of income was not affected (iii) what was transferred to HTIPL was not an asset, as no such asset had been acquired by the assessee. It did not figure in the balance sheet. It was claimed by the assessee that intangible asset had been transferred. In fact, it was found that the customer data base as such was not transferred on an absolute ownership basis. The assessee was not prevented from using the same. What was done was that HTIPL would use the same database henceforth after the termination date. No legal ownership or intellectual copyright was claimed over this database. At least no evidence was placed in support of the claim that customer database was a copyright protected or intellectual property right protected asset. The transfer of employees/staff also was merely a transfer of a resource, which could have been otherwise also built up. This was again a normal business arrangement and was only a condition of joint venture. Further, arrangement with foreign company was only modified vis-a-vis the assessee. Earlier there was an arrangement of foreign company directly with assessee. Now it was again with assessee but in a joint venture. In commercial parlance, nothing had changed except form of relationship which was only a more suitable and convenient trade arrangement. Hence, transfer of employees and staff was not helpful to support the argument that there was a transfer of asset and, hence, the compensation so received was capital in nature; (iv) in fact HTIPL only received certain benefits in terms of resource transfer which would help the joint venture in running the business. [Para 12]

Those resources (employees and customer database) were not the part of balance sheet. They were also not a part of definition of ‘asset’ as given in section 2(14), ‘property’ of any kind held by an assessee. [Para 13]

As held in CIT v. National Insurance Co. Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 37 (Cal.), a property is a bundle of rights, which the owner can lawfully exercise to the exclusion of all others. He is entitled to use and enjoy it as he wishes. The property can be either corporeal or incorporeal. Though it does not always mean physical property but it does mean the right, title, interest in a property. Property also includes rights such as trade marks, copyrights, patents and even intellectual rights capable of transfer or transmission. They also include beneficial rights to a thing considered as having money value especially with reference to transfer/succession and their capacity to be injured. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the revenue had sought to make employees and customer database as same sort of right. For it to be right, there should be (i) possession (ii ) ownership to the exclusion of others; (iii ) transferability/succession (iv) some money value; (v) or created by statute. Employee could not fall under the definition of capital asset as they did not fit under the concept of ‘property’. Though the customer database had been formed over the years but had not been actually transferred to HTIPL. It had been only allowed to be used by it. [Para 15]

So far as the argument of the assessee that what had been received by the assessee was for ‘goodwill’ was concerned, those two items alone did not form goodwill. [Para 16]

In consideration thereof CPC, which had agencies of a number of well-known paper mills, agreed to pay compensation to the assessee by way of rebate/commission at the rate of 5 per cent on the value of the net sales. By another leave and licence agreement dated 24-4-1975 entered into between the assessee and another party CPL, the assessee allotted 400 sq. ft. of the first floor to CPL for a period of 5 years with effect from 1-11-1974. In consideration thereof CPL agreed to pay compensation of Rs. 1,500 per month and make a deposit of Rs. 3 lakhs with the assessee as security for due performance/observance of the terms/conditions of the licence. Sometime during the relevant previous year, i.e., calendar year 1983 corresponding to the assessment year 1984-85, the assessee thought of transferring the first floor to the trustees of eight trusts. The trustees of these trusts insisted on having vacant possession of the first floor and agreed to pay Rs. 55 lakhs in this regard. B y an agreement dated 10-5-1983, entered into between the assessee and CPC, it was agreed that CPC would vacate 2,200 sq. ft. of the first floor allotted to it under the agreement dated 1-11-1974 in consideration of Rs. 37 lakhs by way of compensation. The 10 shares owned by the assessee in the aforesaid society were also transferred and registered in the names of the trustees of the aforesaid 8 trusts in the register of the aforesaid society. The assessee contended that the compensation of Rs. 43 lakhs paid to CPC and CPL should be deducted from Rs. 55 lakhs in working out the capital gain. The ITO, however, rejected the assessee’s claim holding that the parties in question were sister concerns of the assessee and the assessee had merely allowed them to use the premises and no right to them in any form was transferred and, thus, there was no enforceable right for those parties in respect of the premises in any form and the assessee’s claim for payment of compensation was not based on any reason and it could only be construed as a device or adjustment to reduce the tax liability. Profits in lieu of Salary v. Capital Gains

The Delhi High Court in the case of Akash Poddar v. Asstt. CIT [2024] 165 taxmann.com 271 (Delhi) through an interesting and illuminating judgment dated 7th August, 2024 by reversing the order passed by the ITAT Delhi Bench, has held that where assessee received a lump sum amount from company towards full and final settlement of all disputes and differences with it and in terms of settlement agreement, assessee unconditionally and irrevocably relinquished all his rights in respect of registration of shares held by him and to consequently handover share certificates in original to company, the said settlement amount was not liable to be construed as payment connected to termination of assessee's employment and, thus, was liable to be recognized as capital gain.

The assessee, an individual, derived income from salary and capital gains during the assessment year 2014-15. It was submitted before the Assessing Officer that the assessee was offered 50,000 equity shares of TTPL as on 8th June, 2010, in which he was employed with effect from 1st December, 2007 at a purchase cost of NIL and the assessee relinquished the same shares on 23rd January, 2014 for a sum of Rs. 303.75 lakhs thus earning a long-term capital gain of same amount.

The Assessing Officer called for the details of Grant date, Vesting date, Exercise date and Exercise price with reference to the said shares sold. These shares were offered in instalments of 7,500 shares each over a period of four years with 7,500 shares options maturing on completion of each year of service of the company starting from 1st December, 2007. These shares represented 3% of the paid-up capital of the company. The appointment of the assessee was terminated in the month of August 2010 and the assessee approached the Company Law Board against this termination and the Company Law Board vide order dated 29th March, 2012 ordered 'status quo'.

However, an agreement styled as "Settlement Agreement" dated 23rd January, 2014 was entered into between the assessee and TTP Ltd. as a result of which 50,000 shares were allotted to the assessee as on 8th June, 2010.

The Assessing Officer treated the entire money realised by the assessee "as profits in lieu of salary" as defined in Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act.

The assessee was carrying on sub-broking business with 'S' and had about 1800 clients. Said business was transferred to 'S' and for the transfer of goodwill, Rs. 1.11 crores were paid by 'S' to the assessee. Further, since the cost of goodwill was nil and the assessee had purchased the capital bonds with sale proceeds, it claimed deduction under section 54EC. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's claim of sale of goodwill holding that because of changes in the SEBI Regulations regarding share trading assessee could no more act as a sub-broker and, thus, when he could not have continued his business, there was no question of transfer of goodwill. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer taxed the sum of Rs. 1.11 crores under section 28(ii)(c) by treating the same as compensation for termination of agency.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that relationship between 'S' and the assessee was on principal to principal basis and the termination of the agreement between 'S' and the assessee was termination of agreement of two principals. He held that the amount in question was paid by 'S' as compensation for trading infrastructure of business of the assessee, and accordingly, same was to be treated as capital receipt. Accordingly, he directed the Assessing Officer to assess income under the head 'Income from capital gain' and allow exemption under section 54EC to the assessee.

2.2-10c AGENCY RIGHTS/DISTRIBUTION RIGHTS - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : "An 'agent' is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the 'Principal'."

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee's level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature'.

2.2-12 Sale and lease back - It may be noted that if an intangible asset is sold and then taken for use from the transferee, Explanation 4A to section 43(1) may apply if the transferor has already obtained depreciation on the asset. Under this Explanation, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on the written down value of the transferor at time of transfer of the intangible asset, although he may have acquired the intangible asset for a higher sum. To illustrate, if the written down value of an intangible asset is Rs. 20 lakhs in the hands of the transferor and if he sells the asset for Rs. 50 lakhs, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on Rs. 20 lakhs by virtue of the provisions of Explanation 4A.

It may be noted that the aforesaid Explanation does not apply if the transferor has not claimed any depreciation on the intangible asset. In such an event, the actual cost for the transferee shall not be restricted to the written down value of the transferor and he will get depreciation on his cost of acquisition.

The transfer of right or relinquishment of part and parcel of business undertaking of the assessee is nothing but transfer of capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14). Any profit arising from the transfer of capital asset must be chargeable under the head 'capital gain'. The word 'transfer' has been defined in section 2(47). [Para 33] From the definition under section 2(47), it is clear that the word 'transfer' is inclusive of definition, which inter alia provides 6 situations under which there can be transfer in relation to the capital asset. Relinquishment of any rights in the capital asset is one of the situation enumerated in section 2(47). The word 'relinquishment' denotes that relinquishment should be only in the case of capital asset with reference to which the word 'transfer' has been defined. The right of the assessee over the landed property which was part and parcel of the business undertaking of the assessee is a capital asset. The moment assessee losses the right attached to a part of the business undertaking of the assessee, there is relinquishment of right over the said property. The relinquishment of assets or extinguishment of any right in it which may not amount to a sale can also be considered as a transfer. Therefore, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are not acceptable that there is no transfer under section 45 and the assessee has done only business transaction. Accordingly, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue are reversed and it is held that the income accrued to the assessee out of relinquishment of right over the property is to be chargeable under section 45 and computation of capital gain has to be done in accordance with section 48. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to compute the income under the head capital gain on relinquishment of right over the impugned landed property. [Para 34]

In the result, assessee's appeal is partly allowed. [Para 35]

The Assessing Officer held that it was a capital receipt and at the same time taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. Before the Tribunal, the revenue argued that the amount was a revenue receipt. At the same time, it was also contended that even if it was assessed as a capital receipt, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). The Tribunal held that the termination of the agreement affected the business structure of the assessee’s business and the unexpired period of the agreement was sufficiently long and so, it could be inferred that the compensation amount paid was a capital receipt. The Tribunal further held that the agreement originally entered into was not an agency agreement at all but an agreement entered into purely for rendering consultancy services and the agreement was between principal and principal. However, the Assessing Officer considered the entire consideration received as income of the assessee without mentioning the head of income under which he assessed it, which was not proper. [Para 7.5]

Further, there were two agreements of sale—one for 3 acres and another for 7 acres dated 6-1-2006. As per these agreements of sale-cum -general power of attorney, the vendor had delivered the vacant possession of the scheduled property to the vendee. As per the provision of section 2(47 ) transfer takes place as soon as the possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of property Act, 1882. Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : “An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

Under this Explanation, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on the written down value of the transferor at time of transfer of the intangible asset, although he may have acquired the intangible asset for a higher sum. To illustrate, if the written down value of an intangible asset is Rs. 20 lakhs in the hands of the transferor and if he sells the asset for Rs. 50 lakhs, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on Rs. 20 lakhs by virtue of the provisions of Explanation 4A.

It may be noted that the aforesaid Explanation does not apply if the transferor has not claimed any depreciation on the intangible asset. In such an event, the actual cost for the transferee shall not be restricted to the written down value of the transferor and he will get depreciation on his cost of acquisition.

also for facilitating the peaceful possession (including removing encroachment) of 10 acres piece of land to ‘B’. For the purpose, the assessee was compensated with Rs. 2.8 crores by the above firm. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and added the entire sum of Rs. 2.80 crores received by the assessee to his unexplained income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the assessment order.

On second appeal : HELD: It was apparent from records that the consideration received by the assessee, if any, was to be bifurcated into two parts—one for relinquishment of right over the property and another for facilitating the peaceful possession to the vendee. However, the Assessing Officer considered the entire consideration received as income of the assessee without mentioning the head of income under which he assessed it, which was not proper. [Para 7.5]

Further, there were two agreements of sale—one for 3 acres and another for 7 acres dated 6-1-2006. As per these agreements of sale-cum -general power of attorney, the vendor had delivered the vacant possession of the scheduled property to the vendee. As per the provision of section 2(47 ) transfer takes place as soon as the possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of property Act, 1882. Under section 45(1), to attract the capital gains, the following conditions are to be fulfilled :

(1)There should be capital asset.

(2)That capital asset should have been held or owned by the assessee.

(3)Transfer of that capital asset should have been effected.

(4)The transfer should have been effected in the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

(5)Profit and gains should have been from such transfer. [Para 7.6]

If the conditions are satisfied then profit and gains are chargeable to income-tax under head ‘Capital gains’ and would be deemed to be income of the year in which transfer took place. In order to attract tax on capital gain, subject-matter of transfer should be capital asset. [Para 7.7]

A particular thing, right or interest may be a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(14), transaction in relation to which may not give rise to taxable capital gain because of the fact that no transfer as envisaged by the Act was involved. Similarly, certain capital asset can not give rise to capital gain because of the fact that cost of acquisition can (sic-not ) be envisaged in the acquisition of the asset. Any right which can be called property will be included in the definition of ‘capital asset’. A contract for sale of land is capable of specific performance. It is also assignable. Therefore, a right to obtain conveyance of an immovable property is clearly property contemplated by section 2(14). In the instant case, what was said to be relinquished or surrendered was a right in the asset. The giving up of the right to claim specific performance by conveyance of immovable property was held to be relinquishment of capital asset and it was transfer of capital asset within the meaning of the Act. The assessee gave up his right to claim specific performance. By the termination of his oral agreement and allowing the vendor to sell the property to any person at any price, the assessee had given up or relinquished his right of specific performance and what he had received was the consideration for relinquishing that right and the assessee was paid sum of Rs. 1.5 crores. This transfer attracted the tax on capital gain if there was a cost involved to acquire that right. In the instant case, it was not possible to envisage its cost. In any case, such cost had not been specifically determined or brought on record by the Assessing Officer. Though the parties involved stated that there was an advance payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the assessee to the vendor, yet there was no iota of documentary evidence supporting this, other than statement from the parties. Therefore, the amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was a capital receipt, which did not give rise to any capital gain because it was received in respect of relinquishment of right of purchase of property, the cost of which was not determined. It was held in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/ 5 Taxman 1 (SC) that in computing the capital gain it is a condition that to determine the cost of acquisition of the asset on transfer, where such determination fails there can be no capital gain. In view of this, though there was relinquishment of right over asset, there was no transfer of capital asset in accordance with the provisions of section 45. The assessee was not liable for the capital gain. [Para 7.8]

Whether the money received by the assessee based on the settlement which happened in the relevant previous years could be charged to capital gains in assessee's hand? The settlement clearly showed that the AOP as such stood terminated. The differences that cropped up between the members of the AOP is clear from the suit filed by PDP before the Civil Court. This suit show that the parties intended a joint development but were unable to agree on various duties and responsibilities that they had undertaken to do, bringing the project to a limbo and leading to the cancellation of Power of Attorney by the assessee. The parties thought that the joint development was no more feasible. Thus in lieu of the 20 per cent share of profit which would have arisen to the assessee in future, assessee agreed to receive Rs. 14 crores. It can be seen either as the share of profit, the assessee would have received in future from the AOP or a capital receipt. Both parties to the settlement were Private Limited Companies. Even if they had an income of one rupee, it was chargeable to tax at flat rates. It in other words it means that the profit of the AOP was always taxable in the hands of the AOP at maximum rates. Once the profits are taxable in the hands of AOP, by virtue of section 86, read with section 110, the share income is not taxable in the hands of the members. Even otherwise the source of income for the assessee had totally extinguished. Admittedly assessee was having only this project and nothing else. Assessee was not holding any other land or fixed asset as it is clear from the balance sheet. [Para 29]

No doubt, assessee itself had returned capital gains in the impugned assessment year, considering the land to have been transferred by it in the relevant previous year. This however cannot help the case of the revenue. Just because an erroneous admission of income had been made it would not make the assessee liable to tax, for the simple reason that the charge of tax is on income computed in accordance with section 5 and not based on the admission of income where there was no income of the nature admitted. [Para 30]

Since, it has been held that there indeed was an AOP, the question as to whether there was any transfer of subject property from assessee to PDP becomes irrelevant.[Para 31]

Thus, in view of the discussions above, the addition of Rs. 14 crores made under the head 'Capital Gain' was incorrect. Such addition stands deleted. [Para 32]

Adjustment of losses lying unabsorbed

Where business of the assessee is no longer in existence and he has sustained the business losses, not being a loss sustained in specula-tion busi-ness, during the year in which business ceased to exist, such loss can be ad-justed against the income taxable, other than the income taxable as balancing charge, under this provision as deemed business profit. At the time of preparation of the profit and loss account, there may be instances that few receipts being in the nature of capital receipts omitted/ignored to be recorded with a conception that capital receipts do not form part of the business income. Therefore, the purpose of clause 16(e) is that the In-come-tax Department can examine the receipts that are not recorded in the profit and loss account based on the argument that they are capital receipts to deter-mine their classification as either capital or not.

It is well settled that capital receipts are not liable to income tax unless specifically made taxable by the Income-tax Act. The capital receipts that are taxable under section 28 of the Act, if not recorded, are to be reported under clause 16(a). The capital receipts other than these are reported under clause 16(e).

Section 9B provides that any profit and gains arising from deemed transfer of capital asset shall be deemed to be income of the firm of the year in which such capital asset is received by the partner. It shall be charged to tax under the head "Capital Gains".

Further, it provides that fair market value of capital asset on the date of its receipt by the partner shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration while computing capital gain arising from deemed transfer of such capital asset by the firm. Determination of income taxable under the head 'capital gains' depends upon various factors such as nature of capital asset, period of holding, cost of acquisition, full value of consideration, etc. Section 48 prescribes the mode of computation of income taxable under the head 'capital gains'. As per said section, the capital gain is computed by reducing the cost of acquisition, cost of improvement and attributable expense from the full value of consideration of the capital asset.

Section 48 has also been amended by the Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) to mitigate the double taxation arising due to introduction of section 9B and substitution of section 45(4). A new clause (iii) is inserted to provide that profit and gains chargeable to tax under section 45(4) which is attributable to capital asset being transferred by the firm shall be reduced while computing capital gain in the hands of the firm in respect of such capital asset. In other words, the amount of capital gain computed under section 45(4) which is attributable to capital asset being transferred by the firm shall be deducted while computing capital gain in the hands of the firm in respect of such capital asset.

2.2-4 Asset must be a 'capital asset' at the time of transfer

Section 45 is the charging provision which prescribes that the profits and gains from transfer of capital asset effected in the previous year shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head 'Capital gains' and it deems the capital gain to be the income of the previous year in which the transfer takes place.

Under the charging section, the crucial requirements are that there must be a transfer and the transfer must be of a capital asset. The implication is that at the time of the transfer the subject of the transfer must be a capital asset. - M. Venkatesan v. CIT [1984] 16 Taxman 240/[1983] 144 ITR 886/(Mad.)

The character of asset sold must be with reference to the date of its transfer and not the receipt of compensation. A piece of land at the time of transfer may be agricultural and at the time of actual receipt of compensation on compulsory acquisition, it may be a capital asset covered by section 2(14). Since the character of the asset at the time of transfer was not covered by the definition of section 2(14), it could not be taxed by considering its nature at the time of receipt of compensation [A.R. Dahiya v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 141 Taxman 449 (Punj. & Har.); ITO v. Chaman Lal Nagpal [2006] 102 TTJ 890 (Asr. - Trib.)].

The Calcutta High Court in the case of Principal CIT v. ITC Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 88 (Calcutta) held that sum received for relinquishment of right to operate hotel under operating license agreement is revenue receipt.

In this case the assessee-licensee was running the hotel owned by the licensor along with the licensor's employees under an operating license granted by the licensor under an Operating licence agreement, and the licence was terminated by the licensor, and the assessee received the compensation by way of settlement of all disputes in relation to the agreement as per the Arbitrator's award as per consent terms.

The following substantial question was referred to the High Court—

"Whether receipt of money by the Assessee on account of relinquishment of its right to operate a hotel as a licensee would constitute capital receipt exposing the Assessee to capital gains tax or the same shall be treated as business receipt?"

The High Court held that "as it is a compensation received for loss of trading operation of running the hotel under the agreement and not for the loss of any asset of enduring value the amount received is a revenue receipt and not a capital receipt."

Paragraph 29 of this judgment is the highlight of this decision and the same is extracted below—

"Vide in Commissioner of Income Tax, UP, Lucknow v. Gangadhar Baijnath, Generalganj, Kanpur (1972) 4 SCC 28 (para 14) Hon'ble Supreme Court noted that one way of distinguishing capital from revenue receipts, is to take the classical economists' distinction between fixed capital and circulating capital receipts in respect of former is capital while the latter is not. Fixed capital is what is retained by the owner and turned to profit while circulating capital is parted with in order to yield profit. The ITC had not (made) any fixed capital investment to run the hotel under the "Operating Licence Agreement". On the other hand, from perusal of various clauses of the agreement it appears that the ITC has introduced some circulating capital to run the hotel. Therefore, from Classical Economists distinction point of view also, the receipts of Rs. 32.42 crore by the ITC from the ELEL being not for transfer or loss of any capital asset but at best in lieu of circulating capital introduced to operate the hotel, is "revenue receipt" arising from the trading contract i.e. "Operating Lisence Agreement". Mere use of the word "relinquishment" in the "Settlement Agreement" and in the "Consent Terms" without disclosing any rights in any capital asset or relinquishment any rights in any capital assets, is not decisive rather establishes that the receipt is not capital receipt."

YEAR OF TRANSFER/TAXABILITY

Entries in account books - The date of sale or transfer is the date when the sale or transfer takes place, and for the purpose of determining that date, entries in the account books are irrelevant [Alapati Venkataramiah v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 185 (SC)].

Signing of agreement - Capital gains would be charged only on receipt of sale consideration after development of land; and not when agreement was signed for development of land [CIT v. Smt. Najoo Dara Deboo [2013] 38 taxmann.com 258/218 Taxman 473 (All.)].

Registration of sale deed - In order to attract section 45, it should be established that, by the transfer, the title to the property stands passed to the purchaser. If what was sold was immovable property, it should further be established that the same was conveyed by a registered deed. It is the date of execution of the registered deed, and not the date of delivery of possession, that will be relevant in such circumstances, for on that date alone the title to property passes [CIT v. F. X. Periera & Sons (Travancore) (P.) Ltd. [1991] 55 Taxman 242 (Ker.)]. Also see, R. Krishnaswamy v. CIT [2014] 43 taxmann.com 177/222 Taxman 270 (Mad.).

Receipt of part consideration - Where, on transfer of shareholding, assessee received only a part of sale consideration and balance amount was to be received in succeeding years, in such a case, whole of such sale consideration would be chargeable to tax in year of transfer of shares [Potla Nageswara Rao v. DCIT [2014] 50 taxmann.com 137/226 Taxman 173 (Mag.) (AP)].

Contingent payment - Merely because the agreement provides for payment of the balance of consideration upon the happening of certain events, it cannot be said that the income has not accrued in the year of transfer [Ajay Guliya v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 24 taxmann.com 276/209 Taxman 295 (Del.)].

Possession given - Where actual possession of property was given to developer vide agreement dated 30-4-2001, transfer u/s 2(47) would be considered to take place in year of agreement, and not in year when power of attorney was executed to give access to developer to do certain jobs on said land [Dr. Joao Souza Proenca v. ITO [2018] 90 taxmann.com 83/253 Taxman 275 (Bom.)].

Co-operative society - Upon purchase of flat, purchaser certainly acquired right or interest in proportionate share of land but its realisation was deferred till formation of co-operative society by flat owners and transfer of entire property to co-operative society and, hence, capital gains would be chargeable to tax only in the year when land would be sold or transferred to co-operative society formed by flat-owners and not in the year in which individual flats were sold [J. S. & M. F. Builders v. A. K. Chauhan [2020] 117 taxmann.com 228/272 Taxman 359 (Bom.)].

Sale of shares – Where assessees agreed to sell their shares under an agreement and received substantial part of consideration as advance sale consideration towards sale of shares, since share certificates were not delivered to transferees during the relevant previous year, assessees could not be subjected to capital gains tax in the relevant assessment year [PCIT v. Smt. Poornima Shailendra Babu [2023] 149 taxmann.com 50/292 Taxman 340 (Kar.)].

1.3. Tax on receipt of money or capital asset by partner in connection with reconstitution of firm [Section 45(4)]

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has substituted sub-section (4) as proposed to be substituted by the Finance Bill, 2021. This provision provides thatwhere a partner receives during the previous year any capital asset or money or both from a firm in connection with the reconstitution, then any profit and gains arising from such receipt of money by specified person shall be deemed to be the income of the specified entity under the head "Capital Gains' of the previous year in which such capital asset or money or both were received by the specified person. Further, it also prescribes the formula to compute the profit and gains arising to the partner from such receipt of money or capital asset from the firm.

The profit and gains shall be computed in accordance with the following formula:

A = B + C - D

A = Income chargeable to income-tax under this provision as income of the firm under the head 'capital gains';

B = Value of money received by partner on the date of such receipt;

C = Fair market value of the capital asset received by the partner on the date of such receipt; and

D = Balance in the capital account (represented in any manner) of the partner in the books of account of the firm at the time of reconstitution.

Where the value of A is negative, it shall be deemed to be nil.

While computing the balance in the capital account of partner in the books of account of firm, increase in capital account due to the following shall not be taken into account:

(a)

Revaluation of any asset;

(b)

Self-generated goodwill (goodwill acquired without incurring any cost for purchase or which has been generated during the course of business or profession);

(c)

Other self-generated assets.

Explanation2 to Section 45(4) clarifies that when a capital asset is received by the partner from a firm in connection with the reconstitution, the provisions of the said section shall operate in addition to the provisions of section 9B. Thus, the taxation under both the provisions shall be worked out independently.

1.3-1. Analysis of section 45(4)

Section 45(4) provides for the computation of capital gain which arises to a partner on extinguishment or relinquishment of his right in the firm in connection with reconstitution of the firm. Though the income arises to partner but it is deemed as income of the firm. Thus, the firm would be assessed under section 9B for its own income and under section 45(4) for income arising to partner thereof.

1.3-2. Section 45(4) v. Section 9B

Section 9B provides for taxability arising at the time of dissolution or reconstitution, whereas section 45(4) deals with the taxability at the time of reconstitution only. Where any asset or money is transferred to partner or member at the time of dissolution, same amounts to extinguishment or relinquishment of rights. Term "transfer" as defined under section 2(47) covers extinguishment or relinquishment of rights within its ambit. However, since such rights are not extinguished or relinquished in favour of another person in case of dissolution, no one derives any benefit from the same. Thus, section 45(4) does not apply at the time of dissolution.

1.4. Mode of computation of capital gain [Section 48]

Section 9B deals with the taxability of the income arising to the firm on transfer of capital asset to a partner in connection with dissolution or reconstitution. Section 45(4) deals with the income which arises to the partner on receipt of a capital asset in connection with the reconstitution. However, tax in respect of such receipt is charged in the hands of firm only. Thus, in case of reconstitution double taxability will arise once under section 45(1) read with section 9B and second under section 45(4). To remove the impact of such double taxation, Section 48 is amended. This section provides for reduction of cost of acquisition, improvement and expenditure incurred in connection with transfer from full value of consideration of capital asset while computing income chargeable under the head 'capital gains'.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

CIT v. P.N. Panjawani [2012] 21 taxmann.com 458/208 Taxman 22/[2013] 356 ITR 676 (Kar.) Under the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the firm is not recognised as a legal entity. However, the Income-tax Act recognises the firm as a distinct legally assessable entity apart from its partners. Therefore, in the context of the Income-tax Act, the identity of the firm as well as that of the partners for taxability of income are separate and distinct. The firm is a separate taxable entity liable to pay tax on income arising or accruing to it because of its own distinct set of income earning activities and factors. Similarly, in the case of individual partners also if there is a transfer effected by a firm of capital assets i.e., property held by the firm, the capital gain tax arises in the hands of the firm and not in the hands of the partners and vice versa. The admission of the new partners and assignment of right in the firm to the new partners out of the rights of the assessee for consideration does not amount to transfer in the hands of assessee under section 2(47) and consequently not liable to tax under section 45 of the Act.

Extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset

The booklet "How to compute capital gains published by the Income Tax Department" explains 'extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset' as under:

"This covers every possible transaction which results in destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation of all or any bundle of rights in a capital asset."

For example, termination of a lease or of a mortgagee interest in a property. In the case of CIT v. Grace Collis [2001] 115 taxmann 326 (SC) the Supreme Court held that the definition of 'transfer' in section 2(47) also contemplates the extinguishment consequent upon the transfer thereof.

Therefore, the expression 'transfer' does include the extinguishment of rights in a capital asset independent of and otherwise than on account of transfer.

Tracing the history of "extinguishment of rights"

If legislative history is traced, the Indian Income-tax Act 1922(the 1922 Act) did not contain any specific provision corresponding to section 2(47) of the Act defining 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset, though section 12B of the 1922 Act relating to capital gains spoke of "sale, exchange or transfer", as attracting capital gains. The "transfer" was mentioned in juxtaposition of "sale and exchange"- The term juxtaposition means the fact of two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect.

Reference to relinquishment was not mentioned in the said provision. Section 12B of the 1922 Act was recast by the Finance (No.3) Act,1956 wherein it was mentioned that ".the tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head "Capital Gains" in respect of any profits or gains arising from the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer of a capital asset effected after the 31st day of March, 1956, and such profits and gains shall be deemed to be income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place" In other words, the phrase " relinquishment" was added but the other phrase "extinguishment of any rights (therein)" about which this discussion centers around was placed in a separate clause by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1984 with effect from 01-04-1985 when the section 2(47) of the Act was recast apparently with the object of avoiding any ambiguity and repetition of the expression in the charging section though the phrase " extinguishment of any rights (therein)" had also been in the statute book since the inception of the 1961 Act itself.

This clause gives an artificially extended meaning to the expression 'transfer' and expands the same to include the cases of extinguishment of any rights and the compulsory acquisition which were conspicuous by their absence in the 1922 Act.

The Supreme Court as early as 21st February 1978 in the case of Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 803/2 SCC 50 (a Bench consisting of 7 Hon'ble Judges) with regard to transfer of a right in a property by extinguishment observed as under-

destruction of such rights in an asset consequent upon assets ceasing to exist is a situation which is not contemplated either in definition of 'transfer', or in charging section 45 of the Act.

In other words, if the asset is destroyed due to natural calamity the question of "transfer of asset" by "extinguishment of rights" does not arise.

Redemption of preference shares is relinquishment and transfer

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 509 (SC) the Court held that redemption of preference shares is clearly 'sale' by the shareholder to the company and would come within the purview of 'transfer' in view of the following:

A reading of sections 77, 80 and 85 of the Companies Act, 1956 [now sections 67, 55 and 43 of the Companies Act, 2013] makes it clear that when a preference share is redeemed by a company, what a shareholder does is, to sell the shares to the company. Such a transaction is nothing but sale of the preference shares by the shareholder to the company.

That is why after specifically laying down in section 77(1) of the said Act [now section 67(1) of the 2013 Act] that no company shall have the power to buy its own shares, it was necessary to specify in sub-section (5) thereof [sub-section (4) of section 67 of the 2013 Act] that this provision shall not affect the rights of a company to redeem any preference shares issued by it.

If redemption of preference shares did not amount to sale, it would not have been necessary to specifically provide that the restriction imposed upon a company in respect of buying its own shares will not apply to redemption of preference shares issued by the company.

The Court held that the assessee had purchased the preference shares at less than face value. When the shares were redeemed by the company, she received more than what she had paid for the shares. In order to get this amount the assessee had to give up or abandon or surrender the shares held by her. The meaning of the word 'relinquish' as given in Webster's Comprehensive Dictionary International Edition 1984, is: (1) to give up; abandon; surrender, (2) to cease to demand; renounce; to relinquish a claim, (3) to let go (a hold or something held).

The assessee in this case gave up the shares and received in lieu thereof a sum of money. This came clearly within the mischief of section 2(47)(i). That apart, the transaction amounted to sale.

In the instant case, the preference shares were held as capital assets. The excess amount received by the shareholder on redemption of these shares would have to be treated as capital gain in view of section 2(47), read with section 4. Accordingly, the assessee's case squarely came within section 2(47)(i).

6.15-5D Capital gains - Profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset are chargeable to income-tax under the head ‘Capital gains’. The charging section envisages transfer of capital asset and the profits and gains arising on account of such transfer.

The expression ‘transfer’ has been defined in section 2(47) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 as including sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any rights therein, or compulsory acquisition thereof; or conversion of a capital asset into stock-in-trade, or transaction involving the allowance of the possession which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of an immovable property, etc.

Since the transfer as contemplated is one as a result whereof consideration has passed to the assessee or has accrued to him, extinguishment or relinquishment of rights must relate to that ‘capital asset’ corporeal or incorporeal. It is, therefore, obvious that transfer of a capital asset in order to attract liability to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ must be a ‘transfer’ as a result whereof some consideration is received by or accrues to the assessee. If the transfer does not yield any consideration, there can be no question of capital gains. If the transfer takes effect on extinguishment of a right in the capital asset, there must be receipt of consideration for such extinguishment to attract liability to tax.1

The word ‘transfer’ also covers cases which result in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise of all or any of the bundle of rights which a person has in the capital assets.1 It is only when consideration is received in respect thereof.

The word ‘transfer’ is comprehensive and is regarded generally as comprehending within its scope transfers both voluntary and involuntary. In the absence of a distinct genus or category, no presumption can arise that the word ‘transfer’ in section 2(47) must be construed in the sense of a voluntary transfer, because the words ‘sale’, ‘exchange’ and ‘relinquishment’ are in the normal acceptation of those terms voluntary acts, and, therefore, if an existing title of a capital asset is extinguished and a new one created, there is within the meaning of section 2(47) a ‘transfer’ of capital asset, and the fact that the divestiture of title takes place under a law relating to compulsory acquisition of property would make no difference. The compulsory acquisition of capital asset may be a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 2(47), but is not sale. These expressions are not synonymous conveying the same meaning. Had this been so, and also the expression ‘sale’ as embracing within its scope ‘compulsory acquisition’ of an asset, there would have been no need to refer to both these expressions in the inclusive definition of ‘transfer’ in section 2(47). One of the purposes of the inclusive definition is to expand the concept defined. The meaning of the expression ‘transfer’ was extended to cover the compulsory acquisition of an asset along with sale, exchange, relinquishment of an asset, or extinguishment of any right therein, etc.

Sale deed executed by a general power of attorney holder after the death of the original owner was invalid: SC

M. S. Ananthamurthy v. J. Manjula [2025] 172 taxmann.com 7 (SC)

The suit property was originally part of 1 acre 8 guntas of land in Chunchaghatta Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bangalore South Taluk, owned by the original owner, M @ R. He developed the land into individual plots and sold them to various buyers.

The original owner executed a General Power of Attorney (GPA) and an Agreement to Sell in favour of the holder of the GPA. After the owner's death, the holder, in her capacity as a GPA holder, executed a registered sale deed in favour of her son, appellant No. 2.

The respondents contended that the sale deed was executed after the original owner's death and was, therefore, invalid. On the other hand, the respondents claimed that after the death of the original owner, his legal heirs sold the suit property to a person through a registered sale deed.

Later, the person sold the property to another person via another registered sale deed. Finally, the person gifted the suit property to her daughter, the answering respondent, through a registered gift deed.

The High Court ruled in favour of the respondents, and the matter reached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that a power of attorney derives its basic principles from Chapter X of the Contract Act, which provides for 'Agency' along with sections 1A and 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882. The relationship between the executant of a general power of attorney and the holder of the power is one of principal and agent.

A principal is bound by the acts done by an agent or the contracts made by him on behalf of the principal. Likewise, the power of attorney in the nature of the contract of the agency authorizes the holder to do acts specified by the executant or represent the executant in dealings with third persons.

In the present case, it is evident from the contents of the GPA executed by the original owner in favour of the holder that the holder was authorized to manage the property. However, the import of the word 'general' in a POA refers to the power granted concerning the subject matter. The test to determine the nature of POA is the subject matter for which it has been executed. The nomenclature of the POA does not determine its nature. Even a POA termed as a 'general power of attorney' may confer powers that are special in relation to the subject matter. Likewise, a 'special power of attorney' may confer powers that are general in nature concerning the subject matter. The essence lies in the power and not in the subject matter.

The holder of the POA did not choose to register the agreement to sell executed by the original owner in her favour. Even if such an argument were to persuade the Court, the document must have been registered as per section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act. In the absence of such registration, it would not be open for the holder of the POA to contend that she had a valid right, title and interest in the immovable property to execute the registered sale deed in favour of the appellant.

FAQ 13. How to calculate the turnover of a share broker?

When a share broker purchases securities on behalf of his customers, he does not get them transferred in his name, but they are delivered in the name of the customer. The same is true in the case of sales also. The share broker holds the delivery merely on behalf of his customer. The property in securities does not get transferred to the share-brokers. Only brokerage, which is being accounted for in the books of share brokers, should be considered for calculating the turnover. However, in the case of transactions entered into by a share broker on his personal account, the sale value should be considered while calculating the sales turnover. The case of a sub-broker is not different from that of a share broker.

FAQ 14. How to calculate the turnover in case of a speculative transaction?

A 'speculative transaction' means a transaction in which a contract for purchase or sale of any commodity or securities is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery or transfer of commodity or scrips. Thus, in speculative transactions, both positive and negative differences can arise from the settlement of contracts. Each transaction, whether resulting in a positive or negative difference, is an independent transaction. In such transactions, though the contract notes are issued for the full value of the purchased or sold asset, the entries in the books of account are made only for the differences. Accordingly, the aggregate of both positive and negative differences is considered as the turnover.

RIGHTS UNDER A CONTRACT

In CIT v. Anglo India Jute Mills Co. Ltd. [1981] 6 Taxman 54/129 ITR 352 (Cal.) the assessee wanted to purchase certain machinery from abroad. For this purpose, the assessee did all that was necessary for obtaining the permission and getting the import licence. In order to protect itself from fluctuations in the exchange rate, the assessee entered into a forward contract with a bank entitling it to obtain the requisite amount of sterling at the time when the contract came to an end or was required to be performed. The assessee could not get this machinery because the licence expired and, therefore the question of enforcing payment in dollars did not arise. Therefore, the State Bank, pursuant to their commitment, credited the assessee minus the necessary costs, charges and expenses, with the difference between the exchange rate and the assessee got a credit of Rs. 3,13,651. The Court held that the amount was obtained not because the assessee surrendered any licence and not because the assessee gave up its own right under a contract but because the assessee realised its dues or, in other words, the assessee transformed its rights under the contract into money. Therefore, neither was there any transfer nor was there any profit arising therefrom. In that background of facts there was no cost of acquisition and, therefore, there could not be any capital gains in respect of such an asset. Accordingly, the sum of Rs. 3,13,651 could not be considered to be capital gains in terms of section 45. However, it appears that the chargeability to tax under the head 'business' could not be disputed.

TAX LITERATURE/TAXATION OF CAPITAL GAINS

TAXING THE UNTAXED - INSURANCE CLAIM

Gururaj Kulkarni*

In this article, the author discusses the question of taxability of amount received as insurance claim in the light of amendment of the Income-tax Act, 1961 by insertion of sub-section (1A) in section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 by the Finance Act, 1999. The author considers both the legal and the accounting aspects of the issue - EDITOR

Background

1. All revenue receipts are taxable unless specifically exempt; all capital receipts are exempt unless specifically taxable. The profits in lieu of source is a capital receipt. Hitherto, any amount or sum received under an insurance claim was outside the ambit of section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’). With the new budget proposals, this relief is going to witness a complete change, overruling various Supreme Court decisions. A close look at the chargeability of insurance compensation is pertinent, in view of amendment of section 45. Let us cast a brief glance at the present position.

Any profit or gain arising from the transfer of a capital asset is chargeable to tax under the head ‘Capital gains’ in the previous year in which the transfer took place if it is not eligible for exemption under sections 54, 54B, 54EA, 54EB, 54D, etc.

According to section 2(47) of the Act, transfer in relation to a capital asset includes :—

(a)sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset; or

(b)extinguishment of any rights therein; or

(c)the compulsory acquisition thereof under any law; or

(d)conversion of capital asset into stock-in-trade; or

(e)transaction giving possession of immovable property under part-performance of contract of the nature referred in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; or

(f)transaction which has the effect of transferring an immovable property.

The definition of transfer under section 2( 47) is merely inclusive and does not exhaust other kinds of transfer - Sunil Siddharthbhai v. CIT [1985] 156 ITR 509/23 Taxman 14 (SC).

Extinguishment of asset is not transfer

2. Transfer not only includes physical transfer of a capital asset, but also relinquishment or extinguishment of any rights therein. The existence of the asset during the process is a pre-condition to attract the provisions of section 45. If an asset is destroyed, or lost, it would be incorrect to term it as a transfer. The non-existence of the asset after such an accident entails non-application of section 45. Indeed, the right of the owner or possessor of the capital asset is lost but the extinguishment of right in the asset on account of extinguishment of the asset itself is not a transfer of right, but its destruction or loss or cessation. Extinguishment refers not to extinguishment of asset itself but to extinguishment of the holder’s right to the asset - CIT v. East India Charitable Trust [1994] 206 ITR 152/ 73 Taxman 380 (Cal.).

Judicial pronouncements

3. In Vania Silk Mills (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1991] 191 ITR 647/ 59 Taxman 3 , the Apex Court had an occasion to appraise the rationale of taxing the insurance compensation in the light of extinguishment of right. It was held that destruction of a capital asset is not a transfer and, therefore, insurance compensation received from an insurance company does not give rise to capital gains tax liability. A question normally would creep-in regarding the taxability of the sum, when salvage (damaged asset) is taken over by the insurance company. It is held that even in such a case, there is no transfer under section 2(47) and, therefore, capital gains tax liability does not arise - C. Leo Machodo v. CIT [1988] 172 ITR 744/ 38 Taxman 296 (Mad.). Followed Marybong & Kyel Tea Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 589/ 91 Taxman 11 (SC).

When a share broker purchases securities on behalf of his customers, he does not get them transferred in his name but they are delivered in the name of the customer. IT: Where assessee entered into a joint development agreement with developer but did not transfer land owned by it in terms of section 2(47)(v) and there was no intendment to transfer, there could have been no capital gain taxation

GENERAL

Transfer of part asset - The words 'the transfer of a capital asset' occurring in section 45 cannot be interpreted as a transfer of the entire capital asset and not a part of the same [National Products v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 755 (Kar.)].

Capital asset on the date of transfer - It is necessary that property transferred must be a capital asset on date of transfer and not that such property should have been capital asset also on date of its acquisition by the assessee [Arun Sunny v. DCIT [2009] 184 Taxman 498 (Ker.)]. Also see, A. R. Dahiya v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 141 Taxman 449 (P&H).

CAPITAL GAINS OR NOT

Gift for tax avoidance - Where assessee transferred its shareholding, as a gift, in a company to step-down company created in a tax haven country and the said step-down company transferred stake in favour of a third-party investor for a consideration, sole intention of assessee being escape rigour of Indian tax laws, therefore, assessee was liable to tax u/s 45 [PCIT v. Redington (India) Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 136 (Mad.)].

Inherited property - Where assessee inherited certain land, leased out same on payment of ground rent and ultimately sold it after decades, profit arising from sale of land was to be taxed as 'capital gains' [CIT v. Administrator of the Estate of Shri E. F. Dinshaw [2012] 22 taxmann.com 57/208 Taxman 193 (Mag.) (Bom.)].

Intangible assets - Sale of brand names, trademark, copyright and goodwill in journals sold/transferred would clearly be a case of sale of capital asset and exigible to capital gains [CIT v. Mediworld Publications (P.) Ltd. [2011] 11 taxmann.com 374/200 Taxman 1 (Delhi); CIT v. ABB Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 338/[2022] 284 Taxman 350 (Kar.)].

Where collection of assets of undertaking transferred in slump sale included intangible assets like goodwill and intellectual property whose cost of acquisition could not be determined, said sale could not be assessable to capital gains [CIT v. AKZO Noble India Ltd. [2020] 121 taxmann.com 216/[2021] 276 Taxman 259 (Cal.)].

Malba - Proceeds of malba, i.e., material left over after demolition of a structure, would be taxable under the head 'Capital gains' and not under the head 'Income from other sources' [CIT v. Ribu Saggi [2014] 45 taxmann.com 371/223 Taxman 150 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Owelty - Amount of owelty (i.e., compensation deposited to settle inequalities in partition) represents immovable property and would not attract capital gain tax [CIT v. Ashwani Chopra [2013] 30 taxmann.com 299/213 Taxman 490 (P&H)].

Pledge of shares - No capital gains arise where there was no transfer of shares but shares have been pledged for the purposes of obtaining loan [CIT v. Reliance Communication Infrastructure Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 302/[2013] 212 Taxman 177 (Bom.)].

Sale of business as a going concern - Where business is sold as a going concern valuing plant and machinery, etc., surplus arising over and above the difference between WDV and actual cost has to be taxed u/s 45 [CIT v. Artex Mfg. Co. [1997] 93 Taxman 357 (SC)].

Shares - Where assessee-company purchased shares of a private limited company from funds received from its holding company and after some time it had sold said shares to its holding company, profit arising from sale of shares had to be taxed under head 'Capital gains' [CIT v. Renato Finance & Investment Ltd. [2013] 33 taxmann.com 262/218 Taxman 312 (Bom.)].

Where assessee-director received huge amount as non-compete fee but real and true nature of transaction was sale of shares and transfer of control and management of company, amount in question was to be taxed as capital gains in hands of assessee [CIT v. Shiv Raj Gupta [2014] 52 taxmann.com 425 (Del.), SLP granted inShiv Raj Gupta v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 3/244 Taxman 191 (SC)].
